cards.front: A 100 W bulb is connected to a 250 V supply. Find (a) the current and (b) the resistance of the bulb. (Example 3.3)
cards.explain: Use P = V I for current, then Ohm's law R = V/I. The book repeats the same problem as Example 3.5, with the unit misprinted there as W instead of Ω.

steps.explain: From P = V I.
Ohm's law.
Consistent with the rating.

cards.front: An electric kettle has a resistance of 30 Ω. What current flows on a 240 V supply, and what is its power rating? (Example 3.4)
cards.back: Current = 8 A; power = 1,920 W (1.92 kW).
cards.explain: Ohm's law gives the current, and P = V I gives the power. You could also use P = V²/R = 240²/30 = 1,920 W.

steps.explain: Ohm's law.
Electrical power.
Divide by 1,000.

cards.front: A 230 V, 5 kW electric heater is used for hot water. Find the electricity consumed per hour (a) at rated voltage, (b) at 200 V. (Example 3.6)
cards.back: (a) 5 kWh; (b) about 3.78 kWh.
cards.explain: A resistive heater's power varies with the square of voltage (P = V²/R), so P at 200 V = 5 × (200/230)² = 3.78 kW. The book's printed working shows (200/230) × 5 without the square, but its answer of 3.78 kWh is the squared result.

steps.explain: Energy = power × time.

steps.prompt: State how heater power varies with voltage.
steps.answer: P = V²/R, so P ∝ V² (resistance constant)
steps.explain: The heater is a fixed resistance.
Ratio of voltages squared.
Low voltage also means less heat output, so heating takes longer.

cards.front: Write the power-triangle relationships between kW, kVA, kVAr and power factor.
cards.back: kW = kVA cos φ; kVA = kW / cos φ; kVAr = kVA sin φ; PF = cos φ; also kW = √(kVA² − kVAr²).
cards.explain: Active (resistive) power does useful work. Reactive power builds the magnetic flux of inductive devices but is otherwise not usable. Apparent power is the hypotenuse. Only components in the same phase can be added, kW to kW and kVAr to kVAr. In an MCQ, all three expressions for active power are correct ('all of the above').

cards.front: What usually causes current to lag voltage in an AC system?
cards.back: Inductive load, for example motors and transformers, which need reactive current to build their magnetic fields.
cards.explain: A purely resistive load keeps current in phase with voltage, while a capacitive load makes current lead. Lagging reactive power (kVAr) is what lowers the power factor of typical industrial loads.

cards.front: Give the power formulas for balanced three-phase and single-phase loads.
cards.back: Three-phase: P = √3 × V_L × I_L × cos φ. Single-phase: P = V × I × cos φ (V_L = line voltage, I_L = line current).
cards.explain: In industry, single-phase power is mostly used for lighting, fractional-HP motors and electric heaters. Larger motors and process loads are three-phase.

cards.front: A 400 W mercury vapour lamp runs 10 h/day on 230 V, drawing 2 A at PF 0.8. Find the energy consumed per day. (Example 3.7)
cards.back: About 3.7 kWh per day.
cards.explain: For a single-phase AC load, kW = V × I × cos φ / 1,000. Multiply by hours for kWh. The measured input (0.368 kW) is a little below the nameplate 400 W.

steps.answer: kWh = V (kV) × I × cos φ × hours
steps.explain: Single-phase AC power includes power factor.
Voltage expressed in kV.
Energy = power × time.

cards.front: How do you convert a motor's horsepower rating to input kVA?
cards.back: kVA = (HP × 0.746) / (η × PF), where η is motor efficiency and PF is motor power factor.
cards.explain: HP × 0.746 gives output kW. Dividing by efficiency gives input kW, and dividing by PF gives kVA. Smaller motors running at part load are the least efficient and have the lowest power factor.

cards.front: Does a motor's nameplate kW/HP rating show input or output? What about its nameplate volts, amps and PF?
cards.back: Nameplate kW/HP is the output (shaft) power at full load. Nameplate volts, amps and PF describe input conditions at full load.
cards.explain: This is why rated input kW is calculated as √3 × V × I × PF from nameplate values, and the rated efficiency is output kW ÷ that input. Mixing up the two is a common exam trap.

cards.front: A 3-phase induction motor (20 kW) driving a pump is measured at 440 V, 25 A, PF 0.90. Find its energy consumption in one hour. (Example 3.8)
cards.back: About 17.15 kWh.
cards.explain: Measured three-phase input power = √3 × V × I × cos φ. It is input power, so it is compared with rated input (not the 20 kW output rating) when judging loading.

steps.explain: Balanced three-phase load.
Voltage in kV gives kW.
Energy = power × time.

cards.front: A 3-phase, 10 kW motor has nameplate 415 V, 18.2 A, PF 0.9. Running, it measures 415 V, 12 A, PF 0.7. Find rated input, rated efficiency, actual input power and percentage loading. (Example 3.9)
cards.back: Rated input ≈ 11.8 kW; efficiency ≈ 85%; actual input ≈ 6.0 kW; loading ≈ 51%.
cards.explain: Motor loading % = measured input kW ÷ rated input kW × 100. Rated input comes from nameplate V, I and PF because those are full-load input conditions. The 10 kW rating is output.

steps.prompt: Compute rated input at full load.
steps.explain: Nameplate V, I, PF are input conditions.
Rated output ÷ rated input.
Measured values.
Loading = measured input ÷ rated input.

cards.front: A 10 kW motor has a full-load efficiency of 85%. At a particular load it measures 415 V, 10 A, PF 0.68 (3-phase). Find the motor loading in percent. (Chapter question S-2)
cards.back: About 41.6% loading.
cards.explain: When nameplate V/I/PF are not given, find rated input from rated output ÷ efficiency. Then loading = measured input ÷ rated input.

steps.explain: Nameplate kW is output; input = output/η.
Three-phase power formula.
Loading = measured input ÷ rated input.

cards.front: A 250 W sodium vapour street lamp runs 12 h/day on 230 V, drawing 2 A at PF 0.85. Find the energy consumption per day. (Chapter question S-3)
cards.back: About 4.69 kWh per day.
cards.explain: Single-phase: kW = V × I × cos φ. Measured input includes ballast losses, which is why it exceeds the 250 W lamp rating.

steps.explain: Single-phase power with PF.
Energy = power × hours.
The difference is mostly control-gear (ballast) loss.

cards.front: Give the conversions between °C, °F and K.
cards.explain: Water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F at atmospheric pressure. The Kelvin scale has the same 1° step as Celsius but starts at absolute zero (−273.15 °C), and gas-law calculations require absolute temperature in K.

cards.front: Why must absolute pressure, not gauge pressure, be used in gas-law calculations, and at what conditions is standard atmospheric pressure defined?
cards.back: Gas laws relate absolute quantities, so pressure must be absolute (measured from vacuum) and temperature in kelvin. Standard atmospheric pressure is defined at sea level at 273 K (0 °C): 1.01325 bar = 101,325 Pa.
cards.explain: Gauges read the difference from the surrounding atmosphere, and atmospheric pressure varies with temperature and altitude. 20 °C (293 K) is also used as a reference temperature.

cards.front: Define the calorie and give its value in joules.
cards.back: The heat needed to raise 1 g of water by 1 °C. 1 cal = 4.187 J (≈ 4.2 J); 1 kcal raises 1 kg of water by 1 °C.
cards.explain: The joule is now the internationally accepted unit of heat. The kcal is still widely used in Indian fuel and boiler practice, for example in GCV figures in kcal/kg.

cards.front: How many specific heats does a gas have, and why do solids and liquids have just one?
cards.back: Gases could have infinitely many (one per process), but two are defined: c_p (constant pressure) and c_v (constant volume). For solids and liquids, specific heat does not depend on the process.
cards.explain: Specific heat is the heat needed to raise 1 kg by 1 °C (1 K), in kcal/kg °C or J/kg K, and it varies with temperature. Gases expand significantly when heated, so the heat needed depends on whether pressure or volume is held constant.

cards.front: From Table 3.1, give the specific heats (J/kg °C) of lead, copper, iron, aluminium, alcohol and water.
cards.back: Lead 130, mercury 140, copper 390, iron 470, aluminium 910, alcohol 2,400, water 4,200.
cards.explain: Lead has the lowest value and water by far the highest. That is why water absorbs or releases a large amount of heat for a small temperature change, which makes it an excellent heat-transfer and storage medium.

cards.front: What are the latent heat of fusion of ice and the latent heat of vaporisation of water at 100 °C?
cards.back: Fusion: 335 kJ/kg. Vaporisation: 2,257 kJ/kg (≈ 540 kcal/kg).
cards.explain: Latent heat changes state without changing temperature. Q = m × h_fg (or h_if for fusion). The same amount is released on reversal: about 2,257–2,260 kJ/kg when steam condenses at 100 °C, and 335 kJ/kg when water freezes.

cards.front: If the latent heat of fusion of water is 335 kJ/kg, how much latent heat is given up when 10 kg of water at 0 °C freezes to ice at 0 °C? (Example 3.10)
cards.explain: Freezing releases the same latent heat that melting absorbs, at the fusion temperature and with no change in temperature.

steps.explain: Phase change at constant temperature.
Mass and latent heat of fusion.
Heat leaves the water as it freezes.

cards.front: 20 kJ of heat is supplied to 25 kg of ice at 0 °C. How many kg of ice melt? (Example 3.11)
cards.back: About 0.06 kg.
cards.explain: Only the heat supplied limits how much melts. The 25 kg is the amount available, not the amount melted.

steps.explain: Mass melted by a given heat input.
Latent heat of fusion = 335 kJ/kg.
Far less than the 25 kg of ice present.

cards.front: Find the heat needed to vaporise 2 m³ of water at 100 °C if the latent heat of vaporisation is 2,257 kJ/kg. (Example 3.12)
cards.explain: Convert volume to mass (1 m³ of water ≈ 1,000 kg), then Q = m × h_fg.

steps.explain: Density of water ≈ 1,000 kg/m³.
Q = m × h_fg.
Only latent heat, since the water is already at 100 °C.

cards.front: Why is steam superheated in power plants, and how does saturation temperature change with pressure?
cards.back: Superheating (heating steam above saturation temperature at the existing pressure) improves efficiency and avoids condensation in the turbine. The higher the pressure, the higher the saturation temperature.
cards.explain: On the T-S diagram, the area under the dome is the wet water-steam mixture and constant-pressure lines there are horizontal (latent heat region). The region to the right of the x = 1.0 (dry saturated) line is superheated steam.

cards.front: Define dew point and specific humidity (humidity ratio).
cards.back: Dew point is the temperature at which the water vapour in air becomes saturated and starts condensing, equal to the saturation temperature at the vapour's partial pressure. Specific humidity is kg of water vapour per kg of dry air.
cards.explain: Relative humidity, in contrast, is the ratio of the vapour actually held to the vapour the air could hold if saturated at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage. Air at 50% RH holds half the moisture it could hold at that temperature.

cards.front: When are dry-bulb, wet-bulb and dew-point temperatures all equal?
cards.back: When relative humidity is 100% (saturated air).
cards.explain: In unsaturated air, evaporation from the wet wick cools the wet bulb below the dry bulb, and the dew point is lower still. At saturation no evaporation occurs, so all three readings coincide.

cards.front: How does a wet-bulb thermometer differ from a dry-bulb thermometer, and which one reflects relative humidity?
cards.back: The wet bulb is wrapped in a wick soaked in distilled water. Evaporation absorbs latent heat and lowers its reading, so wet-bulb temperature reflects RH. The dry bulb measures sensible heat and is not influenced by RH.
cards.explain: The drier the air, the faster the evaporation and the bigger the wet-bulb depression. Enthalpy of moist air is read from the psychrometric chart using dry- and wet-bulb temperatures.

cards.front: How is the calorific value of a fuel measured, and what makes up the difference between GCV and NCV?
cards.back: In a bomb calorimeter: a sealed, insulated vessel where a known mass is burnt completely and the temperature rise is measured. GCV − NCV = heat of vaporisation of the moisture and of the water formed from hydrogen in the fuel.
cards.explain: Typical heavy fuel oil values are GCV ≈ 10,500 kcal/kg and NCV ≈ 9,800 kcal/kg. The OCR text prints J/kg, but the figures (44,100 and 41,160) are kJ/kg. NCV assumes the water leaves as vapour, so its latent heat is not recovered.

cards.front: In what unit is the rate of heat transfer measured, and name the three modes of heat transfer.
cards.back: Watts (J/s). The three modes are conduction (in solids), convection (fluid to/from a surface) and radiation (needs no medium).
cards.explain: Heat always flows from hot to cold. Energy transferred is in joules; the rate is in watts. An MCQ that offers 'kcal' or 'watts per second' for the rate is a trap.

cards.front: What are the two mechanisms of conduction, and how do forced and natural convection differ?
cards.back: Conduction: molecular motion (higher-energy molecules pass energy to neighbours) and migration of free electrons (mainly in pure metals). Forced convection uses a fan or pump to move the fluid; natural convection is driven by density differences, with hot fluid rising and cold fluid sinking.
cards.explain: Radiation needs no medium. Thermal radiation covers roughly infrared to ultraviolet wavelengths, and radiant energy hitting a surface can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted.

cards.front: Using h_f = c_w (t_s − t₀) with c_w = 4.19 kJ/kg °C and t₀ = 0 °C, find the specific enthalpy of saturated water at atmospheric pressure (t_s = 100 °C). Given h_g = 2,676 kJ/kg, find the latent heat of evaporation.
cards.explain: Specific enthalpy of saturated water is sensible heat above 0 °C. Enthalpy of evaporation is the difference between saturated steam and saturated water enthalpies. At 1 atm these are the steam-table values 419, 2,676 and 2,257 kJ/kg.

steps.explain: Sensible heat of water from the 0 °C reference.
Latent heat = steam enthalpy − water enthalpy.
Matches the latent heat of vaporisation at 100 °C.

cards.front: How is the specific enthalpy of superheated steam calculated, and what specific heat does the guide book use?
cards.back: h_s = h_g + c_ps (t_s − t), where t is the saturation temperature and t_s the superheated temperature. c_ps ≈ 1.860 kJ/kg °C at standard atmosphere (it varies with temperature).
cards.explain: Superheat adds sensible heat to dry saturated steam. Specific enthalpy in general is h = u + p v (internal energy plus pressure × specific volume), and total enthalpy H = m h.

cards.front: State the first, second and third laws of thermodynamics as given in the guide book.
cards.back: First: energy can be neither created nor destroyed, only converted or transferred (conservation of energy). Second: heat flows naturally only from hot to cold, and no heat engine can be 100% efficient. Third: it is impossible to reduce any system to absolute zero (−273 °C).
cards.explain: The second law introduces entropy, a measure of disorder: the more disorderly a system, the less useful work it can do. Some heat from the fuel must always be rejected to the surroundings, which is why heat engines are never 100% efficient.

cards.front: Express the derived SI units pascal, joule, watt, volt, ohm and lux in terms of other units.
cards.back: Pa = N/m²; J = N·m; W = J/s; V = W/A; Ω = V/A; lux = lm/m² (siemens = A/V).
cards.explain: Base units used in the table include metre, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela (plus kilogram). Derived units are built from them, for example a newton is kg·m/s².

cards.front: Give the energy equivalents of 1 BTU, 1 HP and 1 MJ (in Wh) from the conversion table.
cards.explain: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J, which is why 1 MJ ≈ 0.278 kWh. HP × 0.746 converts motor horsepower to kW in the motor kVA formula.

cards.front: Per the Gazette notification of 19-03-2007, what standard calorific values are used for MTOE reporting for 1 kWh, furnace oil, HSD, petrol, LPG and charcoal?
cards.back: 1 kWh = 860 kcal; furnace oil/RFO/LSHS/naphtha 10,050 kcal/kg (0.9337 kg/L); HSD 11,840 kcal/kg (0.8263 kg/L); petrol 11,200 kcal/kg (0.7087 kg/L); LPG 12,500 kcal/kg; charcoal 6,900 kcal/kg, unless the supplier's latest certificate states otherwise.
cards.explain: Coal and coke use the GCV from the supplier's latest certificate. Without certificates, a NABL-accredited, State or Government-recognised lab test is used. 1 kgoe = 10,000 kcal and 1 MTOE = 10⁷ kcal.

cards.front: For MTOE reporting, what calorific value is used for natural gas if the supplier gives no certificate?
cards.back: The average of the 8,000–10,500 kcal/m³ range, about 9,250 kcal/m³.
cards.explain: The actual calorific value from the supplier's latest certificate is preferred. For gaseous fuels, MTOE = (quantity in kg or Nm³ × GCV in kcal/kg or kcal/Nm³) / 10⁷.

cards.front: What is the oil equivalent of 125 t of coal with a GCV of 4,000 kcal/kg? (Chapter objective question 6)
cards.back: 50 toe.
cards.explain: MTOE for solid fuel = (quantity in kg × GCV in kcal/kg) / 10⁷. Answer choices of 40, 400 and 500 are the usual unit-slip traps.

steps.explain: GCV is per kg.
Energy = mass × GCV.
1 toe = 10⁷ kcal.

cards.front: How does the EC Act define an energy audit?
cards.back: The verification, monitoring and analysis of energy use, including a technical report with recommendations for improving energy efficiency, a cost-benefit analysis, and an action plan to reduce energy consumption.
cards.explain: The definition has three parts: measurement/analysis, recommendations with economics, and an action plan. An audit is only useful if it leads to implementation, which is why the report must quantify savings and costs.

cards.front: What is the difference between a preliminary and a detailed energy audit?
cards.back: A preliminary (walk-through) audit is quick and uses existing data to set the consumption baseline, find obvious savings and no-cost or low-cost measures, and set priorities. A detailed audit is a comprehensive, instrument-based study of all major systems, with a full energy balance and costed projects.
cards.explain: A detailed audit is done in three phases: pre-audit, audit and post-audit. It gives the most accurate estimate of savings and costs, and includes a detailed project implementation plan.

cards.front: What are the three phases of a detailed energy audit?
cards.back: Phase I: pre-audit (planning, walk-through, data collection plan). Phase II: audit (detailed measurement, analysis, energy and material balance, identifying options). Phase III: post-audit (implementing recommendations and following up on results).
cards.explain: Typical steps include a kick-off meeting with management, collecting historical data, preparing process flow charts, measurements, techno-economic evaluation of options, and the report with an action plan. Data collection, analysis and reporting are all steps of an audit.

cards.front: Which energy audit instruments measure what: Fyrite, stroboscope, sling psychrometer, Pitot tube, ultrasonic flow meter, lux meter?
cards.back: Fyrite: O₂ or CO₂ in flue gas. Stroboscope: rotational speed without contact. Sling psychrometer: DBT and WBT (→ RH). Pitot tube: velocity pressure in ducts (→ air velocity and flow). Ultrasonic flow meter: liquid flow (transit-time or Doppler method). Lux meter: illuminance.
cards.explain: A power analyser measures kW, kVA, kVAr, PF, harmonics and other quantities directly. A plain ammeter or wattmeter does not give PF on its own. Choosing the right instrument is a frequent objective question.

cards.front: Define Specific Energy Consumption (SEC).
cards.back: SEC = Energy consumed ÷ Production in the same period, e.g. kWh/t or kcal/kg of product. Example: 5 t of coal at 4,000 kcal/kg for 25 t of cement → 20×10⁶ ÷ 25,000 kg = 800 kcal/kg.
cards.explain: SEC is the main plant-level energy performance indicator used for benchmarking and for PAT targets. Compare SEC only at similar capacity utilisation and product mix, because fixed energy is spread over output.

cards.front: How is plant energy performance calculated?
cards.back: Production factor = current year production ÷ reference year production. Reference year equivalent = reference year energy × production factor. Plant energy performance (%) = (reference year equivalent − current year energy) ÷ reference year equivalent × 100.
cards.explain: A positive value means the plant used less energy than expected for its output, so efficiency improved. A negative value means it got worse. The calculation needs current and reference year production and the reference year energy; capacity utilisation is not needed.

cards.front: What is benchmarking in energy management?
cards.back: Comparing a plant's energy performance (SEC or other indicators) with its own past performance (internal) or with similar plants or best practice (external), to find improvement potential.
cards.explain: Fair benchmarking needs comparable boundaries, product mix, capacity utilisation, raw material quality, technology vintage and climate. PAT targets are set by benchmarking each plant's SEC against others in its sector.

cards.front: What does a Sankey diagram show, and why is it useful?
cards.back: It shows energy flows through a system as arrows whose widths are proportional to the energy quantity, so inputs, useful output and losses can be seen at a glance.
cards.explain: Large loss streams stand out visually, which helps the energy manager prioritise where to act. It is a qualitative and quantitative presentation of an energy balance; it does not replace calculations or audits.

cards.front: Reference year (2023) data: production 50,000 t, energy use 30,000 toe. Current year (2024): production 55,000 t, energy use 31,500 toe. Calculate the plant energy performance for 2024 and interpret it.
cards.back: Plant energy performance = +4.55%, so the plant used 4.55% less energy than expected for its production (an improvement).
cards.explain: The production factor scales reference-year energy to what the plant would have used at this year's output. A positive result means the plant performed better than the reference year. A negative result, as in the BEE 2024 question (−5.56%), means performance got worse.

steps.explain: PF = current year production ÷ reference year production.

steps.prompt: Calculate the reference year equivalent energy.
steps.explain: Expected energy at current output = reference energy × PF.
PEP = (Ref. eq. − Current energy) ÷ Ref. eq. × 100.

steps.answer: Positive value: the plant saved 1,500 toe compared with expected consumption.
steps.explain: A negative value would mean worse performance.

cards.front: Give the BEE guide book definition of energy management.
cards.back: The judicious and effective use of energy to maximise profits (minimise costs) and enhance competitive positions.
cards.explain: An alternative definition in the book is the strategy of adjusting and optimising energy, using systems and procedures, to reduce energy requirements per unit of output while holding constant or reducing total costs. The fundamental goal is to produce goods and provide services with the least cost and least environmental effect.

cards.front: What are the three objectives of energy management?
cards.back: 1) Achieve and maintain optimum energy procurement and utilisation throughout the organisation; 2) minimise energy costs/waste without affecting production and quality; 3) minimise environmental effects.
cards.explain: Note that minimising cost must not come at the expense of production or quality. An exam MCQ lists minimising energy costs, minimising waste and minimising environmental degradation, and the answer is 'all the above'.

cards.front: Which three costs are often the top operating costs in industry, and which has the highest potential for cost reduction?
cards.back: Energy (electrical and thermal), labour and materials. Energy has the highest potential for cost reduction.
cards.explain: This is the book's justification for the need for an energy audit. An audit reviews energy costs, availability and reliability of supply, the appropriate energy mix, conservation technologies and retrofits. The book describes the audit as translating conservation ideas into realities within a specified time.

cards.front: Name the three types of energy audit in the BEE guide book.
cards.back: Preliminary audit, targeted energy audit and detailed audit.
cards.explain: The type chosen depends on the type of industry, the depth of audit needed and the potential and magnitude of cost reduction desired. A preliminary audit is quick and uses existing data. A targeted audit studies specific systems. A detailed audit covers all major energy-using equipment.

cards.front: By what two other names is a preliminary energy audit known?
cards.back: Walk-through audit and diagnostic audit.
cards.explain: It is a relatively quick exercise that uses existing or easily obtained data, such as energy bills, invoices and production records. Its outputs include an estimate of the savings scope, immediate no-/low-cost measures, a baseline and areas for more detailed study.

cards.front: List the scope of a preliminary energy audit.
cards.back: Establish energy consumption (from bills); obtain related production data; estimate the scope for savings; identify the easiest areas for attention; identify immediate no-/low-cost savings; set up a baseline; identify areas for detailed study.
cards.explain: The baseline or reference point set up in a preliminary audit is used later to measure progress. Examples of the 'easiest areas' are unnecessary lighting, higher temperature settings and leaks.

cards.front: Classify these as no-cost or low-cost measures: arresting steam/air leaks; shutting idle motors; adjusting the fan damper to control excess air; replacing lamps with appropriate lamps and luminaires.
cards.back: No-cost: arresting leaks, controlling excess air by damper adjustment. Low-cost: shutting equipment when not needed, replacing lamps and luminaires.
cards.explain: The book lists, as areas needing detailed study rather than quick fixes: converting direct to indirect steam heating with condensate recovery, upgrading insulation, modifying the process to reduce steam demand, rescheduling operations to cut peak demand, and evaluating waste heat recovery.

cards.front: Why does a detailed energy audit give the most accurate estimate of savings, and what is its key element?
cards.back: It accounts for the energy use of all major equipment and considers the interactive effects of various projects. Its key element is the energy balance.
cards.explain: The energy balance is based on an inventory of energy-using systems, assumptions of current operating conditions, and measurements and calculations of energy use. A detailed audit includes detailed savings calculations and project implementation costs, and results in a detailed project implementation plan.

cards.front: In BEE's ten-step detailed audit methodology, which steps fall in each phase?
cards.back: Pre-audit phase: steps 1–2 (plan and organise; introductory meeting). Audit phase: steps 3–9 (data gathering to reporting and presentation). Post-audit phase: step 10 (implementation and follow-up).
cards.explain: The audit phase covers: 3 primary data gathering, process flow and utility diagrams; 4 survey and monitoring; 5 detailed trials; 6 energy use analysis; 7 identifying ENCON opportunities; 8 cost-benefit analysis; 9 reporting to top management. The book says the methodology is flexible and can be adapted to the industry.

cards.front: Which detailed trials are done in Step 5 of the ten-step methodology, and how long does a boiler efficiency trial last?
cards.back: 24-hour power monitoring (MD, PF, kWh), load variation trends in pumps, fans and compressors, boiler efficiency trials (4–8 hours), furnace efficiency trials and equipment performance tests.
cards.explain: Step 4 is the broader survey with portable instruments (motors, insulation, lighting), where operating data are confirmed against design data. Step 5 is a focused set of trials on selected major energy equipment.

cards.front: How long should the initial site visit of an energy audit take, and what should it achieve?
cards.back: About one day. It should finalise the audit team, learn management's expectations, identify the main energy-consuming areas and the instrumentation needed, plan the time frame, collect macro data and build support.
cards.explain: During the visit the auditor discusses the aims and economic guidelines of the audit with senior management, analyses major energy data, obtains site drawings and tours the site with a site representative. Proper planning is a prerequisite for an effective audit.

cards.front: Name the baseline data an energy audit team should collect.
cards.back: Quantity and type of raw materials; technology, process and equipment used; capacity utilisation; efficiencies/yield; % rejection/reprocessing; quantity and types of wastes; consumption of fuel, water, steam, electricity, compressed air, cooling and chilled water.
cards.explain: The auditor should specially interview supervisors and equipment operators. The maintenance manager is often the primary person to ask about lighting types, motor sizes, the A/C plant, electrical load and related performance problems.

cards.front: Under which of the four ENCON areas (fuel substitution, energy generation, energy distribution, energy usage by processes) does the major opportunity usually lie?
cards.back: Energy usage by processes. Many of these opportunities are hidden, and process analysis is a useful tool for process integration measures.
cards.explain: Energy generation covers DG sets, boilers, cogeneration and gasifiers. Energy distribution covers transformers, cables, PF improvement and chilled water, cooling water and compressed air networks. Fuel substitution means choosing the appropriate fuel for efficient conversion.

cards.front: Which issues should the technical feasibility of an energy-efficiency measure address?
cards.back: Technology availability, space and skilled manpower; impact on safety, quality, production or process; reliability, service, maintenance requirements and spares availability.
cards.explain: Economic viability is often the key parameter for management acceptance. It can be assessed by payback, IRR or NPV. For low-investment, short-duration measures, the payback method is sufficient.

cards.front: From BEE's economic feasibility worksheet, how are net savings and payback period (in months) calculated?
cards.back: Net savings/year = annual savings − annual operating costs. Payback (months) = investment ÷ net savings per year × 12.
cards.explain: On the worksheet, investment covers equipment, civil works, instrumentation and auxiliaries. Annual operating costs include cost of capital, maintenance, manpower, energy and depreciation. Annual savings cover thermal energy, electrical energy, raw materials and waste disposal.

cards.front: What are the three categories of ENCON measures, and which normally gets priority?
cards.back: Low cost–high return, medium cost–medium return, and high cost–high return. Low cost–high return projects normally get priority.
cards.explain: Process changes almost always involve high costs with high returns. They need careful scrutiny before funds are committed, are complex, and need long lead times before implementation.

cards.front: In BEE's project priority guideline (Table 4.1), what do priorities A, B, C and D mean?
cards.back: A – Good (well defined, attractive, existing technology adequate, no risk). B – May be (marginally acceptable, minor risk). C – Held (poorly defined, marginally unacceptable, doubtful). D – No (clearly not attractive, needs major breakthrough, not feasible).
cards.explain: Each project is rated on economic, technical and risk feasibility. A 'C' project has inadequate existing technology. A 'D' project needs a major technological breakthrough and is not feasible.

cards.front: How should an energy audit report begin, and who is that part written for?
cards.back: With an executive summary giving a brief synopsis of total savings and the highlights of each measure. It should be tailored to non-technical personnel.
cards.explain: The main report then describes the process, presents annual consumption and bills, describes energy inputs and outputs by department and gives the ENCON measures with costs, benefits and payback. It concludes with recommendations for detailed engineering and feasibility studies for high-investment measures.

cards.front: A main cooling tower is rated 5,000 m³/h at 8 °C design range but runs at 3,000 m³/h with a 4 °C range. A separate DG-set cooling tower handles 240 m³/h at 5 °C range and has 2 × 7.5 kW pumps and 2 × 22 kW fans running at 80% load. Merging the DG flow into the main tower needs about 7 kW extra pumping. Find the net savings, annual savings (8,400 h, Rs 4/kWh) and payback on Rs 1.5 lakh of piping.
cards.back: Net saving 40 kW → 3,36,000 kWh/yr → about Rs 13.4 lakh/yr; payback under 2 months.
cards.explain: This is the book's sample of the reporting format for an ENCON recommendation (Table 4.4). It shows that the main tower is only 30% loaded, so it can absorb the small DG-set heat load and the separate tower can be stopped.

steps.prompt: Find the % loading of the main cooling tower.
steps.explain: Loading is the actual heat load (flow × range) over the design heat load.

steps.prompt: Find the heat load of the DG-set cooling tower.
steps.explain: Heat load = water mass (kg/h) × Cp (1 kcal/kg °C) × range.

steps.prompt: Find the power drawn by the DG-set tower.
steps.explain: Both fans and both pumps are taken at 80% load.
The book estimates about 7 kW of extra pumping at the main tower for the added 240 m³/h (66.67 L/s).

steps.prompt: Find the annual kWh and cost savings.
steps.explain: Units saved × tariff gives the cost saving.
Only piping is needed, so the investment is very small.

cards.front: True or false: energy costs are a fixed overhead with little scope for savings.
cards.back: False. Contrary to common belief, energy costs are not a fixed overhead, and there is often huge potential for savings.
cards.explain: Understanding energy costs is vital for awareness creation and saving calculations. Where meters are insufficient, fuel and electricity invoices and the annual company balance sheet (fuel and power cost with production data) are useful sources.

cards.front: In an electricity bill, which charge answers each question: how fast, how much and when is electricity used?
cards.back: How fast: maximum demand charge (kVA). How much: energy charge (kWh). When: time-of-day (TOD) peak/off-peak charges.
cards.explain: The power factor charge reflects real power versus apparent power. Other factors in the final price include HT/LT tariffs, slab rates, consumer category (industrial, commercial, agricultural etc.), regional tariffs, incentives/penalties and tax holidays for new projects.

cards.front: What two features should an energy benchmarking tool have?
cards.back: 1) A common metric irrespective of plant size, most commonly energy intensity (energy use per unit of output). 2) It should be used across a wide range of facilities, to compensate for production differences at similar facilities.
cards.explain: Energy benchmarking compares the performance of a plant or sector against a common metric that represents 'standard' or 'optimal' performance. It forms the basis for monitoring and target setting.

cards.front: What are the three approaches to industrial energy benchmarking?
cards.back: 1) Evaluating an entire industrial sector (vs best available technology, other countries, or over time). 2) Comparing individual plants within a sector. 3) A company using its own historical best performance as the benchmark (internal).
cards.explain: In the second approach, proprietary data is an issue, so indicators must be general enough to reveal nothing confidential. The third approach avoids this because benchmarking is done internally.

cards.front: Which factors must be checked for similarity before external (inter-unit) benchmarking? Is energy price one of them?
cards.back: Scale of operation, vintage of technology, raw material specifications and quality, and product specifications and quality. Energy price is NOT one of them.
cards.explain: External benchmarking compares a group of similar units to identify best practices. If these factors differ, the findings can be grossly misleading. This exact trap appears as an objective question in the book.

cards.front: List the steps in energy conservation benchmarking.
cards.back: 1) Identify the best available technology for each process unit. 2) Understand the process and identify key controlling parameters. 3) Determine the unit's performance. 4) Analyse the gap against the benchmark. 5) Set targets within constraints and implement improvements.
cards.explain: Gap analysis on the key controlling parameters is what turns a benchmark into an action list. Targets must keep practical constraints in view.

cards.front: Give the BEE benchmark parameters for: cement plant, textile unit, power plant, A/C plant, compressed air and DG power plant.
cards.back: Cement: kWh/MT clinker or cement. Textile: kWh/kg yarn. Power plant: kcal/kWh (heat rate). A/C: kWh per ton of refrigeration. Compressed air: kWh/Nm³. DG plant: kWh per litre.
cards.explain: The book splits these into gross production-related parameters (cement, textile, paper, power, fertiliser in Million kcal/MT urea or ammonia, foundry kWh/MT liquid metal) and equipment/utility-related ones (kW/TR, boiler % thermal efficiency, cooling tower % effectiveness, kWh/Nm³, kWh/litre).

cards.front: Which accompanying parameters must be stated when comparing (a) a cement plant's kWh/MT, (b) a boiler's thermal efficiency, (c) an A/C plant's kW/TR?
cards.back: (a) Type of cement, Blaine number (fineness) and process (wet/dry). (b) Fuel quality and type, steam pressure, temperature and flow, and whether efficiency is on a GCV or NCV basis and by the direct or indirect method. (c) Parity of chilled water temperature.
cards.explain: Without these, comparisons among similar industries are not meaningful. Other examples: a power plant's heat rate needs % loading, condenser vacuum and inlet cooling-water temperature. Compressed air must be compared at similar inlet air temperature and generation pressure.

cards.front: Define production factor and reference year equivalent energy use.
cards.back: Production factor = current year's production ÷ reference year's production. Reference year equivalent = reference year energy use × production factor.
cards.explain: The reference year equivalent is the energy the plant would have used to make this year's output if it had operated as it did in the reference year. Comparing it with actual energy use separates efficiency changes from changes in output.

cards.front: Why do equipment capacity and user requirement often mismatch, and give examples of matching energy use to requirement.
cards.back: Designers add safety margins, so equipment is oversized and runs at part load. Examples: trimming impellers, VSDs or resizing to eliminate pump throttling and fan dampers; moderating chilled water temperature to process needs; back-pressure turbines instead of control-valve pressure drops; task lighting instead of area lighting.
cards.explain: Matching comes first in the book's sequence. It is followed by maximising system efficiencies (O&M and best technology), then optimising input energy (heat recovery, cogeneration, renewables), and then fuel/energy substitution.

cards.front: Distinguish fuel substitution from energy substitution, with examples.
cards.back: Fuel substitution replaces a fossil fuel with a more efficient, cheaper or cleaner fuel (e.g. natural gas in fertiliser/power; coconut shells or rice husk for coal; LSHS for LDO). Energy substitution changes the form of energy (e.g. steam heaters for electric heaters; solar for steam-based hot water).
cards.explain: The book names two ways to reduce energy dependency: energy conservation and substitution. Natural gas is increasingly the fuel and feedstock of choice in the fertiliser, petrochemical, power and sponge iron industries.

cards.front: A textile plant replaces a furnace-oil thermic fluid heater (GCV 10,200 kcal/kg, 82% efficiency, fuel cost Rs 1,800/h) with a coconut-chip fired unit (GCV 4,200 kcal/kg, 72% efficiency, Rs 700/h) for the same 15 lakh kcal/h duty. It runs 25 days × 12 months × 24 h. Extra auxiliary power and manpower cost Rs 10 lakh/yr and the new heater costs Rs 35 lakh. Find the net saving and payback.
cards.back: Net saving Rs 70 lakh/yr; payback 6 months.
cards.explain: This is the book's fuel substitution case study. The agro-fuel has less than half the calorific value and lower efficiency, but its far lower cost per hour still gives a very short payback. The plant already handled coconut chips in another boiler, which made the change practical.

steps.explain: Days per month × months × hours per day.

steps.prompt: Find the annual furnace oil cost.
steps.explain: Hourly fuel cost × hours (exactly Rs 129.6 lakh).

steps.prompt: Find the annual coconut chip cost.
steps.explain: Same duty and hours, at the agro-fuel's hourly cost.
Deduct the extra auxiliary power and manpower cost from the gross fuel saving.
Payback = investment ÷ net annual saving.

cards.front: On what method does the Fyrite work, and which reagents absorb CO₂ and O₂?
cards.back: The Orsat method of volumetric analysis. Potassium hydroxide (dyed red) absorbs CO₂, and chromous chloride (blue) absorbs O₂.
cards.explain: A hand bellows pump draws flue gas into the solution, and the change in liquid volume shows the gas percentage. The absorbing fluid is also the indicating fluid, so one vessel does the work of both the measuring burette and the absorption pipette.

cards.front: How do a fuel efficiency monitor and a combustion gas analyser differ?
cards.back: The fuel efficiency monitor measures O₂ and flue gas temperature and uses stored fuel calorific values to calculate combustion efficiency. The combustion gas analyser uses replaceable chemical cells to measure gases such as CO₂, CO, NOx and SOx.
cards.explain: Because a gas analyser can hold a maximum of two sensors, only two or three parameters can be measured at once. It is lighter and easier to handle than a fuel efficiency monitor. The book names the combustion analyser as the instrument for O₂ and CO in flue gas.

cards.front: How is air or flue gas pressure measured in a duct?
cards.back: A digital flexible-membrane manometer combined with a Pitot tube, inserted through a 6 cm monitoring hole in the duct.
cards.explain: Flexible rubber tubes connect the manometer's inlet and outlet probes to the two ends of the Pitot tube, and must be tight to avoid air leakage. This is used for exhaust flue gases from boilers and furnaces and for air from fans and blowers.

cards.front: How does a non-contact infrared thermometer determine temperature, and what must be known about the object?
cards.back: It measures the infrared radiation emitted by the object; knowing the object's emissivity, it calculates the temperature. A lens focuses IR onto a detector that gives an electrical signal, corrected for ambient temperature.
cards.explain: It suits objects in hazardous or hard-to-reach places. By contrast, a contact thermometer is a thermocouple probe inserted into flue gas, hot air or hot water, with a leaf-type probe for surface temperatures.

cards.front: Distinguish transit-time and Doppler ultrasonic flow meters.
cards.back: Transit-time meters send signals with and against the flow; the time difference is proportional to flow rate. They are used for clean liquids. Doppler meters use the frequency shift of signals reflected off particles. They are used for dirty liquids.
cards.explain: Both are non-contact flow meters. An exam MCQ asks which instrument uses the transit-time method: the ultrasonic flow meter.

cards.front: Which instrument gives non-contact speed measurement, and on what principle?
cards.back: The stroboscope. High-intensity flashes at a precise frequency make a rotating object appear slowed or stopped when the flash frequency bears a definite relationship to its speed, giving the RPM.
cards.explain: A tachometer is the simple contact-type alternative, used where direct access is possible. Speed matters in audits because it changes with frequency, belt slip and loading.

cards.front: What do smart energy meters and thermography each provide?
cards.back: Smart meters give real-time detailed usage statistics through wireless communication, viewable or controllable by mobile or internet. Thermography (IR imaging) shows hot and cold spots on surfaces for assessing equipment health and predictive maintenance.
cards.explain: The thermal camera converts IR radiation into electronic video signals that are amplified and shown on a monitor for interpretation. Smart meters can also be used for fuel or water.

cards.front: Under the BEE (Manner and Intervals of Time for Conduct of Energy Audit) Regulations 2008, when must a Designated Consumer's first and subsequent energy audits be done?
cards.back: First audit by an accredited energy auditor within 18 months of the Central Government notification. Subsequent audits every three years, counted from the date the previous audit report was submitted to the DC's management.
cards.explain: A common trap is counting the three years from the audit date or the notification date. The interval runs from submission of the previous report by the accredited energy auditor to the DC's management.

cards.front: Under the 2008 audit regulations, what must each list of recommendations include?
cards.back: A description of each measure; its technical or economic life; known technical risks; a preliminary assessment of financial attractiveness; a tabulated summary by implementation schedule (short, medium, long term); the techno-financially better option where alternatives exist; and impacts on O&M, staff and budget with solutions.
cards.explain: The action plan prepared jointly with the energy manager must include detailed techno-economic analysis, a monitoring and verification protocol for annual reporting to BEE and the SDA, and an agreed time schedule considering finance and equipment availability.

cards.front: Under the 2008 audit regulations, which forms does the accredited energy auditor submit to the Designated Consumer's management?
cards.back: Form 2: the energy audit report. Form 3: an evaluation of the implementation of each measure recommended in the previous audit report.
cards.explain: Both go to the management of the designated consumer. Form 3 makes each audit check whether earlier recommendations were actually carried out.

cards.front: What must the accredited energy auditor certify at the end of the energy audit report?
cards.back: Data collection was diligent and truthful; all monitoring devices are in good condition, calibrated or certified, and untampered; reasonable professional skill and care were taken; adequate training was given to operating personnel after implementation; and the audit followed the 2008 Regulations.
cards.explain: The auditor signs the report under the firm's seal with accreditation and manpower details. The report must include a work schedule sheet signed by both the accredited energy auditor and the DC's energy manager. The report structure is decided jointly by the auditor and the DC.

cards.front: Reference year (2009) energy use was 12 million kcal. The production factor for 2010 is 0.9 and 2010 energy use was 11 million kcal. Find the Plant Energy Performance for 2010 and state your inference.
cards.back: PEP = −1.85%. Performance has marginally worsened, and management must act to improve it.
cards.explain: This is the book's solved example. Even though absolute energy use fell from 12 to 11 million kcal, production fell more (factor 0.9). So the energy per unit of output rose, and PEP is negative.

steps.prompt: Find the reference year equivalent energy.
steps.explain: Reference year energy × production factor is the energy the old practice would need for this year's output.

steps.answer: PEP = (reference year equivalent − current year energy) ÷ reference year equivalent × 100
steps.explain: Positive means improvement; negative means deterioration.
The plant used 0.2 million kcal more than the reference-year practice would have.

steps.answer: Marginally negative: the energy or plant manager must act to improve performance
steps.explain: A falling energy bill alone does not prove better efficiency when production also falls.

cards.front: What principle underlies material and energy balances?
cards.back: Conservation of mass and energy: Input = Output + Accumulation (stored) + Losses. At steady state with nothing stored, Input = Output.
cards.explain: Example: 1,000 kg/h raw material in, with 700 kg product, 200 kg waste and 50 kg stored out → unaccounted loss = 1,000 − 950 = 50 kg/h. Draw a boundary around the process, list every stream crossing it, and balance one component (e.g. solids or fat) at a time.

cards.front: In concentration and drying problems, what quantity is the 'tie element' for the material balance?
cards.back: The non-volatile component (dissolved solids, bone-dry solids or fat), whose mass is the same in feed and product. Example: 100 kg of feed at 6% solids → 6 kg solids → product at 30% = 20 kg, so water evaporated = 80 kg.
cards.explain: Balance the conserved component first to get the product mass, then find the water removed by difference. Moisture on a wet basis = water ÷ (water + solids). The same logic gives salt concentration: 25 kg salt in 100 kg water = 25/125 = 20% by weight.
cards.source: BEE 2025 P1 Q11; BEE 2024 P1 Q37

cards.front: In an energy balance, how is equipment efficiency calculated by the direct method?
cards.back: Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ energy input × 100. Example: boiler with 100 MJ fuel input and 70 MJ in steam → 70%. The losses (flue gas 20 MJ + radiation/unaccounted 10 MJ) make up the other 30 MJ.
cards.explain: In the indirect (loss) method, efficiency = 100 − Σ losses %. A complete energy balance must close: input = useful output + all losses. A large unaccounted figure points to measurement errors or a missed stream.

cards.front: A dryer receives 2,000 kg/h of wet material at 40% moisture (wet basis) and dries it to 5% moisture (wet basis). Latent heat of evaporation is 540 kcal/kg. Ignore the sensible heat of the solids. Find (a) the product rate, (b) the water evaporated, (c) the heat needed for evaporation, and (d) the steam needed if steam gives 520 kcal/kg and the dryer thermal efficiency is 60%.
cards.back: (a) 1,263.2 kg/h; (b) 736.8 kg/h; (c) ≈ 3.98 lakh kcal/h; (d) ≈ 1,275 kg/h of steam.
cards.explain: Bone-dry solids pass through unchanged, so they tie the feed and product together. The water removed is the difference between the feed and product masses. Heat for evaporation is then divided by the useful heat delivered per kg of steam.

steps.explain: Solids fraction = 1 − moisture (wet basis).

steps.prompt: Find the product mass at 5% moisture.
steps.explain: Solids are 95% of the product.
Mass balance: feed = product + vapour.
Q = m × latent heat.
Steam = heat needed ÷ (efficiency × heat per kg of steam).

cards.front: An evaporator is fed 4,000 kg/h of solution containing 2% solids, which is concentrated to 8% solids. Enthalpies: feed 40 kcal/kg, concentrated product 100 kcal/kg, vapour 640 kcal/kg. The heating steam gives up 540 kcal/kg (its condensate leaves at saturation). Find the vapour formed and the steam required per hour, and the steam economy.
cards.back: Vapour = 3,000 kg/h; steam ≈ 3,444 kg/h; steam economy ≈ 0.87 kg vapour per kg steam.
cards.explain: The solids balance gives the product and vapour flows. The heat balance (heat from steam + heat in feed = heat in vapour + heat in product) gives the steam needed. A single-effect evaporator has a steam economy below 1; multiple effects raise it.

steps.prompt: Solids balance to find the product.
steps.explain: Solids in = solids out.
Feed = product + vapour.
Heat in = heat out.
Steam = heat ÷ heat given per kg of steam.
Economy = kg vapour ÷ kg steam.

cards.front: What is the purpose of a material and energy balance?
cards.back: To assess input, conversion efficiency, output and losses; to quantify all material, energy and waste streams in a process or system; and to give a basis for improvement and savings.
cards.explain: An exam MCQ asks whether the objective is input-output, conversion efficiency or losses; the answer is 'all the above'. Energy balances let industry examine each stage of a process, the whole process, or the whole production chain from raw material to finished product.

cards.front: Trace how a material balance is used from the conceptual stage to production.
cards.back: It is estimated at the planning stage, improved during pilot-scale tests, verified during commissioning, and finally used as a control measure during production.
cards.explain: Material balances are fundamental to process control, especially control of product yields. The balance becomes more accurate as real plant data replaces design estimates.

cards.front: In a material balance diagram of a process, on which side is the recycle stream shown?
cards.back: On the input side. A recycle stream is always treated as an input to the process.
cards.explain: In BEE's component diagram, the inputs are raw materials, chemicals, water/air, energy/power and recycled material. The outputs are products, by-products, gaseous emissions, wastewater, liquid waste for recycle, reusable waste for other operations, and solid waste for storage or disposal. A by-product is never an input.

cards.front: Write the general mass balance, and explain what 'losses' means when a balance does not close.
cards.back: Mass in = mass out + mass stored, i.e. raw materials = products + wastes + stored materials. If it doesn't close: raw materials = products + waste products + stored products + losses, where losses are unidentified materials.
cards.explain: The book's sugar plant example: if sugar entering is not matched by purified sugar plus sugar in waste liquors plus sugar accumulated, then sugar is either being chemically changed (burned) or going unnoticed down the drain. With no chemical change, the balance also holds for each individual component.

cards.front: State the general energy balance for a unit operation.
cards.back: Energy in = energy out + energy stored. Energy out includes energy leaving with products, with wastes, and lost to the surroundings.
cards.explain: Energy balances are more complicated than mass balances because forms of energy can be inter-converted (e.g. mechanical energy to heat), but overall the quantities must balance.

cards.front: Distinguish steady-state from unsteady-state, and continuous from batch processes.
cards.back: Steady state: no process variable changes with time. Unsteady state: variables change with time. Continuous: feed and product streams move in and out all the time (e.g. oil refinery, distillation). Batch: feed is charged, processed with no mass added or removed, and products removed at a set time or condition.
cards.explain: In continuous processes, balances are written per unit time. Assuming steady state means flows and vessel hold-ups do not change with time.

cards.front: At what three levels can material balances be developed, and what decides which materials get priority?
cards.back: Overall (whole plant), section-wise (department or cost centre) and equipment-wise. Priority is decided mainly by material cost: costly materials before cheap ones, and products before waste materials.
cards.explain: Section-wise balances help prioritise focus areas for efficiency improvement. Equipment-wise balances help assess equipment performance and identify energy and material losses.

cards.front: What are the typical steps in a material balance procedure?
cards.back: a) Define the basis and units (mass for a batch, flow rate for continuous); b) draw a flowchart with a boundary so streams in and out can be identified; c) write the material balance equations.
cards.explain: First identify materials in, out and stored, then decide whether to balance the gross material or individual constituents. For example, a balance can be done for dry solids alone by splitting the material into water and non-water.

cards.front: Define weight/weight concentration, weight/volume concentration, molar concentration and mole fraction.
cards.back: w/w: weight of solute ÷ total weight of solution. w/v: weight of solute in the total volume of solution. Molar concentration: number of molecular weights of solute (in kg) in 1 m³ of solution. Mole fraction: moles of solute ÷ total moles of all species.
cards.explain: For gases, concentrations are mainly given as weight per unit volume or as partial pressures. For dilute solutions, the mole fraction is close to moles of solute ÷ moles of solvent.

cards.front: What should a process flowchart for a material and energy balance show?
cards.back: Process steps in sequence from raw material to finished product, intermediates and by-products, operating parameters (temperature, pressure, % concentration), flow rates of all streams (m³/h or kg/h), the total cycle time for batch processes, wastes, and the final output.
cards.explain: Identifying and drawing the unit operation or process is a prerequisite for any material and energy balance. Inputs include raw materials, water, steam and energy. An energy and mass balance diagram should be drawn for each step and for the whole plant.

cards.front: A solution containing 10% solids is mixed with a 25% solids solution to give a single 20% solids output. If the 10% solution enters at 5.0 kg/s, find the other flow rates (no accumulation).
cards.back: 25% solution: 10 kg/s; output: 15 kg/s.
cards.explain: This is the book's Example 5.1. Two unknowns need two independent equations: the total mass balance and the solids balance. The liquids balance would give the same result and serves as a check.

steps.explain: No accumulation, so total in = total out.
Solids are conserved across the mixing point.
Eliminate one unknown using the total balance.

cards.front: A refinery input is 80% oil, 15% usable by-products (UBP) and 5% impurities. One output (B) is 92% oil and 6% UBP. The other output (C) is 60% oil at 1,000 L/h. Percentages are by volume, with no accumulation. Find the input flow rate, the composition of C, and the % of the original impurities that end up in C.
cards.back: Input ≈ 2,666 L/h; C is 60% oil, 30% UBP, 10% impurities; 75% of the input impurities leave in C.
cards.explain: This is the book's Example 5.2. The oil balance with the total balance fixes the flows. Separate UBP and impurity balances then give the unknown fractions in C. Stream B's impurities are 100 − 92 − 6 = 2%.

steps.prompt: Write the total and oil balances.
steps.explain: X = input, Y = stream B.
Substitute the total balance into the oil balance.

steps.prompt: Apply the UBP balance to find the UBP fraction v in C.
steps.explain: UBP in = UBP in B + UBP in C.

steps.prompt: Find the impurity fraction w in C.
steps.answer: v + w = 0.40 (since C is 60% oil) → w = 10%
steps.explain: The non-oil part of C is UBP plus impurities.

steps.prompt: Find the % of input impurities in C.
steps.explain: Compare impurity flow in C with impurity flow in the feed.

cards.front: Skim milk contains 90.5% water, 3.5% protein, 5.1% carbohydrate, 0.1% fat and 0.8% ash. The original whole milk contained 4.5% fat. Assuming only fat was removed and there were no losses, find the whole milk composition.
cards.back: Fat 4.5%, water 86.5%, protein 3.3%, carbohydrate 4.9%, ash 0.8%.
cards.explain: This is the book's Example 5.3, a constituent balance. Since only fat was removed, all the other components are tie elements: their masses are the same in whole and skim milk, only diluted by the extra fat.

steps.prompt: Choose a basis and define the unknown.
steps.answer: Basis 100 kg skim milk (0.1 kg fat); let x kg of fat be removed
steps.explain: A 100 kg basis makes percentages read directly as kg.
Original fat over original mass equals 4.5%.
Rearrange the linear equation.
The masses are unchanged; divide each by the larger whole-milk mass.

cards.front: In continuous centrifuging, 35,000 kg of whole milk with 4% fat is separated in 6 hours into skim milk (0.45% fat) and cream (45% fat). Find the flow rates of the two outputs.
cards.back: Skim milk ≈ 5,369 kg/h; cream ≈ 464 kg/h.
cards.explain: This is the book's Example 5.4, a continuous-process balance. Because the process is at steady state (constant hold-up in the centrifuge), the balance is written per unit time.

steps.explain: Continuous balances are written per unit time.

steps.prompt: Write the total and fat balances.
steps.explain: Y = skim milk, Z = cream.
Eliminate Z.
From the total balance.

cards.front: 20 kg of salt is added to 100 kg of water to make a solution of density 1,323 kg/m³. Find the salt concentration as (a) weight fraction, (b) weight/volume, (c) mole fraction, (d) molar concentration (salt molecular weight 58.5).
cards.explain: This is the book's Example 5.5. Because water dominates, the mole fraction is close to moles of salt ÷ moles of water (0.34 ÷ 5.56 = 0.061). This approximation improves as the solution becomes more dilute.

steps.explain: Solute mass over total solution mass.
1 m³ of solution weighs 1,323 kg, and 1/6 of that is salt.
Moles of solute over total moles.
Molecular weights of solute (in kg) per m³ of solution.

cards.front: In a textile mill, an evaporator concentrates liquor from 6% solids (w/w) to 30% solids. How much water is evaporated per 100 kg of feed?
cards.back: 80 kg of water per 100 kg of feed.
cards.explain: This is the book's Example 5.6. Solids are the tie element because they pass through unchanged. Only water leaves as vapour.

steps.explain: The solids pass through unchanged.
The same 6 kg is 30% of the concentrate.
Mass in − mass out as product = vapour.

cards.front: Air is 77% N₂ and 23% O₂ by weight. Find (a) the mean molecular weight, (b) the mole fraction of O₂, and (c) the O₂ concentration at 1.5 atm and 25 °C (R = 0.08206 m³·atm/kg-mole·K).
cards.back: (a) 28.8; (b) 0.21; (c) about 0.4 kg O₂ per m³ (≈0.013 kg-mole/m³).
cards.explain: This is the book's Example 5.7. The mean molecular weight is the mass of a sample divided by its total moles. The gas law then gives moles per m³ at the stated pressure and temperature.

steps.explain: Basis of 100 kg.
Mass ÷ moles.
O₂ moles over total moles.

steps.prompt: Moles of air per m³ at 1.5 atm, 298 K.
steps.explain: Ideal gas law with V = 1 m³.
23% of the air mass is oxygen.

cards.front: A soft drink is carbonated with CO₂ equal to 3 volumes of gas per volume of water at 0 °C and 1 atm. Ignoring other components, find the mass fraction and mole fraction of CO₂.
cards.back: Mass fraction ≈ 5.9 × 10⁻³; mole fraction ≈ 2.41 × 10⁻³.
cards.explain: This is the book's Example 5.8. For a gas dissolved in a liquid, find the moles of gas from the gas law, then the moles of liquid directly.

steps.explain: Take one volume of water.
Ideal gas law at 0 °C and 1 atm.
Molecular weight of CO₂ is 44.
CO₂ mass over total mass.
Water is 55.6 moles per 1,000 kg.

cards.front: A bag filter receives 1,69,920 m³/h of gas with 4,577 mg/m³ of dust. The outlet is 1,85,040 m³/h with 57 mg/m³. How much ash must be removed per hour from the hopper?
cards.back: About 767 kg/h.
cards.explain: This is the book's Example 5.9, a dust balance. The outlet gas volume is higher than the inlet (e.g. air in-leakage), so you must balance dust mass, not concentration.

steps.explain: m³/h × mg/m³ ÷ 10⁶ gives kg/h.
Same conversion.
Inlet dust = outlet dust + hopper ash.

cards.front: What is the general form of the first law for a system exchanging heat and work, and what does it become over a complete cycle?
cards.back: ΣQ + ΣW = ΔU (net heat supplied plus net work input equals the change in internal energy). Over a complete cycle ΔU = 0, so ΣQ + ΣW = 0.
cards.explain: Heat supplied to the system and work done on it are positive. For the steam power cycle: ΣQ = Q_in (boiler) − Q_out (condenser), and ΣW = W_in (feed pump) − W_out (turbine). So Q_in + W_in = Q_out + W_out.

cards.front: A system receives 75 units of energy but only 60 units go out. What has happened to its storage?
cards.back: Its stored energy increased by 15 units.
cards.explain: With no change in storage, input equals output. If input exceeds output the system gains energy (storage increases). If output exceeds input the system must have lost that much from storage.

cards.front: In an energy balance, what are 'sinks', and how does the book's example reach 22.5% efficiency?
cards.back: Sinks are depositories of leakage or rejected energy, usually low-grade heat (e.g. boiler radiation losses, heat carried off by cooling water). Example: inputs 15 + 185 = 200; useful output 45; sink 155; efficiency = 45 ÷ 200 = 22.5%, so losses are 77.5%.
cards.explain: Outputs represent useful work. With no internal storage, outputs plus sinks must equal inputs. Thermodynamic efficiency is always below 100%.

cards.front: What causes the loss of usable energy in mechanical, electrical and fluid systems?
cards.back: Mechanical: friction. Electrical: resistance. Fluid: turbulence, viscosity or mixing.
cards.explain: Energy 'lost' really means it has changed into a form that is not counted, most often heat and wear from work done against friction. No energy is actually destroyed.

cards.front: Why do practical energy balances usually become heat balances, and what is enthalpy referred to?
cards.back: Because forms of energy inter-convert, so all energy streams (oil, gas, coal, steam, chilled water, electricity) are converted to equivalent heat energy, ignoring internal energies. Enthalpy is always referred to a reference level (datum).
cards.explain: Working out a heat balance then needs only the quantities of materials, their specific heats and their changes in temperature or state (latent heat). It assumes no appreciable heat is converted to other forms such as work.

cards.front: Into which three areas can every plant energy or utility system be classified for system analysis?
cards.back: Generation, distribution and utilisation.
cards.explain: Energy (coal, oil, gas, electricity) enters the facility and is converted to convenient forms (steam, compressed air, chilled water, thermic fluid, DM water). It leaves mostly as heat and motion. For example, electricity is bought as HT and converted to LT, and fuels become steam or electricity.

cards.front: A 2-tonne furnace shell (Cp 0.2 kcal/kg °C) must be cooled from 90 °C to 55 °C using water at 28 °C, allowed to rise by at most 5 °C. Neglecting heat loss, how much water is required?
cards.back: 2,800 kg of water.
cards.explain: This is the book's Example 5.10. Two energy streams are set equal: the heat given up by the shell equals the heat picked up by the water. The allowed 5 °C rise fixes the water quantity.

steps.prompt: Heat to remove from the shell.
steps.explain: Q = m·Cp·ΔT.

steps.prompt: Heat picked up by X kg of water.
steps.explain: The water may rise only from 28 to 33 °C.
Energy stream 1 = energy stream 2.

cards.front: A textile dryer uses 4 m³/h of natural gas (800 kJ/mole). It dries 60 kg/h of wet cloth from 55% to 10% moisture. Using only the latent heat of evaporation (2,257 kJ/kg), estimate its thermal efficiency.
cards.back: About 48%.
cards.explain: This is the book's Example 5.11. A fuller evaluation would add sensible heat of the cloth and moisture and changes in combustion air temperature and humidity. Latent heat dominates, so this quick balance is useful.

steps.prompt: Find bone-dry cloth and initial moisture.
steps.explain: Split the wet feed into water and solids.
The dry cloth is 90% of the dried product.
Moisture removed × latent heat.
At STP, 1 mole occupies 22.4 L.
Heat needed ÷ heat supplied.

cards.front: A paper machine produces 340 TPD, 24 h/day. Inlet dryness is 40% and outlet dryness is 95%. Evaporated moisture has an enthalpy of 632 kcal/kg, and supply steam has a latent heat of 513 kcal/kg. Find (a) the moisture evaporated and (b) the steam required per hour.
cards.back: (a) ≈ 19.47 t/h evaporated; (b) ≈ 23,984 kg/h (≈ 24 t/h) of steam.
cards.explain: This is the book's Example 5.12. The fibre (dry paper) is the tie element. The steam must supply at least the total heat carried away by the evaporated moisture, 632 kcal/kg for sensible plus latent heat at 80 °C.

steps.explain: Convert TPD to TPH.
Outlet is 95% dry.

steps.prompt: Moisture before and after the dryer.
steps.explain: At the inlet, fibre is 40% and water 60%.
Difference between in and out.
Steam latent heat must supply the heat in the evaporated moisture.

cards.front: What does a Sankey diagram's arrow width represent?
cards.back: The width of each arrow is proportional to the size of the actual energy flow.
cards.explain: A Sankey diagram, drawn after the energy balance calculations, shows the entire input and output energy flow of equipment such as boilers, fired heaters and furnaces. It shows outputs (benefits) and losses visually, so energy managers can prioritise improvements better than with numbers or tables.

cards.front: In BEE's Sankey diagram for an internal combustion engine, how is 100% fuel energy split, and what improvements follow?
cards.back: 25% effective power, 5% friction and parasitic losses, 30% coolant, 40% exhaust gas. The exhaust is the priority, so a waste heat boiler should be part of the system; coolant heat can drive vapour absorption refrigeration.
cards.explain: Engines run hot, so exhaust gases leave at high temperatures and system efficiency is poor. The lower the exhaust temperature, the higher the system efficiency.

cards.front: An evaporator is fed 10,000 kg/h of a 1% solids solution at 38 °C, concentrated to 2% solids. Steam enters at 640 kcal/kg and condensate leaves at 100 °C. Enthalpies: feed 38.1, product 100.8, vapour 640 kcal/kg. Find the vapour formed and the steam used per hour.
cards.back: Vapour 5,000 kg/h; steam ≈ 6,154 kg/h.
cards.explain: This is the book's end-of-chapter solved example. The solids balance gives the product and vapour flows. The heat balance then gives the steam. Each kg of steam gives up 640 − 100 = 540 kcal as it condenses to 100 °C water.

steps.explain: Solids are the tie element.
The solids are 2% of the product.
Mass × enthalpy.
Heat from steam + heat in feed = heat in vapour + heat in liquor.
Divide by the heat given up per kg of steam.

cards.front: What is the first step in an energy action plan?
cards.back: Getting top management commitment, usually by forming an energy management cell and appointing an energy manager, with the backing of a written energy policy.
cards.explain: BEE's sequence is: make a commitment, assess performance and opportunities, set goals and targets, create an action plan, implement it, evaluate progress, and recognise achievements. Without management backing, resources and authority for projects never arrive.

cards.front: What is force field analysis in energy action planning, and which approach is usually more effective?
cards.back: It lists the positive (driving) and negative (restraining) forces acting on a goal. Minimising the negative forces (barriers) is usually more effective than strengthening the positive ones.
cards.explain: Pushing harder on driving forces tends to provoke more resistance. Removing barriers such as lack of funds, skills or ownership lets change happen with less friction. The analysis is used when planning energy-saving changes in an organisation.
cards.source: BEE 2024 P1 Q13; BEE 2025 P1 Q12

cards.front: What are the essential elements of a written energy policy?
cards.back: A statement of management commitment, clear objectives and targets for energy performance, responsibilities and accountability (energy manager or cell), allocation of resources, and a commitment to monitor, report and continually improve.
cards.explain: The policy is signed by top management and communicated to all staff. Under ISO 50001 it must also commit to legal compliance and to supporting procurement of efficient products and design for energy performance.

cards.front: Why is an Energy Management System (EnMS) such as ISO 50001 adopted?
cards.back: To manage energy use systematically through a Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle (policy, baseline, EnPIs, objectives and targets, action plans, monitoring, review), so that energy performance improves continually.
cards.explain: Cost savings and efficiency follow from the system, but the defining reason is systematic management rather than one-off projects. Key ISO 50001 terms: energy review, significant energy uses (SEUs), energy baseline (EnB) and energy performance indicators (EnPIs).

cards.front: In Total Productive Maintenance (TPM), what are the 'six big losses'?
cards.back: Breakdowns, setup and adjustment losses, idling and minor stoppages, reduced speed, process defects, and reduced yield at start-up. Excessive overtime is NOT one of them.
cards.explain: The six losses fall into three groups: availability (breakdowns, setup), performance (minor stops, reduced speed) and quality (defects, start-up yield). Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) = Availability × Performance × Quality.

cards.front: How does an organisation with an energy action plan differ from one that only has periodic energy audits?
cards.back: Audit-only organisations implement a few findings and then do little until the next audit. Organisations with an action plan make continual efforts to monitor and improve energy efficiency, integrated with their existing management techniques.
cards.explain: The book gives planning two major functions. A good plan shields the programme from disruptions. Scheduling events through the year (training, audits, planning sessions, demonstrations, lectures) keeps continuous emphasis on the programme and keeps it active.

cards.front: List the six steps of energy action planning in order.
cards.back: 1) Top management commitment and support; 2) assessing energy profile and establishing baseline; 3) energy policy and planning; 4) implementation; 5) evaluating energy performance; 6) recognising achievements.
cards.explain: This is BEE's Figure 6.1 cycle. Incorporating energy action planning into overall strategic planning legitimises the programme at top management level and provides funding and personnel. An exam trap: 'conduct safety audit' is not a step.

cards.front: What are the four vital requirements for a successful energy management programme?
cards.back: Top management support, a well-charted strategy plan, an effective monitoring system, and adequate technical ability to analyse and implement savings options.
cards.explain: Of these, top management support comes first. If top management accepts that energy efficiency is good business, the programme can be integrated with existing management of manpower, raw materials etc. 'Security of plant' is a distractor that is not one of the four.

cards.front: How is top management commitment to energy management shown in practice?
cards.back: Senior executives demonstrate commitment through actions and take part in organising and planning the campaign. They give visible support, especially by authorising resources and attending meetings, to the energy committee and the energy manager.
cards.explain: Responsibility for implementing the programme is usually assigned at two levels: the energy committee and the energy manager. In companies without an energy-efficiency ethic, good communication downwards from senior management is vital.

cards.front: Through awareness, employees support energy management when informed of which six things?
cards.back: 1) The amount of energy they use; 2) its costs; 3) the critical part energy plays in their job's viability; 4) the many ways they can save energy; 5) the relationship between production rate and energy consumption; 6) the seriousness of the energy problem and its impact on the country's economy.
cards.explain: The book calls awareness one of the most successful means of motivating employees. Recognition and rewards (cash awards or certificates) are other effective ways.

cards.front: What are the three key factors of motivation in the BEE guide book?
cards.back: 1) Motivation is already within people, and the manager's task is to bring it out, not to provide it. 2) The energy and enthusiasm people invest in work varies by individual. 3) The personal satisfaction to be gained determines how much energy an employee will invest in the job.
cards.explain: This is why the book stresses involving people personally in setting targets, and giving them recognition.

cards.front: Who should decide departmental energy conservation goals: senior management or the operating department?
cards.back: The operating department. Goals must not be dictated by senior management. People are committed when personally involved in setting realistic but challenging targets.
cards.explain: Healthy competition between departments and plants should be encouraged. Each department's goals should come with a documented programme of activities and assigned responsibilities. Energy management can also be made part of each supervisor's performance standards.

cards.front: What concept should the purchase department use when buying equipment, according to the energy action planning chapter?
cards.back: Life-cycle costing: weigh the annual savings from more efficient equipment against its higher purchase cost.
cards.explain: The book treats purchasing as one of the motivation and management levers in an energy programme, alongside awareness, recognition and rewards.

cards.front: Why must a company designate an energy manager, and where should that person report?
cards.back: If no one has energy management as a specific part of their job, it gets lower priority than other duties. The energy manager should report as high as possible in the organisation without losing line orientation.
cards.explain: The energy manager should be strong, dynamic, goal-oriented and a good manager, supported with resources including staff. In BEE's textile mill example, the energy manager reports to the factory manager, alongside the production, utilities/maintenance and finance managers.

cards.front: Name five responsibilities of an energy manager listed by BEE.
cards.back: Any five of: prepare an annual activity plan of attractive investments; establish an energy conservation cell; improve monitoring and process control; analyse equipment efficiency; ensure instruments are working and calibrated; run internal workshops; disseminate consumption data to shop level; establish an SEC calculation method; manage training; build a knowledge bank; coordinate external audits and projects; network with other energy managers.
cards.explain: BEE separates responsibilities (a broad list of 15) from duties (5, linked to the EC Act). A long-answer question asks for at least 5 duties and 3 responsibilities.
