cards.front: List the five duties of an energy manager under BEE.
cards.back: 1) Report to BEE and the State Designated Agency once a year on energy consumed and action taken on the accredited auditor's recommendations; 2) establish improved data recording, collection and analysis; 3) support the accredited energy audit firm; 4) provide information to BEE as demanded under the Act; 5) prepare and implement a scheme for efficient use of energy as per the EC Act regulations.
cards.explain: Trap: 'create a knowledge bank on sectoral and national energy efficiency developments' is a responsibility, not a duty. The book's MCQ uses exactly this distractor.

cards.front: What is one of the most important roles of the energy manager, and how can claimed savings be made credible?
cards.back: Marketing (selling) the energy management programme. Savings goals can be shown to be realistic with data and quotes from other companies, published in literature or obtained by contacting their energy managers.
cards.explain: Without internal marketing, the programme struggles to get resources and cooperation from departments.

cards.front: Why do most successful energy management programmes have an energy committee, and who is on it?
cards.back: Not all the talent needed resides in one person or discipline. The committee has members with strong technical backgrounds (chemical, industrial, electrical, civil, mechanical engineers etc.) who give technical help to the energy manager and plant staff.
cards.explain: The energy manager may be full-time, but the committee usually works part-time and is called on as needed; in multi-plant organisations it may be full-time. A committee encourages sharing of ideas, gets agreement on cross-departmental projects and gives a stronger voice to top management than one energy manager.

cards.front: How often does an energy committee normally meet, and what does it review?
cards.back: Normally monthly. It reviews monthly production and energy consumption against targets, budgets and previous months, and the status of conservation projects implemented or planned.
cards.explain: The frequency depends on how important energy costs are in the company's cost structure and what projects are under way.

cards.front: What are the BEE requirements for collecting energy data to build an energy profile?
cards.back: Account for all energy sources (electricity, steam, oil, gas, waste fuels), purchased or self-generated, in physical units and cost. Assemble at least two years of data, summarised monthly, using more recent data if available.
cards.explain: The data must be complete and accurate, since it is used for analysis and goal setting. It comes from utility bills and sub-meters, by measurement, calculation or estimation. Non-energy data (building size, production, operating hours) are also tracked to set Energy Performance Indicators.

cards.front: What is normalisation of energy data, and give normalisation factors for industry and for commercial buildings.
cards.back: Removing the impact of factors other than efficiency (season, occupancy, raw material quality etc.) so energy performance can be compared. Industry: inputs, product type, output, production process. Commercial buildings: climate zone, building area, energy choice, energy cost, occupancy, operating hours.
cards.explain: Exam trap: 'maintenance cost' is not a common normalising factor for industrial facilities.

cards.front: What is the minimum data period for an energy baseline, and what is preferable?
cards.back: A minimum of 12 months of data. An average over the past two to three years is more desirable.
cards.explain: The baseline is the reference point from which progress is measured. Identify energy performance indicators (e.g. kcal/ton, kcal/kWh, total energy cost/ton), and publish and share the baseline with managers and key stakeholders.

cards.front: Distinguish quantitative and qualitative reviews when analysing energy use patterns.
cards.back: Quantitative: find consumption peaks and valleys and link them to operations or events; compare the performance of similar facilities. Qualitative: interviews and informed opinions, lessons learned, in-house audits and surveys, and reviewing policies and operating procedures.
cards.explain: The analysis identifies significant energy uses, meaning those accounting for a high proportion of total consumption. The energy profile must be updated at set intervals and after major changes in facilities, equipment or processes.

cards.front: What are the components of energy planning in the BEE guide book?
cards.back: Developing an energy policy, setting objectives and targets, preparing detailed action plans, allocating management resources, and using management techniques (5S, TPM, TQM, Kaizen, ISO 50001) for implementation.
cards.explain: Planning rests on the premise that strategic goals are only achieved if they are driven by day-to-day actions.

cards.front: What two roles does a formal written energy policy play?
cards.back: 1) A public expression of the organisation's commitment to energy management. 2) A working document that guides energy management practice and provides continuity.
cards.explain: The energy policy provides the foundation for setting performance goals and integrating energy management into the organisation's culture and operations. Ideally it is a formal written declaration with stated objectives, an action plan and clear responsibilities.

cards.front: How should an energy policy be drafted and adopted, and who publishes it?
cards.back: All departmental representatives should be invited to contribute when it is first formulated and when it is reviewed. It should then be formally adopted and ratified by the head of the organisation; publishing the policy is a top-management role.
cards.explain: Wider participation gives wider acceptance. The policy usually states goals and concrete targets, often with major measures and timetables, and must match the company's mission statement or overall strategy.

cards.front: What first-year energy reduction goal does BEE consider adequate, and why are yearly goals usually better than multi-year goals?
cards.back: First-year goals of 3–6% reduction in energy consumption or SEC are adequate for most companies. Yearly goals let rewards be seen sooner, success be celebrated more often, and corrections be made more frequently, especially if production changes.
cards.explain: A good rule is to start with small goals. Goals must be measurable, time-bound and formally approved by senior management. They can be based on audit findings, technical or economic feasibility, or benchmarking. An example of a multi-year goal is 20% savings over 3 years.

cards.front: What does SMART mean for energy targets in the BEE guide book?
cards.back: Specific and Measurable; Ambitious (committing the organisation to continual improvement); Realistic, so they can be achieved within specified Time limits.
cards.explain: Targets are normally set at departmental level to achieve organisational goals, and should be attainable but challenging. They are expressed through energy performance indicators such as energy per item, per kg, per m² or %.

cards.front: In BEE's ISO 50001 cement plant example, how do goal, objectives and targets differ?
cards.back: Goal: the broad policy aim (reduce energy per output by 15% vs 2015 by 2017). Objectives: steps towards it (cut coal use 10% by 2016; cut clinker SEC from 90 to 85 kWh/t). Targets: the specific measures (e.g. online O₂ analyser for kiln excess air, cooler waste heat recovery, waste tyres as fuel, efficient raw mill fan, VFD on dust collector fan).
cards.explain: Each target then gets an action plan with time, actions, responsibility and resources. In the example, the online O₂ analyser target has the General Manager overall responsible and a budget of Rs 5,00,000.

cards.front: What is internal benchmarking, and when is it used for setting targets?
cards.back: Using the company's own historical best performance as the basis for targets. It is used when external benchmarking is impractical because of confidentiality or lack of detailed comparable data.
cards.explain: External benchmarking needs very detailed data on energy and on processes, raw materials and products. Comparisons not made on the same basis give misleading results.

cards.front: List the steps in creating an energy action plan.
cards.back: a) Evaluate audit reports and identify gaps between current and desired performance; b) list the activities needed to close each gap; c) list resources and time required; d) designate overall responsibility; e) facilitate budget negotiations and confirm budget availability.
cards.explain: Action plans are energy management programmes. To avoid duplicating resources, they should be built into normal business operations, and communicated to all departments involved (utilities, operations, HR, purchase, engineering, EHS etc.).

cards.front: Classify each as a positive or negative force for 'reduce energy per unit of production': high energy price; competing corporate priorities; available efficient technology; lack of awareness; incentive for high power factor; insufficient finance.
cards.back: Positive: high energy price, efficient technology available, PF incentive. Negative: competing corporate priorities, lack of awareness, insufficient financial resources.
cards.explain: Other forces in BEE's Figure 6.4: positive are top management commitment and energy being a high share of product cost; negative are absence of a corporate energy policy and insufficient skills. The book's tip: it is usually more effective to minimise negative forces than to strengthen positive ones.

cards.front: List the steps of force field analysis.
cards.back: 1) State the goal and the direction towards it; 2) identify barriers (negative forces), internal or external; 3) identify positive forces; 4) estimate the relative strength of each (low, medium, high); 5) prioritise the forces the action plan can most effectively strengthen or weaken.
cards.explain: It is done before creating the action plan, to gain insight into the change process. External barriers can include energy rate structures or government regulation.

cards.front: What two major areas should employee training address in an energy management programme?
cards.back: 1) Developing new skills in technologies (in-house or outside training). 2) Adopting new attitudes towards energy wastage and waste reduction.
cards.explain: Training is called the key to sustaining energy conservation. It must be continuous, not a one-off session, so it both informs and changes attitudes. Trained technical staff should in turn train operators in-house.

cards.front: Give good practices for building energy awareness and motivation.
cards.back: Top management announces an energy policy and backs the team; incentives and recognition for successful projects; announcing results to all employees; participation at every step; divisional working groups; monthly evaluation of energy consumption and savings; in-house training; an annual energy conservation week with seminars, exhibitions and contests.
cards.explain: Communication methods include informal dialogue, work group meetings, posters, newsletters, bulletin boards and intranet sites. New employees get basic energy information during orientation.

cards.front: What features should an energy performance tracking (information) system have?
cards.back: A suitable frequency of data collection (daily, weekly or monthly); easy to use, update and maintain; used to communicate performance to all parts of the organisation to motivate change; formats understandable across the organisation that make reporting easy.
cards.explain: It can range from a simple spreadsheet to detailed databases and IT systems. Metering and sub-metering are needed for effective monitoring. Sharing results across departments promotes healthy competition.

cards.front: What are the levels and examples of internal recognition, and give an example of external recognition.
cards.back: Levels: individual, team (department or group) and facility. Types range from certificates and formal acknowledgements to salary increases, cash bonuses or shields, ideally given by senior management at an award ceremony. External: a National Energy Conservation Award.
cards.explain: Recognition criteria include best energy-saving idea, highest reduction in energy use, or savings increased by a quantified amount. External recognition validates the programme and enhances public image, making the organisation more attractive to customers, lenders and other stakeholders.

cards.front: Name the five Japanese words of 5S and their English meanings.
cards.back: Seiri – housekeeping (separate needed from unneeded items); Seiton – workplace organisation (a place for everything); Seiso – cleanup; Seiketsu – cleanliness (constant state of readiness); Shitsuke – discipline.
cards.explain: 5S is a simple but effective method of organising the workplace. Implementing it reduces hidden waste, improves quality and safety, and cuts lead time and cost.

cards.front: What do the letters PQCDS stand for as the benefits of 5S, and which cycle is used to implement 5S?
cards.back: P – increase Productivity; Q – improve product Quality; C – reduce manufacturing Costs; D – ensure on-time Delivery; S – provide a Safe working environment. Implementation follows the PDCA (Plan–Do–Check–Action) cycle.
cards.explain: Plan: organise a committee, plan each S, announce the programme. Do: training, a clean-up day, an organise-your-workplace day. Check: evaluate results. Action: self-examination and corrective action.

cards.front: What does KAIZEN mean, and what are its implementation steps?
cards.back: KAI = change, ZEN = good (for the better): continuous improvement involving everyone. Steps: 1) the operator identifies and writes down a problem; 2) the operator develops an improvement idea and goes to the supervisor; 3) the supervisor or Kaizen team reviews it, encourages action and fills the Kaizen form; 4) the idea is implemented and checked; 5) the operator is rewarded.
cards.explain: Kaizen events that target energy directly, such as steam or compressed air leak events where operators detect and fix leaks on the spot, give immediate returns. They also enrol employees in future conservation efforts.

cards.front: What is the principle of Small Group Activities (SGA) in energy management?
cards.back: Members discuss, think and judge based on facts and data rather than experience, intuition or gut feeling. Cross-functional shop-floor teams conceptualise, measure and implement energy projects.
cards.explain: This creates awareness and gives a sense of ownership and achievement. Plants using SGA developed a culture of energy savings and better sustained the savings. Planning runs from forming groups and defining roles, through setting targets and running meetings, to reporting and presenting the problems solved.

cards.front: According to BEE, what share of energy costs can be saved by eliminating TPM's six big losses with proper maintenance, and what are the four strategies for integrating energy into TPM?
cards.back: An estimated 25% of energy costs. Strategies: integrate energy reduction into autonomous maintenance; train employees to identify energy wastes; conduct energy kaizen events; build energy best practices into safety, health and environment management systems.
cards.explain: TPM aims to maximise overall production system effectiveness and eliminate all accidents, defects and breakdowns, with everyone from top executive to shop floor taking part. Autonomous maintenance means operators maintain their own equipment: daily inspection, lubrication, parts replacement, simple repairs, abnormality detection and precision checks.

cards.front: Give energy-reduction checklist items for combustion and steam generation systems from BEE's TPM section.
cards.back: Combustion: run furnaces and boilers near design capacity, reduce excess air, clean heat transfer surfaces, cut radiation losses from openings, insulate properly, install air preheat or heat recovery. Steam: better water treatment to minimise blowdown, optimise deaerator venting, repair leaks, minimise vented steam, maintain steam traps.
cards.explain: For process heating, the checklist adds: seal openings to stop air leakage, keep a slightly positive furnace pressure, reduce material-handling fixtures, and recover exhaust heat for lower-temperature processes.

cards.front: Which phrase is associated with TQM, and why does TQM complement energy management?
cards.back: 'Doing the right things right, first time'. Rejects waste the energy used to make them, e.g. a casting with blow holes must be scrapped.
cards.explain: TQM requires involvement of everyone from worker to top executive, visible management commitment, 'document what you do, then do what you documented', written and displayed mission and vision statements, people satisfaction as first priority, and emphasis on long-term needs.

cards.front: What framework does ISO 50001:2011 require organisations to follow?
cards.back: Develop a policy for more efficient energy use; fix targets and objectives to meet the policy; use data to understand and decide on energy use; measure the results; review how well the policy works; continually improve energy management.
cards.explain: An EnMS addresses energy supply, measurement, documentation and reporting of energy use, and procurement and design practices for energy-using equipment. An exam MCQ answer is 'all of the above'.

cards.front: How does ISO 50001 relate to other ISO standards, and how much of world energy use could it influence?
cards.back: It uses the same continual-improvement management system model as ISO 9001 (quality) and ISO 14001 (environment), so it integrates easily with them. It could influence up to 60% of the world's energy use.
cards.explain: In ISO 50001:2011, clause 4.3 is the energy policy, 4.4 planning (energy review, legal requirements, objectives and targets), 4.5 implementation and operation, 4.6 checking performance, and 4.7 management review. The book summarises ISO 50001 as 'saying what you do and doing what you say', since action plans are documented and audited.

cards.front: What is simple payback period and what are its limitations?
cards.back: Simple payback = First cost (investment) ÷ Net annual cash savings. It does not account for the time value of money or for savings after the payback period.
cards.explain: It is quick and easy to understand, which makes it useful for screening low-cost energy measures. Two projects with the same payback can have very different lifetime value, so use NPV or IRR for larger investments.

cards.front: How is Return on Investment (ROI) calculated?
cards.back: ROI (%) = Annual net cash flow ÷ Capital cost × 100. Example: ₹20,000 per year on ₹1,00,000 → 20%.
cards.explain: ROI is the reciprocal of simple payback (×100). Like payback, it ignores the time value of money. For a project to be worthwhile, ROI should exceed the interest rate on borrowed money or the cost of capital.

cards.front: Define Net Present Value (NPV).
cards.back: NPV = Σ CFₜ ÷ (1 + i)ᵗ for t = 0 to n, the sum of all cash flows discounted to today at the discount rate i, with the investment entered as a negative cash flow at t = 0. Accept the project if NPV > 0.
cards.explain: The present value factor 1/(1+i)ᵗ converts future savings into today's money. NPV tells you how much value the project adds beyond the required return. Among mutually exclusive projects with no capital limit, choose the highest NPV.

cards.front: Define Internal Rate of Return (IRR).
cards.back: IRR is the discount rate at which the NPV of a project's cash flows equals zero. Accept the project if IRR > cost of capital.
cards.explain: IRR is found by trial and interpolation: IRR = r₁ + NPV₁ × (r₂ − r₁) ÷ (NPV₁ − NPV₂), where NPV₁ > 0 at the lower rate r₁ and NPV₂ < 0 at r₂. Both NPV and IRR account for the time value of money; simple payback and ROI do not.

cards.front: Two projects of equal life: X has IRR 40%, NPV ₹50,000; Y has IRR 30%, NPV ₹1,20,000. With no capital limit, which do you choose?
cards.back: Project Y, because it has the higher NPV.
cards.explain: When NPV and IRR rankings conflict for mutually exclusive projects and funds are not limited, NPV is preferred: it measures the absolute value added. IRR is a percentage and favours small projects, and it assumes cash is reinvested at the IRR.
cards.source: BEE 2025 P1 Q14; BEE 2024 P1 L3

cards.front: What do these terms mean: net operating cash inflow, economic life, salvage value, depreciation?
cards.back: Net operating cash inflow: annual savings minus operating and maintenance costs (after tax where applicable). Economic life: the period over which the project gives useful savings. Salvage value: what the asset can be sold for at the end of its life (a cash inflow in the final year). Depreciation: the decrease in an asset's value over time.
cards.explain: Depreciation is not a cash outflow, but it lowers taxable profit and so affects after-tax cash flows. Include salvage in the last year's cash flow and any mid-life reinvestment in the year it happens.
cards.source: BEE 2024 P1 L3; BEE 2025 P1 Q15

cards.front: What is sensitivity analysis in project financial evaluation?
cards.back: Testing how NPV, IRR or payback change when key assumptions change: energy price, fuel cost, savings achieved, capital cost, project life, discount rate, or tax rate (a macro factor).
cards.explain: It shows which variables the project's viability depends on most, and how robust the decision is. Energy price escalation and the level of savings achieved are usually the most influential variables in energy projects.

cards.front: What are the options for financing energy efficiency projects?
cards.back: Debt financing (loans), equity, retained earnings (internal funds), capital lease, true (operating) lease, and performance contracting through ESCOs.
cards.explain: In performance contracting, the ESCO's payment is tied to the energy savings achieved, which lowers the client's risk. A stock buyback is not a financing option. Public schemes such as EEFP under NMEEE help channel finance to energy efficiency.

cards.front: How do 'guaranteed savings' and 'shared savings' ESCO contracts differ?
cards.back: Guaranteed savings: the client arranges the finance, and the ESCO designs and implements the project and guarantees a level of savings. Shared savings: the ESCO finances the project and is repaid from an agreed share of the savings.
cards.explain: In guaranteed savings, the ESCO carries the performance risk and the client carries the credit risk. In shared savings, the ESCO carries both. Measurement & Verification (M&V) checks that the guaranteed or shared savings were actually achieved.

cards.front: Why is life-cycle costing better than comparing purchase prices?
cards.back: It includes the operating (energy), maintenance and disposal costs over the asset's whole life, not just the first cost.
cards.explain: For motors, pumps and compressors, energy cost over the life can be many times the purchase price. A cheaper but inefficient unit can therefore cost far more in total.

cards.front: A 37 kW pump motor runs at 70% load with 90% efficiency for 20 h/day, 330 days/year. A VFD costing ₹2,50,000 is expected to cut its energy use by 15%. Power costs ₹8/kWh. Find the annual energy use, savings, simple payback and ROI.
cards.back: Energy ≈ 1,89,933 kWh/yr; savings ≈ 28,490 kWh = ₹2,27,920/yr; payback ≈ 1.1 years (~13 months); ROI ≈ 91%.
cards.explain: Input power = rated output × load ÷ efficiency. Savings are a percentage of current consumption. Payback and ROI are reciprocals; a payback near one year makes this an attractive low-risk measure.

steps.explain: Input = output × loading ÷ efficiency.
Energy = power × operating hours (6,600 h).

steps.prompt: Find the energy and cost savings.
steps.explain: Savings = % reduction × energy × tariff.
Payback = investment ÷ annual savings.
ROI = annual savings ÷ investment × 100.

cards.front: Two mutually exclusive projects each have a 5-year life. Project A costs ₹5 lakh and saves ₹1.6 lakh/yr. Project B costs ₹9 lakh and saves ₹2.75 lakh/yr. At a 12% discount rate, compare them by simple payback and by NPV. Which should be chosen if funds are not limited?
cards.back: Payback: A 3.13 yr, B 3.27 yr. NPV: A ≈ ₹0.77 lakh, B ≈ ₹0.91 lakh. Choose B (higher NPV).
cards.explain: Simple payback favours A, but payback ignores the time value of money and the absolute value created. NPV shows that B adds more wealth. With no capital constraint, NPV decides.

steps.explain: Payback = cost ÷ annual savings.

steps.prompt: Find the cumulative PV factor at 12% for 5 years.
steps.explain: Uniform annual savings: PV = savings × Σ 1/(1+i)ᵗ.
NPV = PV of inflows − investment.

steps.answer: NPV(B) > NPV(A), so choose B, even though its payback is longer.
steps.explain: With no capital limit, select the project with the higher NPV.

cards.front: An energy-efficiency project costs ₹10 lakh and gives net savings of ₹3 lakh per year for 5 years, with no salvage value. Find the IRR by interpolation between 15% and 16%.
cards.explain: IRR is the rate at which NPV = 0. Calculate NPV at two rates either side of zero and interpolate linearly. If the company's cost of capital is below 15.24%, the project is acceptable.

steps.explain: NPV = Σ CF/(1+r)ᵗ − investment.
The sign has changed, so the IRR lies between 15% and 16%.
IRR = r₁ + NPV₁ (r₂ − r₁) ÷ (NPV₁ − NPV₂).

steps.answer: Accept if the cost of capital is below 15.24%.
steps.explain: IRR > cost of capital → project adds value.

cards.front: According to the BEE guide book, what is the biggest constraint in increasing the number of energy projects?
cards.back: Lack of finance.
cards.explain: The book notes that alternative finance arrangements can overcome the 'initial cost' obstacle and let firms implement more energy management proposals. It also observes that many energy managers rely only on simple payback, which does not reveal the added value of after-tax benefits.

cards.front: When an energy auditor puts forward a proposal, what two questions will management ask, and why do they matter?
cards.back: How much will the proposal cost? How much money will it save? The energy project competes with many other projects for limited capital.
cards.explain: Senior management's job is to put capital where it earns the greatest return, so an energy project is only one of many candidates. The book notes that in practice management often demands a higher rate of return from energy projects than from core, directly profit-making investments.

cards.front: True or false: an organisation should demand a faster rate of return from energy-efficiency investments than from its other investments.
cards.back: False. Energy-efficiency investments should be judged by exactly the same criteria as all other investments.
cards.explain: Section 7.3 says investment in energy efficiency is in most respects no different from any other area of financial management, so a faster or more attractive return should not be demanded. (Section 7.2 observes that management often does demand a higher return in practice; the book's recommendation is that it should not.)

cards.front: Before making any energy-saving investment, what should be ensured first?
cards.back: That existing plant gives its best performance, energy is bought at the lowest possible tariffs, the best energy forms (fuel or electricity) are used efficiently, and good housekeeping is practised regularly.
cards.explain: Low-cost technical and housekeeping measures often cut waste without capital. Spending money before these are in place can mean paying for savings that were available for free.

cards.front: Besides energy savings, what benefits of an energy project should be presented to senior management?
cards.back: Lower operating costs, low risk/reward ratio, reduced environmental cost, improved productivity, better product or service quality, and potential to improve the company's share value.
cards.explain: Framing the project in these business terms makes it easier to compete for capital with other proposals. The book adds that a systematic financial approach must still be used to rate options against expected savings.

cards.front: What are the three groups of basic criteria for financial investment appraisal, and what does each tell you?
cards.back: 1) Payback period – how long until the investment recovers itself (sets the needed financing term). 2) NPV and cash flow – financial planning of money inflows and outflows over time. 3) ROI and IRR – comparison with other investment options.
cards.explain: Each criterion answers a different management question. Payback is about liquidity and loan term; NPV and cash flow fit the project into the corporate financial system; ROI and IRR express returns as a rate that can be compared with alternatives and the cost of money.

cards.front: Why is the word 'simple' used in 'simple payback period'?
cards.back: Because the time value of money is not considered in its calculation.
cards.explain: Simple payback = capital cost ÷ annual net savings, where annual net savings are the savings left after all operating costs. Cash inflows are just added without discounting.

cards.front: What are the two limitations of ROI given in the BEE book?
cards.back: It ignores the time value of money, and it does not account for year-to-year variation in net cash inflows.
cards.explain: In the book's example (₹1,00,000 outlay, ₹25,000 a year) the 25% ROI would be strictly valid only if ₹25,000 came in every year in perpetuity – not a realistic condition.

cards.front: If money earns 10% interest, what is ₹100 today worth in one year, and what is ₹100 received one year from now worth today?
cards.back: ₹110 in one year; ₹90.91 today.
cards.explain: FV = PV × (1 + i)ⁿ and PV = FV ÷ (1 + i)ⁿ. So 100 × 1.1 = 110, and 100 ÷ 1.1 = 90.91. Relating cash flows at different times in this way is called discounting, or the present value concept.

cards.front: State the NPV decision rule. What does a zero NPV mean?
cards.back: Accept if NPV is positive, reject if negative. A zero NPV is value-neutral.
cards.explain: A negative NPV means the project does not reach the required return and would cause an economic loss if implemented. Among alternatives, the higher the NPV the more attractive the project.

cards.front: What should the discount rate used in NPV reflect, and how should it be set relative to the borrowing rate?
cards.back: It should reflect the risk of the project; it is prudent to set it slightly above the interest rate at which the capital is borrowed.
cards.explain: The credibility of NPV depends entirely on a realistic discount rate, which is often hard to predict. Setting it a little above the cost of borrowing builds in a margin.

cards.front: When is an investment judged sound by IRR, and how is IRR used to choose among alternatives?
cards.back: It is sound if the IRR is greater than the current interest rate. Among alternatives, choose the one with the highest rate of return.
cards.explain: IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV = 0. Finding it is iterative (trial and error) and usually done with a spreadsheet; Excel has an IRR function.

cards.front: Give the interpolation formula for IRR.
cards.back: IRR = lower rate + [NPV at lower rate × (higher rate − lower rate)] ÷ (NPV at lower rate − NPV at higher rate).
cards.explain: Find one discount rate giving a positive NPV and a nearby rate giving a negative NPV, then interpolate linearly between them. The result can also be read from a graph of NPV against discount rate where the curve crosses zero.

cards.front: What limitation of IRR does the BEE book state?
cards.back: IRR cannot distinguish between lending and borrowing, so a high IRR is not necessarily a desirable feature.
cards.explain: Its advantages are that it accounts for the time value of money, uses the whole cash-flow stream, and gives a rate of return that business people find easier to think about than an absolute NPV figure.

cards.front: What is the key difference between the NPV and IRR methods?
cards.back: NPV assumes the discount rate (cost of capital) is known and finds the value; IRR sets NPV to zero and finds the discount rate. NPV is a tool for comparing several projects; IRR tests whether a single project reaches a target rate of return.
cards.explain: Both discount cash flows, so they look similar. But they answer different questions: 'how much value at this rate?' versus 'what rate does this project earn?'

cards.front: How do expenses differ from capital investments, and what do initial capital costs include?
cards.back: Expenses are routine, ongoing costs of normal operation; capital investments are strategic, long-term, usually decided by senior management and taxed differently. Initial capital cost includes purchase plus installation and preparation costs.
cards.explain: Initial costs are usually non-recurring and may be spent at once or over several years. Funds for capital projects are generally limited, which is why appraisal is needed.

cards.front: What are the conventions and requirements of a cash flow diagram?
cards.back: Time runs along the horizontal axis; upward arrows are inflows (revenue or savings), downward arrows are outflows (costs); arrows point away from the axis and can be summed within a year. A good diagram is complete, accurate and legible.
cards.explain: The economic life sets the horizontal scale, usually in years. Showing timing clearly makes it more likely that time-value-of-money concepts are applied correctly.

cards.front: A project is feasible with energy cost savings escalating at 10% a year, but sensitivity analysis shows break-even at 9%. What does this mean?
cards.back: The project carries a high degree of risk, because it becomes unviable if energy-cost inflation falls only slightly, below 9%.
cards.explain: Sensitivity analysis is recommended especially for marginal projects. It identifies uncertain parameters to which the NPV or IRR decision is sensitive, and 'switching values' show how much a variable must change to flip acceptance to rejection.

cards.front: In sensitivity analysis, what is the difference between micro and macro factors? Give examples.
cards.back: Micro factors are within the firm's control: operating expenses, capital structure, cost of debt and equity, form of finance (e.g. leasing), project life. Macro factors are economy-wide and cannot be changed by management: interest rates, tax rates, accounting standards, depreciation rates, regulations, energy prices, technology changes.
cards.explain: Macro variables affect the whole industry in which the company operates. The book also lists extension of government-subsidised projects and general employment or salary trends as macro factors.

cards.front: Why is the cost of equity (stock) higher than the cost of debt financing?
cards.back: Equity holders share in profits, and interest on debt is tax-deductible while stock dividends are not.
cards.explain: The two main sources of debt capital are loans and bonds; the two main sources of equity are stocks and retained earnings. Retained earnings carry the same cost of capital as stock because they truly belong to the stockholders.

cards.front: How does a capital lease differ from a true lease?
cards.back: A capital lease is midway between debt and equity and gives a lower cost of capital with third-party participation. A true lease gives use of equipment without ownership risk, suits short-term use, has tax-deductible payments, but gives no depreciation benefit and no ownership even at the end.
cards.explain: A true lease reduces the risk of poor performance, poor service and obsolescence because the lessee never owns the asset.

cards.front: What is the unique feature of energy performance contracting, and why does it lead to a wider scope of work?
cards.back: The contractor is paid only from the performance of the installed equipment, i.e. after it actually reduces expenses. This removes any incentive to cut corners and encourages exceeding savings, so contracts tend to be facility-wide.
cards.explain: With a facility-wide scope, several improvements (e.g. lighting and air conditioning) can be done together, giving a 'multiplier effect' on cost reduction. The client invests very little money up-front.

cards.front: In a fixed-fee ESCO contract, what does the ESCO do and how does its risk compare with savings-based contracts?
cards.back: It audits, designs and either helps implement or simply advises, for a fixed lump-sum fee. It bears less risk because its fee does not depend on the savings achieved.
cards.explain: The three common ESCO options are fixed fee, shared savings and guaranteed savings; a part-fixed-fee, part-shared-savings combination is also used. Guaranteed savings gives the client most security but usually costs more.

cards.front: Which of these is NOT a typical performance contract: shared savings, guaranteed savings, fixed fee, hire purchase?
cards.back: Hire purchase.
cards.explain: Shared savings, guaranteed savings and fixed fee are the three ESCO contract options in the BEE book. Hire purchase is an ordinary purchase-finance arrangement whose payments do not depend on energy savings.

cards.front: What are the pros and cons of performance contracting for the host company?
cards.back: Pros: use of equipment with reduced installation/operating risk, poor performance, service and obsolescence risk; host can focus on its core business. Cons: potentially binding contracts, legal expenses, higher administrative cost, and savings must be shared.
cards.explain: Tax benefits of depreciation must also be negotiated. Because complex contracts leave more room for error, the book stresses choosing an ESCO with a good reputation and experience in similar facilities.

cards.front: What three conditions must an asset meet to be depreciable?
cards.back: It must be held by the business to produce income, it must wear out or be consumed in use, and it must have a life longer than one year.
cards.explain: Depreciation allowances are deductions from taxable income that tax law permits because most business assets lose value over time.

cards.front: List the services an ESCO usually offers.
cards.back: Investment grade energy audit; financing (own funds or via banks); purchase, installation and maintenance of the equipment; training of O&M staff; monitoring of operations and savings; measurement and savings verification; and a guarantee of savings.
cards.explain: The investment grade audit identifies savings, assesses risks and mitigation, and calculates cost-effectiveness over time. ESCO services have become customer-driven, so the client picks from this menu.

cards.front: What benefits does an industry get from working with an ESCO?
cards.back: Immediate upgrade and lower operating costs without initial capital; access to ESCO expertise; positive cash flow; capital freed for core business; better O&M; ESCO takes on several business risks including guaranteed equipment performance for the contract life; services paid from money otherwise spent on wasted energy.
cards.explain: The guarantee covers performance for the whole contract, not just a warranty period. The book also mentions a more comfortable, productive environment.

cards.front: What is an investment grade energy audit (IGA), and how do single-step and two-step ESCO engagements differ?
cards.back: An IGA identifies efficiency opportunities and translates the technical findings into financial terms, presenting a bankable project that can secure a loan. Single step: ESCO does the IGA and implements the measures. Two step: ESCO only does the IGA and reports; the organisation prioritises measures.
cards.explain: In the two-step route the organisation ranks measures by time, capital investment and payback period. If a bank finances the project, detailed cash flow, IRR, debt service coverage ratio and sensitivity analysis are prepared.

cards.front: How does contract duration affect the risk of an ESCO contract?
cards.back: The longer the duration, the higher the risk and uncertainty.
cards.explain: Contracts have rewards and penalties built in through guarantees. The organisation can contract with the ESCO under one of three payment mechanisms: fixed fee, shared savings or guaranteed savings.

cards.front: How are energy savings calculated in a performance contract, and how are energy price changes handled?
cards.back: Energy saved = Baseline − Current ± Adjustments. Cost savings use a price agreed in the contract (a set price, or a formula such as average monthly energy cost) so they reflect only the efficiency measures.
cards.explain: Adjustments bring current-period energy use to the same conditions as the baseline period. Without an agreed price, savings in rupees would swing with tariff changes that have nothing to do with the project.

cards.front: In the BEE case study of the ABC building ESCO project, what were the baseline consumption, savings potential and guaranteed savings?
cards.back: Baseline about 21,28,545 kWh/year; potential 39% reduction in energy use and 33% in the energy bill; guarantee of at least 7,93,250 kWh/year, which is 95% of the proposed ≈8,35,000 kWh saving.
cards.explain: Main loads were lighting and air conditioning. Measures included task lighting, replacing window/split ACs with a centrifugal-chiller central AC (also used for winter heating), efficient pumps, and LPG instead of electric heating in the canteen.

cards.front: In the BEE ABC building case study, what were the contract term and savings-sharing ratios?
cards.back: 5-year term. Savings shared 95% contractor : 5% owner for the first three years, and 90% : 10% in years four and five; the assets then pass to the owner at a nominal cost.
cards.explain: The owner also pays a fixed sum for maintaining the measures. Contractor payments are tied to actual bill reduction, so the contractor also carries out O&M, and whole-facility performance measurement and verification is done jointly.

cards.front: Why is performance contracting attractive for municipalities, and what is the estimated saving potential in municipal water pumping?
cards.back: Municipal budgets lack funds for efficiency upgrades; performance contracting needs no upfront investment because the cost is paid from savings. Water pumping alone has at least 25% saving potential.
cards.explain: ESCOs bring managerial, technical and turnkey skills plus the ability to structure financing. The steps include a walk-through self-assessment, an Expression of Interest (EOI), a Request for Proposal (RFP) to firms that responded, IGA, contract, and monitoring and verification.

cards.front: A cogeneration system will cut a company's annual energy bill by ₹23 lakh. It costs ₹90 lakh, and annual operating and maintenance costs are ₹5 lakh. Find the simple payback period.
cards.back: 5 years.
cards.explain: Annual net savings must deduct the operating costs from the gross bill reduction. Using ₹23 lakh instead of ₹18 lakh would wrongly give about 3.9 years.

steps.explain: Simple payback uses net savings: benefits minus yearly costs.

steps.answer: Simple payback = capital cost ÷ annual net savings
steps.explain: Time value of money is ignored, hence 'simple'.
After 5 years the capital is recovered and later savings are clear profit.

cards.front: Projects A and B each cost ₹1,00,000. A saves ₹50,000, 30,000, 20,000, 10,000, 10,000 in years 1–5. B saves ₹20,000, 20,000, 20,000, 40,000, 50,000, 60,000 in years 1–6. Find each payback and say what it shows about the payback method.
cards.back: A: 3 years; B: 4 years. Payback prefers A even though B has much larger inflows in years 5 and 6 – it ignores savings after payback.
cards.explain: This is the book's example of the main drawback of payback: it ignores everything after the payback point. B's total savings (₹2,10,000) far exceed A's (₹1,20,000).

steps.prompt: Cumulate A's savings until they reach ₹1,00,000.
steps.explain: Payback is the time to recover the investment.
B recovers its cost one year later.
B's large later inflows are ignored by payback.

steps.answer: Payback picks A, though B is clearly better over its life
steps.explain: Payback favours early cash inflows and discriminates against projects with large later inflows.

cards.front: An outlay of ₹1,00,000 on equipment gives an after-tax cash flow of ₹25,000 a year for six years, with no significant fluctuation. Find the ROI.
cards.explain: ROI = annual net cash flow ÷ capital cost × 100. The book warns this 25% is strictly valid only if ₹25,000 came every year in perpetuity, because ROI ignores the time value of money.

steps.answer: ROI = annual net cash flow ÷ capital cost × 100
steps.explain: ROI is the inverse of payback, as a percentage.
Use the average annual operating cash flow and net investment.

steps.answer: ROI = 25%; it must exceed the cost of money to be attractive
steps.explain: Payback here is 4 years, the inverse of 25%.

cards.front: Two projects each cost ₹30,000 and have a 10-year life; discount rate 8%. Project 1 saves ₹6,000 every year. Project 2 saves ₹6,600 in years 1–2, ₹6,300 in years 3–4, ₹6,000 in years 5–6, ₹5,700 in years 7–8 and ₹5,400 in years 9–10. Both total ₹60,000. Which is better by NPV?
cards.back: NPV₁ ≈ ₹10,254; NPV₂ ≈ ₹10,867. Project 2 is preferred.
cards.explain: Total savings are equal, but Project 2 earns more in the early years, and money received earlier is worth more after discounting. Comparing total savings alone could not separate these two projects.

steps.prompt: List the 8% discount factors 1/(1.08)ᵗ for years 1–10.
steps.explain: Factor for year 0 (the investment) is 1.
Equal yearly savings can be multiplied by the sum of the factors.
Each pair of years has the same saving.
The book shows ₹10,867 (rounding of factors).
Front-loaded savings are worth more in present-value terms.

cards.front: A project costs ₹20,000 and returns ₹6,000, 5,500, 5,000, 4,500, 4,000 and 4,000 in years 1–6. The firm's cost of capital is 8%. Find the NPV at 8% and the IRR by interpolation between 12% and 13%.
cards.explain: IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV zero; you raise the rate until NPV changes sign, then interpolate. The printed book shows +₹495 at 12%, but its own factors give about +₹460; either value interpolates to ≈ 12.88%. Since IRR exceeds the 8% cost of capital, the project is sound.

steps.explain: Positive NPV, so the IRR is above 8%; increase the rate.
Still positive, so IRR > 12%.
Negative, so IRR lies between 12% and 13%. (At 16% NPV ≈ −₹1,508.)
IRR = lower rate + NPV_low × (rate gap) ÷ (NPV_low − NPV_high).
A project is sound when IRR exceeds the cost of money.

cards.front: An oil-fired reheating furnace heats 12 t/h of steel billets from 40°C to 1220°C at 28% efficiency, 4,700 h/year. Billet specific heat 0.12 kcal/kg°C; furnace oil GCV 10,000 kcal/kg, density 0.94 kg/L, cost ₹45/L. Ceramic fibre insulation (₹20 lakh) raises efficiency to 30%. Find the oil use per tonne, hourly saving, simple payback, and the maximum justified investment at 16% over 6 years.
cards.back: ≈53.8 L oil/t; saving ≈ ₹1,936/h (₹91 lakh/yr); payback ≈ 0.22 yr (≈2.6 months); maximum investment ≈ ₹3.35 crore.
cards.explain: The book's working shows the payback as 0.352 years (4.2 months), but 20,00,000 ÷ (1,936 × 4,700) = 0.22 years, so 0.22 years is the figure its own data support. Part (e) is the present value of ₹91 lakh/year for 6 years at 16%: the most you could invest and still earn a 16% IRR.

steps.prompt: Heat needed by the billets per hour.
steps.explain: Sensible heat of the stock.

steps.prompt: Furnace oil per tonne of billets at 28%.
steps.explain: Input = useful heat ÷ efficiency.

steps.prompt: Hourly saving when efficiency goes to 30%.
steps.explain: Fuel needed falls in the ratio of the efficiencies.

steps.answer: Annual saving = 1,936 × 4,700 = ₹91.0 lakh; 20 lakh ÷ 91.0 lakh ≈ 0.22 yr ≈ 2.6 months
steps.explain: Capital ÷ annual net savings.

steps.prompt: Maximum investment for 16% IRR over 6 years.
steps.explain: At this investment the NPV at 16% is zero, i.e. IRR = 16%.

cards.front: Find the NPV at 16% of a project costing ₹50,000 at the start of year 1 that saves ₹23,000 at the end of year 1 and ₹36,000 at the end of year 2.
cards.back: NPV ≈ −₹3,419 (negative, so the project fails at 16%).
cards.explain: This is the chapter's objective question 7; the magnitude matches option (d) 3,419, but the sign is negative because the discounted savings are less than the investment.

steps.explain: PV = FV ÷ (1 + i)ⁿ with n = 1.
The investment at t = 0 is not discounted.

steps.answer: Negative NPV → reject at a 16% discount rate
steps.explain: NPV < 0 means the return standard is not met.

cards.front: ₹10,000 is deposited at the start of a year at 6% annual interest. How much is in the account at the end of year 5 if nothing is withdrawn?
cards.explain: This is compounding, the reverse of discounting. Simple interest would give only ₹13,000, a common wrong option.

steps.explain: Interest earns interest each year.
n = 5 years.

cards.front: A company invests ₹10 lakh at the start of year 1 in an energy project giving a constant net cash flow of ₹2 lakh a year for 10 years. It expects an IRR of at least 26%. Does the project meet this, and what is its IRR?
cards.back: No. NPV at 26% ≈ −₹3.07 lakh; the IRR is about 15%.
cards.explain: For equal annual cash flows, the IRR is the rate at which the annuity factor equals investment ÷ annual flow (here 5). A 26% rate gives a 10-year factor of only about 3.47, far short of 5.

steps.explain: At the IRR, 2 × (sum of discount factors) = 10.
Negative NPV, so IRR < 26%: expectation not met.
Sign changes between 15% and 16%.
About 15%, well below the 26% target.

cards.front: An energy-saving retrofit costs ₹1,00,000. It saves 6,000 kWh/year at ₹3/kWh, ₹3,800/year in demand charges and ₹2,000/year in maintenance. Rates stay constant and life is 10 years. Find the NPV at 12%.
cards.back: NPV ≈ +₹34,475, so the retrofit is worthwhile.
cards.explain: All three saving streams are added into one annual net cash flow. With equal annual flows, NPV = −investment + annual saving × sum of discount factors.

steps.explain: kWh saved × energy rate.
Include demand and maintenance savings.

steps.prompt: Sum of 12% discount factors for 10 years.

steps.explain: Positive NPV → accept.

cards.front: 100 fused 60 W incandescent bulbs are replaced by 12 W CFLs instead of new incandescent bulbs, for 4,000 h/year. Energy charge ₹4/kWh; demand charge ₹250/kVA/month (take unity power factor). Find the annual cost saving. Incandescent bulb ₹10 (life 1,000 h), CFL ₹100 (life 4,000 h): find the simple payback.
cards.back: Saving ≈ ₹91,200/year (₹76,800 energy + ₹14,400 demand). Extra lamp cost ₹6,000/year, so payback ≈ 0.066 yr (about 3–4 weeks).
cards.explain: This is the book's short question S-1; the book gives no answer, so this solution assumes unity power factor (kVA = kW) and that each bulb's demand counts every month. Over 4,000 h one CFL replaces four incandescent bulbs, so the extra outlay is only ₹100 − ₹40 per point.

steps.explain: Saving per lamp is 48 W.
kW × hours × tariff.
Demand charge is per kVA per month.
Compare against the alternative of buying new incandescent bulbs.
Capital (extra cost) ÷ annual net saving.

cards.front: What is a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)?
cards.back: A hierarchical breakdown of a complex project into smaller, manageable tasks or work packages that can be scheduled, costed and assigned.
cards.explain: The WBS is the basis for estimating time and cost and for building network diagrams. The lowest level should be a work package that one person or team can own.

cards.front: What is the main limitation of a Gantt chart?
cards.back: It does not clearly show logical dependencies between activities, so it cannot identify the critical path.
cards.explain: Gantt (bar) charts show each activity's start, duration and finish against a calendar, which makes them good for communicating progress. Network methods (CPM/PERT) are needed to analyse dependencies and float.

cards.front: How does CPM differ from PERT?
cards.back: CPM is deterministic: each activity has one fixed duration, and the method is often used for time-cost trade-offs. PERT is probabilistic: it uses three time estimates per activity, te = (a + 4m + b) ÷ 6, with variance ((b − a)/6)².
cards.explain: PERT suits R&D or new projects where durations are uncertain. It gives the probability of finishing by a target date. CPM suits repetitive projects such as construction where durations are well known. Both identify the critical path.

cards.front: What is the critical path, and which common statement about it is false?
cards.back: The critical path is the longest-duration path through the network. Its length is the minimum time needed to complete the project, and its activities have zero float. False statement: 'it is the maximum time required to complete the project'.
cards.explain: Any delay to a critical activity delays the whole project, so management attention goes there. There can be more than one critical path, and the critical path can shift as activities progress.

cards.front: How is slack (float) of an activity calculated? Is an activity with ES = 8 and LS = 10 critical?
cards.back: Slack = LS − ES = LF − EF. Here slack = 10 − 8 = 2 days, so the activity is NOT critical (critical activities have zero slack).
cards.explain: Example: LS = 8, LF = 12, EF = 9 → slack = LF − EF = 12 − 9 = 3 weeks. The forward pass gives ES/EF (take the maximum of predecessors' EF); the backward pass gives LS/LF (take the minimum of successors' LS).

cards.front: Why is a dummy activity used in a project network (activity-on-arrow) diagram?
cards.back: To show a logical dependency, or to keep two activities that share the same start and end nodes distinct. A dummy has zero duration and uses no resources.
cards.explain: Dummies are drawn as dashed arrows. They only preserve correct precedence logic; they do not change the project duration.

cards.front: Activities (duration in weeks; predecessors): A 4 (–), B 6 (–), C 3 (A), D 5 (A), E 4 (B, C), F 2 (D, E). Find ES, EF, LS, LF and slack for each activity, the critical path, and the project duration.
cards.back: Critical path A–C–E–F, duration 13 weeks. Slack: B = 1 week, D = 2 weeks; all others 0.
cards.explain: The forward pass gives the earliest times (take the maximum EF of predecessors). The backward pass from the project end gives the latest times (take the minimum LS of successors). Activities with zero slack form the critical path, the longest path through the network.

steps.prompt: Forward pass for A, B, C, D.
steps.answer: A: ES 0, EF 4; B: ES 0, EF 6; C: ES 4, EF 7; D: ES 4, EF 9
steps.explain: EF = ES + duration; ES = maximum EF of predecessors.

steps.prompt: Forward pass for E and F.
steps.answer: E: ES = max(6, 7) = 7, EF 11; F: ES = max(9, 11) = 11, EF 13 → project = 13 weeks
steps.explain: Project duration = EF of the last activity.

steps.answer: F: LF 13, LS 11; E: LF 11, LS 7; D: LF 11, LS 6; C: LF 7, LS 4; B: LF 7, LS 1; A: LF = min(4, 6) = 4, LS 0
steps.explain: LS = LF − duration; LF = minimum LS of successors.

steps.prompt: Find slack and the critical path.
steps.answer: Slack (LS − ES): A 0, B 1, C 0, D 2, E 0, F 0 → critical path A–C–E–F = 4+3+4+2 = 13 weeks
steps.explain: Zero-slack activities are critical.

cards.source: BEE 2025 P1 L1; BEE 2024 P1 L5 (modified)

cards.front: PERT time estimates in weeks (optimistic a, most likely m, pessimistic b): A (start) 2-4-6; B (after A) 3-5-13; C (start) 4-6-8; D (after C) 2-3-4; E (after B and D) 1-2-3. Find the expected time of each activity, the critical path, the expected project duration, and its standard deviation.
cards.back: te: A 4, B 6, C 6, D 3, E 2. Critical path A–B–E = 12 weeks; σ ≈ 1.83 weeks.
cards.explain: PERT uses a beta-distribution approximation: te = (a + 4m + b)/6 and variance = ((b − a)/6)². Add up the variances along the critical path and take the square root to get the project's standard deviation, which is used to estimate the probability of meeting a deadline.

steps.explain: The critical path is the longest path.
Add variances (not standard deviations), then take the square root.

cards.front: How does the BEE book define a project, and why is a project 'temporary' and 'unique'?
cards.back: A 'temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product or service'. Temporary because it has a definite beginning and end; unique because its output differs in some distinguishing way from similar products or services.
cards.explain: The book's example is designing, installing and commissioning a cogeneration system in an industry. A project manager oversees the contractors and manages the schedule and budget.

cards.front: What is the objective of project management?
cards.back: To optimise project cost, time and quality.
cards.explain: Project management principles and techniques help finish projects on schedule, within budget and to specification, while supporting other organisational goals such as productivity, quality and cost-effectiveness.

cards.front: Name the six steps of the Project Development Cycle (PDC).
cards.back: 1) Project identification and screening, 2) Technical design, 3) Financing, 4) Contracting, 5) Implementation, 6) Performance monitoring.
cards.explain: The chapter is organised around these steps. Energy-related projects are noted as generally low-risk, both in the means of achieving change and in its result.

cards.front: How do internal and external identification of energy-saving projects differ?
cards.back: Internal: the facility manager identifies opportunities during day-to-day energy management or from detailed audits. External: systematic audits by a reputable energy consultant, ESCO or industry organisation.
cards.explain: Both routes feed the first step of the project development cycle, after which the opportunities are screened and ranked.

cards.front: What criteria should be used to screen and rank energy-saving project opportunities?
cards.back: Economic feasibility (IRR, NPV, cash flow, average payback); sustainability of savings over equipment life; ease of quantifying, monitoring and verifying savings; availability of technology and ease of adapting it to Indian conditions; other environmental and social benefits (e.g. lower GHG and SO₂ emissions).
cards.explain: Screening ensures that limited capital goes to projects whose savings are real, lasting and measurable, not just economically attractive on paper.

cards.front: What must a technical feasibility study for an energy project identify?
cards.back: Proposed technologies and measures; supply chain for products and materials; special technical difficulties and skills needed; preliminary designs with schematics, manufacturer details and capital cost estimates; and an organisational and management plan with timetable, staffing, training and logistics.
cards.explain: A sound technical feasibility study is what makes the project a viable investment in the eyes of management and lenders.

cards.front: Which internal sources of project funds does the BEE book list, and when may the revenue budget be used?
cards.back: Direct cash from company reserves, the revenue budget (if payback is less than one year), and new share capital.
cards.explain: Low-cost measures, treated as mini-projects, should get top priority, and the present system should be running efficiently before money is spent. Very short-payback measures can be funded from the operating (revenue) budget instead of capital.

cards.front: List the external sources of funds for an energy project.
cards.back: Bank loans, leasing arrangements, payment by savings (a deal with the equipment supplier), energy services contracts, and private finance initiatives.
cards.explain: Lenders such as banks or national development banks will want, besides company assets and credit lines, a pro forma financial worksheet showing project cash flows, NPV and IRR.

cards.front: What good practices does the BEE book recommend for managing contracts in a project?
cards.back: Ensure every contractor is competent (one weak link can delay all); make contractors and suppliers prepare realistic, detailed resource and time plans matching the project plan; impose (graduated) penalties and offer incentives; help them with genuine problems as partners; keep the right to off-load contracts in time if delays are expected.
cards.explain: A substantial part of most projects is done through contracts, so contract management is critical to successful implementation.

cards.front: In a traditional (fixed-price or lump-sum) contract, who carries the risk, and when is it appropriate?
cards.back: The contractor takes the risk of unforeseen problems in exchange for a larger profit. It suits dealing with unknown vendors or work the project manager expects to be risky.
cards.explain: All specifications are given to the contractor, who buys and installs equipment at a fixed price or at cost plus a mark-up.

cards.front: What are 'extended technical guarantee/service' and 'extended financing terms' contracts?
cards.back: Extended guarantee/service: extended performance guarantees on selected equipment and/or service and maintenance agreements. Extended financing: the contractor offers an extended lease or other financing with payments based on expected savings.
cards.explain: These sit between a traditional contract and full performance contracts, in which savings themselves are guaranteed or shared.

cards.front: In a shared savings performance contract (as described in the project management chapter), who provides finance and how is the contractor paid?
cards.back: The contractor provides the financing and is paid an agreed fraction of actual savings as they are achieved; this payment pays down the debt cost of equipment and services.
cards.explain: In a guaranteed saving performance contract, all or part of the savings is guaranteed by the contractor, and all or part of the cost of equipment and services is paid down out of savings as they are achieved.

cards.front: Why is a performance monitoring system needed, and what three principles should it follow?
cards.back: It helps anticipate deviations from the plan, analyse emerging problems and take corrective action. It should focus sharply on critical aspects, emphasise physical milestones rather than financial targets, and be kept simple.
cards.explain: The exam likes the trap that monitoring should stress financial targets – the book says physical milestones.

cards.front: Once a project is commissioned, how is a periodic performance review useful?
cards.back: It shows how realistic the project's assumptions were, gives a documented log of experience for future decisions, suggests corrective action from actual performance, and helps uncover judgmental biases.
cards.explain: The review compares actual with projected performance and acts as a feedback device.

cards.front: When is the Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) developed relative to other planning steps, and how can it be displayed?
cards.back: Before dependencies are identified and activity durations estimated; it is used to identify tasks before building Gantt charts and CPM/PERT networks. It can be shown as a tree, list or table.
cards.explain: The level of breakdown depends on the type of project and the management style. In budgeting, costs are estimated at the work-package level and rolled up to higher WBS levels.

cards.front: Who developed the Gantt chart, what was an early application, and what form does it take?
cards.back: Henry Gantt, during the era of scientific management; an early use was tracking shipbuilding projects. It is a horizontal bar chart with time on the horizontal axis.
cards.explain: Each task is a bar whose length shows its duration; rows show start and end dates. Time units are typically weeks or months.

cards.front: How can a basic Gantt chart be enhanced to show more information?
cards.back: A vertical line marking the present date (showing tasks running together and simultaneous resource needs); shading bars as progress is made; link lines or colour codes for dependencies; resource allocation per task; milestones.
cards.explain: The basic chart's weakness is that it does not show logical dependencies well; network diagrams show logic clearly but have no time-scale axis.

cards.front: Define activity, event and network in project networking.
cards.back: Activity: a task required by the project that uses resources and consumes time. Event: the beginning or ending point of one or more activities (a node). Network: the combination of all project activities and events.
cards.explain: A project network shows graphically which tasks must precede or follow others, making it a powerful planning and control tool.

cards.front: How do activity-on-arrow (AOA) and activity-on-node (AON) networks differ? Which is used in software packages?
cards.back: AOA: activities are arrows joined at event nodes (circles). AON: activities are nodes, with dependencies drawn as arrows between them. AON is used in project management software.
cards.explain: In AOA a dashed dummy activity is needed when two activities would share the same start and end events, to show the correct dependency. The CPM network was originally developed as AON.

cards.front: Who developed the Critical Path Method (CPM), when, and for what purpose?
cards.back: DuPont, in 1957, to manage shutting down chemical plants for maintenance and restarting them.
cards.explain: CPM gives a graphical view of the project, predicts the time required, and shows which activities are critical to the schedule and which are not.

cards.front: List the six steps in CPM project planning.
cards.back: 1) Specify individual activities, 2) determine their sequence, 3) draw the network diagram, 4) estimate each activity's completion time, 5) identify the critical path (longest path), 6) update the diagram as the project progresses.
cards.explain: The activity list comes from the WBS, and the project should have a single start and a single finish activity. Updating can reveal a new critical path.

cards.front: True or false: CPM is a probabilistic model that uses three time estimates for each activity.
cards.back: False. CPM is deterministic and uses one fixed time per activity; PERT is the probabilistic model with three estimates.
cards.explain: CPM time estimates come from past experience or knowledgeable people and ignore variation. PERT uses optimistic, most likely and pessimistic times.

cards.front: Define ES, EF, LS and LF, and state the formulas linking them.
cards.back: ES: earliest start once predecessors finish. EF = ES + t. LF: latest finish without delaying the project. LS = LF − t.
cards.explain: ES and EF come from a forward pass from the start; LS and LF from a backward pass from the finish. Slack = LS − ES = LF − EF; on the critical path ES = LS and EF = LF.

cards.front: State the earliest-start rule (forward pass) and the latest-finish rule (backward pass) at a node.
cards.back: Earliest start of an activity leaving a node = the LARGEST EF of all activities entering it. Latest finish of an activity entering a node = the SMALLEST LS of all activities leaving it.
cards.explain: Mixing up largest and smallest is a classic error. The forward pass waits for the slowest predecessor; the backward pass must not delay the earliest-needed successor.

cards.front: What is project crashing, and where should resources be added or saved?
cards.back: Crashing is shortening the project by adding resources to critical-path activities. To speed up, add resources only to critical activities; to save resources, lengthen only non-critical activities, within their float.
cards.explain: Shortening a non-critical activity does not shorten the project, because the critical path sets the minimum completion time.

cards.front: When and for what project was PERT developed, and what kind of model is it?
cards.back: In the late 1950s for the US Navy's Polaris project, which had thousands of contractors. It is a probabilistic network model that allows for randomness in activity times.
cards.explain: PERT steps are like CPM except for time estimation: it uses optimistic, most likely and pessimistic times and assumes a beta distribution for them.

cards.front: Give the PERT formulas for expected time, standard deviation and variance of an activity. How is the project's variance found?
cards.back: Tₑ = (Tₒ + 4Tₘ + Tₚ)/6; σ = (Tₚ − Tₒ)/6; V = σ². Project variance = sum of the variances of the activities on the critical path.
cards.explain: Assuming the critical-path duration is normally distributed (reasonable when it has enough activities), this variance gives the probability of finishing by a given date.

cards.front: What information does PERT provide?
cards.back: Expected project completion time; probability of completion before a specified date; the critical activities; activities with slack that can lend resources to critical ones; and activity start and end dates.
cards.explain: The PERT chart is not final; estimated times are replaced by actual times as the project unfolds, and the chart is revised if delays need extra resources.

cards.front: What are the limitations of PERT, and why does it tend to underestimate project duration?
cards.back: Time estimates are subjective; the real distribution may not be beta; and PERT assumes the project completion time distribution equals that of the critical path. Since other paths can become critical if delayed, PERT consistently underestimates the expected completion time.
cards.explain: Near-critical paths with high variance can end up longer than the expected critical path, which a single-path calculation ignores.

cards.front: Before implementing a project, what should top management identify, and how should each be handled?
cards.back: Strengths and weaknesses (internal forces) and opportunities and threats (external forces). Strengths and opportunities should be exploited; weaknesses and threats must be overcome.
cards.explain: Monitoring should be in place before implementation starts, appear on the work plan and involve all stakeholders. The implementation plan should include a schedule or timeline, such as the book's boiler milestones from component delivery to testing and commissioning.

cards.front: What are the three categories of project costs? Give an example of each.
cards.back: Human resource costs (salaries and benefits of project staff); administrative costs (everyday support costs such as local telephone, copier paper, heating, support staff); resource costs (materials, equipment leases, long-distance calls, travel – specific to the project).
cards.explain: The budget is used throughout the project to compare money actually spent with estimates for each activity.

cards.front: Distinguish direct and indirect project costs, with examples.
cards.back: Direct costs can be attributed directly to project work, e.g. team salaries, equipment rentals, team training. Indirect costs are not specific to the project, e.g. lease of a building shared with other staff, or administrative/procurement staff who help but have no assigned tasks.
cards.explain: Each organisation has its own way of accounting for indirect costs; the finance or accounts department advises how to include them in the budget.

cards.front: What is the difference between analogous estimating and bottom-up estimating?
cards.back: Analogous: estimate based on the actual costs of previous similar projects of comparable size and scope. Bottom-up: estimate each task individually and add them up.
cards.explain: Bottom-up estimating uses the WBS work packages. Inadequate budget is one reason projects fail; the finance manager usually sets the cost and the project manager negotiates within it.

cards.front: What is project construction (commissioning), and to which projects does it apply?
cards.back: The process of assuring that all systems and components are designed, installed, tested, operated and maintained to the user's operational requirements. It applies to new projects and to existing units being expanded, renovated or revamped.
cards.explain: Commissioning checks, inspects and tests every component from individual instruments up to subsystems and systems, and spans design, procurement, construction, assembly and handover, sometimes including assisted operation.

cards.front: Give the general M&V equation for energy savings. What does the adjustments term do, and what conditions does it usually cover?
cards.back: Energy savings = Base-year energy use − Post-retrofit energy use ± Adjustments. Adjustments bring both periods to the same conditions, commonly weather, occupancy, plant throughput and related equipment operation.
cards.explain: Adjustments come from identifiable physical facts and can be routine (weather) or as needed (e.g. a second shift added). M&V is central when contract payments or guarantees depend on the size of savings.

cards.front: An activity has an optimistic time of 15 days, most likely 18 days and pessimistic 27 days. Find its PERT expected time, standard deviation and variance.
cards.back: Tₑ = 19 days; σ = 2 days; V = 4 days².
cards.explain: The expected time is pulled above the most likely value because the pessimistic estimate is far from it. (A simpler book question with 10, 15, 20 days gives exactly 15 days, because the estimates are symmetric.)

steps.explain: Weighted average for a beta distribution.
Not the simple average (20) or the most likely (18).
One-sixth of the range.
Variances add along a path; standard deviations do not.

cards.front: CPM, weeks (duration; predecessors): A 5 (–), B 6 (–), C 4 (A), D 3 (A), E 1 (A), F 4 (E), G 14 (D, F), H 12 (B, C), I 2 (G, H). Find ES/EF, LS/LF, slack, the critical path and the project duration.
cards.back: Critical path A–E–F–G–I, 26 weeks. Slack: B 6, C 3, D 2, H 3; A, E, F, G, I have zero slack.
cards.explain: The activity durations add up to 51 weeks, but parallel work (e.g. A and B together) cuts the project to 26 weeks. Non-critical activities can be delayed up to their slack without delaying completion.

steps.prompt: Forward pass (EF = ES + t; ES = largest EF of predecessors).
steps.explain: The project finishes at EF of I = 26 weeks.

steps.prompt: Backward pass (LS = LF − t; LF = smallest LS of successors).
steps.explain: Start from LF = 26 for the last activity.
E.g. C: 8 − 5 = 3 weeks.
The zero-slack activities form the longest path.

cards.front: PERT, expected times in days (predecessors): a 20 (–), b 20 (–), c 10 (–), d 15 (a), e 10 (b, c), f 14 (b, c), g 4 (b, c), h 11 (c), i 18 (g, h), j 8 (d, e). Find ES/EF, LS/LF, slack and the critical path.
cards.back: Critical path a–d–j, 43 days. Slack: b 1, c 4, e 5, f 9, g 1, h 4, i 1; a, d, j zero.
cards.explain: Once expected times are found from the three estimates, the PERT network is worked exactly like CPM. Path b–g–i (42 days) has only 1 day of slack, so it could easily become critical if b, g or i slips.

steps.explain: Project end = latest EF = 43 (j); f and i also end the project.
LF = smallest LS of successors.
Zero slack marks critical activities.
The longest path through the network.

cards.front: Expected times in weeks (predecessors): A 7 (–), B 9 (A), C 12 (A), D 2 (B), E 10 (D, C), F 3 (C), G 2 (F), H 8 (E, G), I 2 (H). List all paths with their durations and identify the critical path.
cards.back: A–B–D–E–H–I = 38; A–C–E–H–I = 39; A–C–F–G–H–I = 34. Critical path A–C–E–H–I, 39 weeks.
cards.explain: Listing every start-to-finish path and adding durations is a quick way to find the critical path in small networks. The longest path sets the minimum project time.

steps.prompt: Trace the paths from A to I.
steps.explain: E needs both D and C; H needs both E and G, so three routes reach I.
Sum of expected times.
Sum of expected times.
Sum of expected times.
Longest path = expected project duration.

cards.front: What principle is energy Monitoring & Targeting (M&T) based on?
cards.back: 'You can't manage what you don't measure.' Energy use is related to its driver (production, degree-days), and actual consumption is compared with expected consumption so that deviations can be found and acted on.
cards.explain: The M&T elements are recording (measuring), analysing (correlating with production), comparing (against a baseline or target), setting targets, monitoring, reporting and controlling. M&T turns energy from an overhead into a managed variable cost.

cards.front: How is fixed (non-production) energy consumption found from data?
cards.back: Plot energy (y) against production (x) on an XY scatter chart and fit E = m·P + c. The intercept c is the fixed energy consumption, and the slope m is the variable energy per unit of production.
cards.explain: Fixed energy (lighting, HVAC, idle running, losses) is used regardless of output. That is why SEC rises at low capacity utilisation. Reducing c is often the cheapest saving.

cards.front: Why is an energy baseline established in M&T?
cards.back: To fix a reference point (expected energy for a given production) against which later energy performance improvements are measured.
cards.explain: The baseline is usually a regression E = mP + c from a representative period before the energy-saving measures. The baseline and energy performance indicators are core requirements of ISO 50001 and of M&V for ESCO contracts.

cards.front: What is CUSUM, and how do you interpret its graph?
cards.back: CUSUM = cumulative sum of (actual − predicted) energy, period by period. A falling line means savings (actual below predicted). A rising line means excess consumption. A horizontal line means actual = predicted (no change in performance).
cards.explain: Predicted energy comes from the baseline equation, e.g. E = 2.2·P + 10,000. The final CUSUM value gives the total savings (if negative) over the period. Changes in slope mark when performance changed, for example when a measure was implemented or a fault appeared.
cards.source: BEE 2025 P1 Q43, L4; BEE 2024 P1 L1

cards.front: The baseline relationship for a plant is E = 120·P + 20,000 (E in kWh, P in tonnes). After an energy-saving programme, the monthly data (production in t / actual energy in kWh) are: Apr 400/66,000; May 420/70,000; Jun 380/63,000; Jul 450/73,500; Aug 410/67,000; Sep 390/64,500. Build the CUSUM table and find the total savings.
cards.back: CUSUM after six months = −10,000 kWh, i.e. 10,000 kWh saved.
cards.explain: For each month, predicted energy comes from the baseline equation. The monthly difference (actual − predicted) is added up cumulatively. A steadily falling CUSUM line confirms sustained savings; a flat stretch would mean performance had returned to baseline.

steps.explain: Use the baseline regression.
Negative = consumed less than expected.
CUSUMₙ = CUSUMₙ₋₁ + (Eₐ − Eₚ).

steps.answer: Total savings over 6 months = 10,000 kWh; the CUSUM line slopes down throughout.
steps.explain: A downward slope means savings; a horizontal line means no change.

cards.source: BEE 2025 P1 L4; BEE 2024 P1 L1 (modified)

cards.front: Why is an energy audit alone not enough to keep control of a plant's energy consumption?
