cards.back: An audit gives only a 'picture' of past consumption. A monitoring programme is needed to keep control, and it must be paired with targeting (setting targets and making planned improvements) to actually improve performance.
cards.explain: The book stresses that monitoring by itself only records consumption and so has limited value. Improvement comes when targets are set and actual use is compared against them, which is why the technique is always 'Monitoring and Targeting' together.

cards.front: By what typical percentage have M&T programmes reduced annual energy costs in industry?
cards.back: Typically 5–15% of annual energy costs.
cards.explain: BEE Book 1 cites typical reductions in annual energy costs of 5 to 15% across various industrial sectors from M&T programmes. The savings come mainly from better management control rather than capital investment.

cards.front: Under M&T, how are plant utilities such as fuel, steam, compressed air, water and electricity treated?
cards.back: As controllable resources, managed the same way as raw materials, finished-product inventory, personnel and capital.
cards.explain: M&T is primarily a management technique that uses energy information to eliminate waste, reduce and control current energy use and improve operating procedures. It combines the principles of energy use and statistics, so energy stops being treated as a fixed overhead.

cards.front: Distinguish 'monitoring' from 'targeting' as defined in the BEE guide book.
cards.back: Monitoring establishes the existing pattern of energy consumption and explains deviations from it. Targeting identifies a desirable consumption level and works towards achieving it.
cards.explain: Targets are based on historical data (average or best) collected during monitoring, and on benchmarking against similar organisations. Monitoring keeps the existing pattern under control; targeting moves it to a better level.

cards.front: What are Energy Account Centres (EACs), and who should be accountable for them?
cards.back: EACs are departments, processes or cost centres set up for energy accounting before starting M&T. The operational manager responsible for each EAC is accountable for its energy consumption.
cards.explain: Setting up EACs is the first organisational step in M&T. It assigns energy use to the people who control it, so variances can be traced to an area and to a manager.

cards.front: M&T schemes are classified by number of sites and level of metering. Name the four types and how EACs are formed in each.
cards.back: 1) Single site, central utility metering: treat as one EAC. 2) Single site with sub-metering: split into several EACs. 3) Multi-site, central metering at each site: each site is a separate EAC. 4) Multi-site with sub-metering: divide each site into several EACs.
cards.explain: The level of metering decides how finely energy can be allocated. Sub-metering is what allows a site to be broken into several accountable centres.

cards.front: List the six key elements of a Monitoring & Targeting system.
cards.back: Recording, Analysing & comparing, Setting targets, Monitoring, Reporting, and Controlling.
cards.explain: Recording collects reliable energy data for each EAC. Analysing relates it to output to get standard performance. Targets improve on that standard. Monitoring compares actual use with target. Reporting tells management about variances, and Controlling corrects them.

cards.front: How is 'standard energy performance' of an EAC established, and what if historical data does not exist?
cards.back: By regression analysis relating energy use to a measured output (e.g. production) over 12–24 months of historical data. If no data exists, an energy audit is done to establish it.
cards.explain: Standard energy performance is the baseline for judging future performance and can serve as the initial target. Achievable targets are then set to improve on it, based on external benchmarking or the organisation's own best (least) historical consumption.

cards.front: Name five things an M&T system particularly involves.
cards.back: Checking the accuracy of energy invoices; allocating energy costs to departments (EACs); determining energy performance/efficiency; recording energy use so efficiency projects can be checked for results; highlighting performance problems in equipment or systems.
cards.explain: These are the routine functions that make M&T a management tool. Invoice checking and cost allocation are accounting tasks; performance tracking and fault highlighting drive technical action.

cards.front: Besides lower energy cost, name five benefits of M&T.
cards.back: Any five: explain increases or decreases in energy use; show trends (weekly, seasonal, operational); improve energy budgeting against production plans; see how the organisation reacted to past changes; predict future use when planning changes; diagnose specific areas of waste; develop performance targets for energy action plans; manage energy instead of accepting it as a fixed cost.
cards.explain: The ultimate goal of M&T is reducing energy cost through better efficiency and management control. The other benefits mostly come from having a reliable energy–production relationship that can be used to explain, predict and plan.

cards.front: At what four levels can energy information be obtained, and from what sources?
cards.back: Plant level: financial accounting systems (utilities cost centre). Plant department level: comparative data for similar facilities, service-entrance meter readings. System level (e.g. compressor house): sub-metering. Equipment level: nameplate data, run-time and schedules, sub-meters on specific equipment.
cards.explain: All these data can be processed to yield information about facility performance. The finer the level, the more useful the data is for finding where energy is wasted.

cards.front: What standard conversion factors to kcal does Table 9.1 use for electricity, HSD, furnace oil and LPG?
cards.back: Electricity 860 kcal/kWh; HSD 10,500 kcal/kg; furnace oil 10,200 kcal/kg; LPG 12,000 kcal/kg.
cards.explain: For the annual-consumption analysis, all energy is first converted to a common unit (usually kcal). The data is then tabulated and shown as percentage breakdowns and pie charts of energy share and cost share.

cards.front: What is the main limitation of the annual energy consumption percentage-breakdown (pie chart) analysis?
cards.back: It makes no allowance for variable factors that influence energy use (e.g. production, climatic zone or occupancy of buildings), so it cannot be used to compare different organisations.
cards.explain: The analysis is quick and shows energy and cost breakdown and trends. In the book's example, furnace oil was 62% of energy but 66% of cost, while electricity was 18% of energy but 20% of cost. It still says nothing about why consumption changed.

cards.front: What does a time-dependent energy analysis (energy plotted against month) show, and what are its limitations?
cards.back: It shows general trends, seasonal patterns and base load, and lets exceptions be spotted immediately. But it cannot explain why trends occur, and it is only a comparative tool, not an absolute one.
cards.explain: In the book's example, the base load was about 10,500 kWh/month, and a rise in Nov–Jan pointed to loss of control over electricity use. Finding the reason needs further analysis, such as relating energy to production. A bar chart of current year vs previous year has the same weakness: it does not clearly show trends.

cards.front: What is a norm chart, and what is it good for?
cards.back: A sequential plot of actual energy consumption overlaid on target consumption. It has little analytical value but is useful for highlighting exceptions and communicating them to managers.
cards.explain: Because a norm chart is a simple historical record, senior and operational managers find it easy to understand. It is a communication tool rather than a diagnostic one.

cards.front: In a deviance chart, how is a month plotted when actual consumption exceeds target, and why are limit lines added?
cards.back: Deviance = actual − target, so higher-than-target use plots as a positive value and lower use as negative. Upper and lower limit lines separate normal variation from serious deviations.
cards.explain: Deviance charts are particularly good at highlighting problems so remedial action can be taken, and they can trigger detailed exception reports.

cards.front: In a chart of monthly SEC together with production, the lowest SEC occurred in the month of record production. What does this indicate?
cards.back: That the plant has fixed energy consumption, i.e. energy used regardless of production level, which is spread over more output when production is high.
cards.explain: SEC alone (Figure 9.7) showed only a trend. Adding production (Figure 9.8) made the cause clear. Fixed consumption means SEC is not constant and falls as output rises, which is why energy vs production regression is preferred to SEC alone.

cards.front: What is a Moving Annual Total chart and what are its advantages?
cards.back: Each point is the sum of the previous 12 months of data, so each point covers the full range of seasons and holidays. It also smooths out errors in the timing of meter readings.
cards.explain: If energy and production Moving Annual Totals track each other, there is no cause for alarm. Any divergence of the energy line is an early warning of waste, or confirmation that efficiency measures are working.

cards.front: How does linear regression analysis overcome the limitation of time-dependent analysis? Give two typical variable pairs.
cards.back: It removes the 'time' element and focuses on the variables that influence energy use. Typical pairs: furnace oil vs units of production; electricity vs production; water vs production; lighting electricity vs hours of occupancy.
cards.explain: Regression establishes standard equations for energy consumption, often from data that would otherwise be meaningless. Table 9.4 gives influencing factors: air volume delivered for compressors, steam generated for boilers, production volume for process steam.

cards.front: True or false: if a regression analysis shows no significant relationship between energy and a variable, then no relationship exists.
cards.back: False. Absence of a significant relationship does not necessarily mean none exists. The result depends on the quantity and quality of data and on the variables chosen.
cards.explain: The book warns that regression depends heavily on data quality and should be treated with care. Poor metering, too few points or a wrong choice of variable can all hide a real relationship.

cards.front: In an energy vs production XY scatter diagram, what does a low degree of scatter indicate? What does a poor fit indicate when a relationship is known to exist?
cards.back: Low scatter = good fit. A poor fit where a relationship should exist = poor level of control, and hence potential for energy savings.
cards.explain: The scatter diagram is the first step in building the energy–production relationship. Wide scatter means the same production is being made with very different amounts of energy, which points to poor operational control.

cards.front: In the energy–production equation y = c + mx, what do y, x, c and m represent?
cards.back: y = energy consumed in the period (dependent variable); x = production in the same period (independent variable); c = intercept on the y-axis, i.e. fixed (base-load) energy; m = slope, i.e. energy per unit of production.
cards.explain: Energy for the period = c + m × production. The best-fit line is found by least squares (minimising the sum of squared distances of points from the line). Once established, it predicts future consumption and serves as the standard for targets and CUSUM.

cards.front: Write the two 'normal equations' used to find c and m for the best-fit line y = c + mx through n data points.
cards.back: Σy = n·c + m·Σx and Σxy = c·Σx + m·Σx².
cards.explain: These come from the least-squares fit. You tabulate x, y, x² and xy, sum each column and solve the two simultaneous equations for c (intercept) and m (slope).

cards.front: Example 9.1 – A foundry's 9 months of data (production x t/month; energy y toe/month): (380,340), (440,340), (460,380), (520,380), (320,300), (520,400), (240,280), (620,424), (600,420). Find the best-fit line y = c + mx.
cards.explain: Solving the normal equations gives the energy–production relationship for the foundry furnace. The intercept, 180 toe/month, is the theoretical base load used regardless of production; each extra tonne costs about 0.4 toe.

steps.prompt: Tabulate and sum x, y, x² and xy for the 9 months.
steps.explain: These sums are all the normal equations need.
Σy = nc + mΣx; Σxy = cΣx + mΣx².

steps.prompt: Eliminate c and solve for m.
steps.explain: Substitute c from the first equation into the second.

steps.prompt: Find c and write the line.
steps.explain: The book rounds to E = 0.4P + 180, with a theoretical furnace base load of 180 toe/month.

cards.front: What does the Pearson correlation coefficient (r) tell you in M&T, and what is its formula?
cards.back: How well the best-fit line matches the data, i.e. the reliability of the line (1 = 100% correlation). r = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) / √[Σ(x−x̄)² · Σ(y−ȳ)²].
cards.explain: Scattered data can still give a regression equation that is meaningless, so r is checked before the equation is used for targets. The book treats r as ranging from 0 to 1. The value is compared with a minimum acceptable r for the number of data points.

cards.front: For the foundry data of Example 9.1 (x̄ = 455.56 t, ȳ = 362.67 toe), Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) = 50,346.67, Σ(x−x̄)² = 127,022.22 and Σ(y−ȳ)² = 20,832. Find the correlation coefficient and judge it.
cards.back: r = 50,346.67 / √(127,022.22 × 20,832) ≈ 0.98. This is far above the minimum (~0.8 for 9–10 samples), so the fit is very good.
cards.explain: An r of 0.98 means production explains energy use almost completely, so the equation E = 0.4P + 180 is reliable for targeting and CUSUM.

steps.prompt: Multiply the two sums of squares.
steps.explain: This is the denominator before the square root.
The denominator normalises the covariance term.
Close to 1 means a strong linear relationship.

steps.answer: Minimum r for 10 samples is 0.767; 0.98 exceeds it comfortably.
steps.explain: The book concludes the correlation is very good.

cards.front: Per Table 9.5, what is the minimum acceptable correlation coefficient for 10, 20 and 50 data samples?
cards.explain: The more data points you have, the lower the r needed to show a real relationship. Other values: 15 → 0.641, 25 → 0.506, 30 → 0.464, 40 → 0.402.

cards.front: What equation describes multi-variable analysis of energy consumption, and how should it be solved?
cards.back: y = c + m₁x₁ + m₂x₂ + … + mₙxₙ, where x₁…xₙ are the variables influencing y. It is hard to solve by hand, so specialist computer software is advised.
cards.explain: Energy often depends on several drivers at once (e.g. production and climate). Single-variable analysis uses one independent variable; multi-variable analysis fits a separate coefficient for each driver.

cards.front: Why are CUSUM charts particularly useful for diagnosing energy problems?
cards.back: Because they identify the date when energy performance changed, which helps pin-point the problem so its root cause can be analysed.
cards.explain: CUSUM is the Cumulative Sum of differences between actual and baseline (standard) consumption. The baseline equation is derived from data collected before any intervention, and the CUSUM line changes slope at the moment something changes.

cards.front: List the steps of CUSUM analysis used in the foundry heat-recovery example.
cards.back: 1) Plot energy vs production for the baseline months; 2) draw the best-fit line; 3) derive its equation; 4) calculate standard (predicted) consumption for each month; 5) find actual − standard; 6) compute the cumulative sum; 7) plot CUSUM vs time; 8) estimate savings.
cards.explain: These eight steps (asked as 'list at least 5 steps' in the exam) turn raw monthly data into a savings estimate. Only the pre-intervention months are used to build the baseline equation.

cards.front: On a CUSUM chart (actual − predicted), what does a horizontal line, a rising line and a falling line each mean?
cards.back: Horizontal: actual and calculated consumption are the same. Rising: performance is worse than standard (specific energy consumption going up). Falling: energy savings are being made.
cards.explain: A typical CUSUM line oscillates around zero until something changes the consumption pattern, such as an energy saving measure (line falls) or poor control, housekeeping or maintenance (line rises). Site knowledge is needed to link each change of direction to an event.

cards.front: A foundry furnace (baseline E = 0.4P + 180 toe) got heat recovery during month 9. Months 10–18 (E actual, P t): (400,560), (360,440), (320,360), (340,420), (372,480), (380,540), (280,280), (280,260), (380,500). CUSUM at month 9 is +4. Find the savings.
cards.back: CUSUM goes +4 (m9) → 0 → +4 (m11) → 0 → −8 → −8 → −24 → −36 → −40 → −40 (m18). Savings ≈ 44 toe over the last 7 months (from +4 to −40), almost 2% of energy use.
cards.explain: The CUSUM oscillated around zero for a few months and then fell steadily after month 11. The book reads this as the heat recovery system taking about two months to commission, after which steady savings were achieved. Total savings are the drop in CUSUM from where the trend started.

steps.prompt: Calculate standard consumption E = 0.4P + 180 for months 10–18.
steps.explain: The baseline predicts what the furnace would use without the change.

steps.prompt: Find actual − standard for each month.
steps.explain: Negative means less energy than predicted.
CUSUM is the running total of the differences.

steps.prompt: Read the savings off the CUSUM.
steps.answer: From +4 at month 11 to −40 at month 18 = 44 toe.
steps.explain: The steady downward slope begins after month 11.

steps.answer: Actual use in months 12–18 = 2352 toe; 44/2352 ≈ 1.9%, i.e. almost 2%.
steps.explain: The book quotes 'almost 2% of energy consumption'.

cards.front: Baseline (Jan–Jun 2011): E = 0.5P + 220 toe. Waste heat recovery was installed at end of June. Jul–Dec actual (E toe, P t): (590,760), (605,820), (670,940), (582,750), (512,610), (540,670). Find energy savings and the reduction in SEC.
cards.explain: Every month after installation used less energy than the baseline predicted, so the CUSUM falls steadily. Dividing the total saving by the total production for the same six months gives the average drop in specific energy consumption.

steps.prompt: Compute predicted energy E = 0.5P + 220 for each month.
steps.answer: Jul 600, Aug 630, Sep 690, Oct 595, Nov 525, Dec 555 toe.

steps.explain: All negative: savings every month.
The final CUSUM is the total saving.
Needed to express the saving per tonne.
Saving in toe divided by production in tonnes.

cards.front: A food plant's baseline: energy = 1.8 × production (kg) + 15,000 kWh/month. Measures were taken in June 2010. Jul–Dec (production kg, actual kWh): (62,000, 113,600), (71,000, 139,000), (75,000, 158,000), (59,000, 119,300), (62,000, 123,700), (73,000, 143,600). Use CUSUM to find savings.
cards.explain: This is the book's end-of-chapter exercise L-1, worked here with the baseline it gives. September used more than predicted (CUSUM rises that month), but the six-month cumulative result is a net saving.

steps.answer: E = 1.8P + 15,000 kWh (variable 1.8 kWh/kg plus 15,000 kWh fixed).
steps.explain: Fixed plus production-related energy.
A positive value means a worse month.
Running total of the differences.
The final CUSUM value is the cumulative saving.

cards.front: Measures were implemented before Jan 2011. Production averaged 1000 MT/month in Jan–Jun 2011. Actual vs predicted SEC (kWh/MT): Jan 1203/1121, Feb 1187/1278, Mar 1401/1571, Apr 1450/1550, May 1324/1284, Jun 1233/1233. Use CUSUM to find energy saved.
cards.back: Differences (actual − predicted): +82, −91, −170, −100, +40, 0. CUSUM: +82, −9, −179, −279, −239, −239 kWh/MT. Savings = 239 kWh/MT × 1000 MT ≈ 2,39,000 kWh.
cards.explain: This is the book's end-of-chapter exercise L-2, worked here. Because production is a constant 1000 MT/month, the CUSUM of SEC differences can be multiplied directly by monthly production to get the energy saved.

steps.prompt: Find actual − predicted SEC each month.
steps.explain: Negative means better than predicted.
The running total is the CUSUM.
Each month's SEC difference applies to 1000 MT.

steps.answer: About 2.39 lakh kWh saved in Jan–Jun 2011 (Jan and May were worse than predicted).
steps.explain: The overall CUSUM trend is downward.

cards.front: List the generic features of commercial Energy Management Information System (EMIS) software.
cards.back: A database for large long-term data; recording all utility types from meters and invoices; handling complex tariffs; handling related variables (degree days, production); statistical data analysis; quick reporting; and in advanced packages, an interface with Building Management Systems (BMS) for automatic (e.g. hourly) data capture.
cards.explain: The big advantage is the database, which lets historical data and data from many sources be compared instantly. Under-performing EACs can then be spotted quickly and remedial action taken.

cards.front: True or false: an EMIS computer package can replace the energy manager in an M&T programme.
cards.back: False. Computers are simply tools for storing and analysing large amounts of data quickly; they are not a replacement for the energy manager.
cards.explain: The book is explicit on this point. The software handles data and reports, but interpreting events and starting corrective action stays with people.

cards.front: How often should M&T reports go to operational managers vs senior management, and what is 'reporting by exception'?
cards.back: Operational managers may need weekly reports; senior management may need only a quarterly review. Reporting by exception means generating reports only when energy performance falls outside predetermined limits (very poor or very good).
cards.explain: Monthly reports suit large multi-site organisations, while weekly reports suit complex, high-energy facilities. Too-frequent reporting swamps managers with irrelevant information, which reporting by exception avoids while also cutting everyone's workload.

cards.front: What qualities should energy management reports have to ensure prompt action?
cards.back: Simple; highlight where waste is occurring; published regularly; succinct; in a standard format generated automatically by computer; tailored to the reader's level.
cards.explain: Reports are how action is started in an organisation. A standard automatic format cuts preparation time and makes managers familiar with the information. If the reporting period is too short, though, the system becomes over-complex.

cards.front: Which six greenhouse gases are covered by the Kyoto Protocol?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs) and sulphur hexafluoride (SF₆).
cards.explain: CO₂ is the largest contributor by volume. The fluorinated gases have very high Global Warming Potentials. Emissions are reported in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent (tCO₂e) = mass × GWP.

cards.front: Which greenhouse gas has the longest atmospheric lifetime and very high GWP?
cards.back: Sulphur hexafluoride (SF₆), with an atmospheric lifetime of about 3,200 years and a GWP in the tens of thousands relative to CO₂.
cards.explain: SF₆ is used as an insulating gas in high-voltage switchgear, so leak prevention and recovery matter. PFCs also last thousands of years. CO₂ has no single lifetime, because it is removed by several processes over very different timescales.

cards.front: What causes stratospheric ozone depletion, and what does the ozone layer filter?
cards.back: Mainly chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and other halogenated compounds. The ozone layer absorbs harmful UV-B radiation.
cards.explain: Chlorine released from CFCs by UV light destroys ozone catalytically. The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out CFCs and is phasing out HCFCs, and the Kigali Amendment covers HFCs. Ozone depletion and global warming are separate problems, but some gases contribute to both.
cards.source: BEE 2025 P1 Q8; BEE 2024 P1 Q29

cards.front: What are the basic objectives of sustainable development?
cards.back: Economic security and prosperity, social development and advancement, and environmental sustainability, all three together.
cards.explain: The Brundtland definition: development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Energy efficiency supports all three objectives.

cards.front: What is carbon sequestration?
cards.back: Capturing CO₂ from point sources (e.g. power plants) or the atmosphere and storing it long term, for example in geological formations, oceans, or biomass and soils.
cards.explain: Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage (CCUS) handles point sources. Forests and soils act as natural carbon sinks.

cards.front: How do you convert fuel carbon content to CO₂ emissions?
cards.back: CO₂ (kg) = mass of carbon burnt (kg) × 44/12. Each kg of carbon gives 3.67 kg of CO₂.
cards.explain: The 44/12 comes from molecular weights: CO₂ = 44, C = 12. Example: 1,000 kg of natural gas with 74% carbon → 740 × 3.67 ≈ 2,713 kg CO₂. For electricity, multiply the kWh saved by the grid emission factor, e.g. 1,000 kWh × 0.8 kg/kWh = 800 kg CO₂.
cards.source: BEE 2025 P1 L6; BEE 2024 P1 Q1

cards.front: What are India's updated NDC targets under the Paris Agreement (submitted 2022), and its net-zero year?
cards.back: Reduce the emissions intensity of GDP by 45% by 2030 from the 2005 level; reach about 50% of cumulative installed electric power capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030; net-zero emissions by 2070.
cards.explain: The Paris Agreement (COP21, 2015) aims to keep warming well below 2°C and to pursue 1.5°C, using nationally determined contributions. It followed the Kyoto Protocol (1997), which set binding targets only for developed countries and created the Clean Development Mechanism.

cards.front: A 50 MW coal-fired power plant raises its efficiency from 30% to 33% through renovation and modernisation. Coal GCV is 3,600 kcal/kg, the plant runs 8,000 h/year at full load, and the emission factor is 1.5 kg CO₂ per kg of coal. Find the annual coal saving and the CO₂ avoided.
cards.back: Coal saving ≈ 28,956 t/yr; CO₂ avoided ≈ 43,434 t/yr.
cards.explain: Heat rate (kcal/kWh) = 860 ÷ efficiency, and specific coal consumption = heat rate ÷ GCV. The fall in specific coal consumption multiplied by generation gives the coal saved, and the emission factor converts that to CO₂ avoided. A 3-point efficiency gain cuts fuel use by about 9%.

steps.explain: SCC = 860 ÷ (η × GCV).
Energy = capacity × hours.
Saving = ΔSCC × generation.
CO₂ = coal saved × emission factor.

cards.front: Name the six principal emissions from fuel combustion that affect the air environment.
cards.back: Carbon dioxide, particulate matter (dust), sulphur oxides, nitrogen oxides, hydrocarbons and carbon monoxide.
cards.explain: These are by-products of burning hydrocarbon fuels in industry. CO₂ dominates total emissions by quantity, while SOx, NOx and particulates are the main local and regional air pollutants.

cards.front: What is the main source of each: particulate matter, SOx, NOx and CO from combustion?
cards.back: Particulates: ash content of solid fuels (coal, lignite, biomass). SOx: sulphur in oil and coal. NOx: nitrogen from both the fuel and the combustion air. CO: incomplete combustion.
cards.explain: SOx and NOx are flagged as major global air pollutants because they cause acid rain, a trans-boundary problem. CO points directly to poor combustion, which is also an efficiency loss.

cards.front: True or false: carbon dioxide is classed as an air pollutant in the BEE guide book.
cards.back: False. CO₂ is not considered a pollutant, but it is a major contributor to global warming and climate change.
cards.explain: CO₂ comes from the oxidation of carbon in fuel and dominates total combustion emissions. Its concern is climatic rather than toxic, which is why it is treated under global warming, not air pollution.

cards.front: Name the four key environmental issues of global significance. Is suspended particulate matter one of them?
cards.back: Acid rain, ozone layer depletion, global warming and climate change, and loss of biodiversity. Suspended particulate matter is not a global issue (it is a local one).
cards.explain: Global issues affect all mankind regardless of country, so they need international effort. That raises the question of who should do what, which is the basis of agreements such as UNFCCC and Kyoto.

cards.front: How is acid rain formed, and name four of its effects.
cards.back: SOx and NOx from fossil fuel combustion mix with water vapour to form sulphuric and nitric acids. Effects: acidification of lakes, streams and soils; release of metals such as aluminium that wash away plant nutrients; killing of trees, crops and aquatic life; decay of buildings, paints and statues; respiratory, skin and eye problems.
cards.explain: Deposition can be wet (rain, snow, sleet) or dry (particles and gases). Because the pollutants travel far before falling, acid rain crosses national borders.

cards.front: Where is the ozone layer, and at what UV wavelengths is ozone naturally formed and destroyed?
cards.back: In the stratosphere, about 10–50 km above the earth. Ozone forms when O₂ absorbs UV below 240 nm and is destroyed when it absorbs UV above 290 nm.
cards.explain: Natural formation and destruction used to be in balance. The layer blocks the sun's UV-B radiation; depletion lets more harmful radiation reach the surface.

cards.front: Which ozone-depleting substances release chlorine and which release bromine? How many ozone molecules can one chlorine atom destroy?
cards.back: CFCs, HCFCs, carbon tetrachloride and methyl chloroform release chlorine; halons and methyl bromide release bromine. One chlorine atom can destroy 10,000–100,000 ozone molecules before it is removed.
cards.explain: It is the free chlorine or bromine atom, not the intact ODS molecule, that destroys ozone. Strong UV in the stratosphere breaks the ODS apart after it diffuses up there.

cards.front: Describe the chain reaction by which a CFC destroys ozone.
cards.back: UV breaks a C–Cl bond in the CFC, freeing a Cl atom. Cl + O₃ → ClO + O₂. A free O atom then breaks ClO, releasing Cl again, which repeats the cycle.
cards.explain: Because chlorine is regenerated, it acts as a catalyst, so a single CFC molecule can destroy up to about 100,000 ozone molecules. The thinning was first measured seasonally over the South Pole.

cards.front: Name the five categories of effects of ozone layer depletion described in the guide book.
cards.back: Effects on human and animal health (eye disease, skin cancer, infections); on terrestrial plants; on aquatic ecosystems (phytoplankton, larvae); on bio-geo-chemical cycles; and on air quality.
cards.explain: More UV-B changes species composition in forests and grassland, harms the early life stages of fish and shrimp, and changes sources and sinks of greenhouse gases. It also raises photo-dissociation in the troposphere, increasing harmful oxidants such as hydrogen peroxide.

cards.front: What countermeasures to ozone depletion does the guide book list?
cards.back: International agreement (Montreal Protocol) to phase out ozone-depleting chemicals; tax on ozone-depleting substances; ozone-friendly substitutes HCFC and HFC (lower ozone depleting potential, shorter life); recycling of CFCs and halons.
cards.explain: Note that HCFCs and HFCs, though gentler on ozone, are still greenhouse gases, so they are now counted alongside other GHGs for global warming.

cards.front: What would the earth's average surface temperature be without the natural greenhouse effect, compared with today?
cards.back: About −18°C instead of the present 15°C.
cards.explain: Water vapour, CO₂, methane and nitrous oxide absorb the long-wave infrared radiation emitted by the warm earth and re-emit part of it downwards. Short-wave solar radiation passes through relatively unimpeded. This natural warming is what made life on earth possible.

cards.front: What is the 'enhanced' greenhouse effect, and why is water vapour not counted among the gases driving it?
cards.back: The extra warming from human increases in greenhouse gases (CO₂ from fossil fuels, plus deforestation), on top of the natural effect. Water vapour is a GHG, but its atmospheric amount is not changed directly by human activity.
cards.explain: The human-influenced gases named are CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide, CFCs and ozone. The book estimates the earth's average temperature has risen by 0.75°C since 1880 because of human GHG emissions.

cards.front: According to the book's 2014 figure, what was the atmospheric CO₂ concentration, and why is cement a major CO₂ source?
cards.back: 397 ppm (Mauna Loa Observatory, November 2014). Cement emits CO₂ both from fuel combustion and from calcination of limestone.
cards.explain: CO₂ is the most important GHG because of its abundance, and it persists for over 100 years. Coal-based power plants are the major CO₂ source in many countries, followed by vehicles; deforestation both releases stored carbon and leaves fewer trees to absorb CO₂.

cards.front: How much carbon do the oceans and terrestrial biomass hold compared with the atmosphere, and how much excess human CO₂ do they absorb?
cards.back: Oceans hold about 50 times more carbon than the atmosphere; terrestrial biomass (trees, grasses) about 3 times more. Together they absorb about half of the excess CO₂ from human activity.
cards.explain: These natural sinks complement man-made carbon sequestration, which captures CO₂ from large point sources and stores it in depleted oil/gas reservoirs, deep coal seams or saline reservoirs.

cards.front: Name the main natural source and four anthropogenic sources of methane.
cards.back: Natural: wetlands. Anthropogenic: leakage in coal mining, natural gas pipelines and petroleum wells; rice cultivation; livestock (ruminant) digestion and wastes; landfills of municipal solid waste; wood burning.
cards.explain: Methane forms by anaerobic decomposition of organic matter (without oxygen). The book names landfills, livestock and wetland rice cultivation as the leading anthropogenic sources.

cards.front: Name four human sources of nitrous oxide (N₂O) and its approximate atmospheric lifetime.
cards.back: Nitrogen fertiliser and manure; biomass burning; fossil fuel combustion in power plants; chemical industry (e.g. nylon production); ploughing that releases N₂O from soil; car catalytic converters. Lifetime is about 120 years (Table 10.1: 114 years).
cards.explain: N₂O has a GWP of 300 in the book's table, so even small emissions matter. Its concentration rose from a baseline of 275 ppb to 326 ppb.

cards.front: What are the largest man-made sources of perfluorocarbons (PFCs), and what are the main uses of SF₆?
cards.back: PFCs: primary aluminium production and semiconductor manufacture. SF₆: electrical insulation and power transmission equipment, the magnesium industry, semiconductor manufacture, and as a tracer gas for leak detection.
cards.explain: PFCs last several thousand years in the atmosphere, so all emissions accumulate. The book calls SF₆ the most potent greenhouse gas.

cards.front: Why are HCFCs and HFCs, which replaced CFCs, still a climate concern, and how are HFC emissions best contained?
cards.back: They are less destructive to ozone but are still greenhouse gases, and their production could increase greatly. HFC emissions (leaks from refrigeration and AC, end-of-life disposal, aerosols) are best contained by recycling the refrigerants.
cards.explain: Their shorter lifetime and lower concentration mean less warming per unit emitted than CFCs. CFCs themselves stay in the atmosphere for about 100–200 years because they are so chemically unreactive.

cards.front: Define Global Warming Potential (GWP).
cards.back: The ratio of the warming (radiative forcing) from one unit mass of a greenhouse gas to that from one unit mass of CO₂ over a period of time, i.e. its warming potential per unit mass relative to CO₂ (GWP of CO₂ = 1).
cards.explain: GWP accounts for both how strongly a molecule absorbs infrared and how long it stays in the atmosphere. Some gases are 140 to 23,900 times more potent than CO₂ over 100 years, so even tiny amounts of SF₆ or HFC-23 matter.

cards.front: Give the GWPs in Table 10.1 for CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide, perfluoromethane (PFC) and SF₆.
cards.back: CO₂ 1; CH₄ 23; N₂O 300; perfluoromethane 5,700; SF₆ 22,000.
cards.explain: Among methane, N₂O, CFCs and PFCs, methane has the lowest GWP (a common exam trap). Lifetimes in the same table: CH₄ 12 years, N₂O 114, perfluoromethane 50,000, SF₆ 3,200.

cards.front: What share of global GHG emissions comes from CO₂ from fossil fuels and cement, and how large were global fuel-combustion CO₂ emissions in 2013?
cards.back: Almost 70% of global GHG emissions; fuel combustion emitted almost 36 Gt CO₂ in 2013.
cards.explain: Energy use is by far the largest source of GHGs. Agriculture (CH₄ and N₂O from livestock and rice) and non-energy industrial processes (fluorinated gases, N₂O) are smaller shares. For 2010, Figure 10.8 shows 91% of human CO₂ from fossil fuels and cement and 9% from land-use change; of it, about 50% stays in the atmosphere, 26% goes to land and 24% to the oceans.

cards.front: Per the guide book (2013 data), what was India's share of global emissions, its rank, total CO₂ and per-capita emissions?
cards.back: About 7% of global emissions; third largest CO₂ emitter after China and the USA; about 2.5 Gt CO₂ in 2013; per capita only about 1.6 t/year.
cards.explain: Coal-based power generation accounted for almost 70% of India's coal-related CO₂ emissions. These are the book's 2013 figures and have since changed.

cards.front: By how much did average sea level rise in the 20th century, and what was the largest contributor?
cards.back: About 20 cm. The largest contribution was thermal expansion of warming ocean water.
cards.explain: The book predicts a further 10–20 cm rise by 2030 and up to 1 m by 2100, with low-lying countries such as Bangladesh most at risk. Melting ice adds to the rise and also loses the reflective cooling of white ice caps.

cards.front: Name six impacts of global warming and climate change described in the guide book.
cards.back: Any six: rising ocean temperature and sea level; snow and ice melting (glacier retreat); altered rainfall patterns; more extreme weather events; more severe heat waves; loss of biodiversity; spread of diseases (e.g. malaria); dwindling freshwater supply; food shortages.
cards.explain: Indian examples in the book: rising rainfall on the west coast and north Andhra Pradesh, falling monsoon rain in north-east India and parts of Gujarat and Kerala, and more extreme weather in West Bengal, Gujarat and Kerala.

cards.front: When and where was the UNFCCC signed, when did it come into force, and what is its stated objective?
cards.back: Signed by over 160 countries at the UN Conference on Environment and Development (Earth Summit), Rio de Janeiro, June 1992; came into force in 1994. Objective: stabilise GHG concentrations at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic (human) interference with the climate system.
cards.explain: Its short-term aim was for developed countries to return GHG emissions, especially CO₂, to 1990 levels by 2000. Long-term, stabilisation should come within a time frame that lets ecosystems adapt, keeps food production safe and lets economic development proceed sustainably. Developed countries were to take the lead.

cards.front: When and by whom was the IPCC formed, and what did its 1995 report conclude?
cards.back: Formed in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and the United Nations. The 1995 report said the observed warming is 'unlikely to be entirely natural in origin' and that there is a 'discernible human influence on global climate'.
cards.explain: It also projected a 1.4–5.8°C rise in the 21st century (about 75% due to CO₂) and a further 0.1–0.9 m sea-level rise. The report changed the world's view of climate change and led to the 1997 Kyoto Protocol.

cards.front: What is the Conference of Parties (COP), and which COP produced the Kyoto Protocol?
cards.back: The COP is the supreme body of the UNFCCC, where the Parties meet annually to promote and review implementation of the Convention. COP 3 produced the Kyoto Protocol in 1997.
cards.explain: Meetings held between COPs are called intersessional meetings. Kyoto set legally binding emission targets for developed (Annex I) countries for six GHGs, to be met over 2008–2012.

cards.front: What did the Kyoto Protocol commit industrialised countries to, and how does it differ from the Convention?
cards.back: Binding targets for 37 industrialised countries and the European Community to cut GHG emissions by an average of 5% below 1990 levels over 2008–2012. The Convention only encouraged them to stabilise emissions; the Protocol commits them to it.
cards.explain: It places a heavier burden on developed nations under 'common but differentiated responsibilities', because they caused most of today's GHG levels through more than 150 years of industry. It entered into force in 2005 after Russia ratified; the USA (about 25% of global GHGs) did not ratify.

cards.front: What is a Party's 'assigned amount' under Kyoto, and what was the EU 'bubble'?
cards.back: Assigned amount: the maximum emissions (in CO₂ equivalent) a Party may emit over the commitment period to meet its target. Bubble: the 15 EU states shared one overall target and redistributed it among themselves as different individual targets.
cards.explain: Table 10.2 targets (vs 1990): EU-15 and several others −8%, USA −7%, Canada, Hungary, Japan and Poland −6%, Croatia −5%, New Zealand, Russia and Ukraine 0%, Norway +1%, Australia +8%.

cards.front: Distinguish Annex I, Annex II and Non-Annex I Parties under the UNFCCC.
cards.back: Annex I: industrialised OECD countries plus economies in transition (EIT, e.g. Russia, Baltic and Central/Eastern European states). Annex II: the OECD members of Annex I (not EITs), who must provide finance and technology transfer to developing countries. Non-Annex I: mostly developing countries.
cards.explain: Developing countries are recognised as especially vulnerable, for example those with low-lying coasts or prone to drought. Their needs are addressed through investment, insurance and technology transfer.

cards.front: Name the three market-based mechanisms of the Kyoto Protocol.
cards.back: Emissions trading ('carbon trading'), the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), and Joint Implementation (JI).
cards.explain: Countries must meet their targets mainly through national measures. The mechanisms are a supplement that lets them meet targets more economically and stimulates green investment. Emissions trading lets countries with spare emission units sell them to countries over their targets.

cards.front: How do CDM and Joint Implementation differ? What credit does each earn?
cards.back: CDM: a country with a Kyoto commitment funds an emission-reduction project in a developing country (no commitment) and earns Certified Emission Reductions (CERs). JI: a project in another Annex I country (both have commitments) earns Emission Reduction Units (ERUs). Each credit = 1 tonne CO₂.
cards.explain: A JI project must give reductions or removals additional to what would otherwise happen; the host gains investment and technology. Most CDM projects have been renewable energy, followed by waste handling and disposal. CDM reductions from 2000–2007 could count towards 2008–2012 commitments.

cards.front: List the stages of the CDM project cycle in order.
cards.back: 1) Project preparation (identification, feasibility); 2) Project Idea Note (PIN); 3) Project Design Document (PDD); 4) host country approval by the DNA; 5) PDD made public for 30 days; 6) validation by a DOE; 7) validation report submitted; 8) registration by the CDM Executive Board; then implementation and monitoring, yearly verification, and certification and issuance of CERs.
cards.explain: The last three stages run throughout the project's life. Project preparation uses approved UNFCCC methodologies to show the project is real, measurable and additional.

cards.front: Name the three types of small-scale CDM projects eligible for fast-track approval, with their limits.
cards.back: Type I: renewable energy projects up to 15 MW capacity. Type II: energy efficiency projects cutting energy use by up to 15 GWh/year (54 TJ) vs business-as-usual. Type III: other projects emitting less than 15 kt CO₂/year.
cards.explain: A fast track exists because the normal CDM process is too costly for small projects. Small projects also give big local sustainable-development benefits, small technologies (solar, wind, fuel cells) are promising, and CDM could lose public support if biased toward large capital-intensive projects.

cards.front: What is a Project Idea Note (PIN) in CDM, and what does it contain?
cards.back: An optional note of about five pages that informs the host country DNA and potential CER buyers. It covers project type and size; location; expected GHG reduction vs business-as-usual; suggested crediting lifetime; suggested CER price (US$/tCO₂e); financial structure; and other socio-economic or environmental benefits.
cards.explain: A PIN is not required, but it helps obtain early feedback on host-country sustainability requirements and buyer interest before the full CDM process. A feasibility study is also optional but helps prove additionality and shows ROI with and without CDM.

cards.front: What is the key mandatory document of the CDM cycle, and what crediting-period options does a project have?
cards.back: The Project Design Document (PDD). Crediting period: either one fixed period of 10 years, or up to three periods of 7 years each, with revalidation every seventh year.
cards.explain: The baseline methodology and baseline scenario in the PDD set how many CERs the project earns. The PDD goes to a DOE for validation and then to the CDM Executive Board for registration. Credits normally count from project start (from registration if the project began before it was registered).

cards.front: Who is India's National CDM Authority, and why is host-country approval required?
cards.back: The Ministry of Environment & Forests (MoE&F). Approval ensures governments keep sovereignty over their natural resources and confirms that the project meets the host country's sustainable development criteria.
cards.explain: The Designated National Authority (DNA) in the non-Annex I country evaluates and approves the project and is the point of contact. The completed PDD and reports are submitted to it.

cards.front: How does validation differ from verification in a CDM project?
cards.back: Validation is done at the outset by a DOE, which checks the PDD against CDM requirements (after 30 days of public comment). Verification is the periodic (usually annual) ex-post check of the monitored emission reductions during operation, which form the basis for CERs.
cards.explain: Registration with the CDM Executive Board becomes final within a maximum of eight weeks unless a review is requested. After verification, the DOE issues a certification report, and CERs are issued unless a project participant or three Executive Board members request a review within 15 days.

cards.front: In CDM, what is 'leakage', and for how long must a project be monitored?
cards.back: Leakage is an indirect increase or decrease in emissions outside the defined project boundary (e.g. changed consumer behaviour or reduced transport). Monitoring continues for the whole crediting period (3 × 7 years or 10 years).
cards.explain: At minimum, monitoring must cover project output, related GHG emissions, environmental impact and leakage, following the monitoring plan in the PDD. The monitoring report includes an estimate of the CERs generated.

cards.front: What levy applies to CERs from CDM projects, and what is it for?
cards.back: A 2% levy, used to help particularly vulnerable developing countries adapt to the adverse effects of climate change.
cards.explain: The book also notes that public funding for CDM must not divert official development assistance (ODA). Carbon funds come from international tenders, voluntary corporate initiatives, multilateral funds, EU purchase commitments and bilateral negotiations.

cards.front: What were the EU's '20-20-20' targets for 2020?
cards.back: A 20% cut in GHG emissions from 1990 levels; 20% of EU energy from renewables; and a 20% improvement in energy efficiency.
cards.explain: EU leaders set them in March 2007 and enacted them through the binding climate and energy package in 2009, aiming for a highly energy-efficient, low-carbon economy.

cards.front: How does the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) 'cap and trade' work?
cards.back: A cap is set on total emissions from covered installations and is reduced over time. Companies receive or buy allowances, which they can trade. Each year they must surrender enough allowances to cover their emissions or face heavy fines; spare allowances can be kept or sold.
cards.explain: The book says it covers over 11,000 power stations and industrial plants in 31 countries, plus airlines. Trading means emissions are cut where it is cheapest. Covered emissions were to be 21% below 2005 in 2020, with 43% proposed for 2030.

cards.front: How did the Brundtland Commission (1987) define sustainable development?
cards.back: 'Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.'
cards.explain: The report was 'Our Common Future'. A fuller definition is 'living on the Earth's income rather than eroding its capital', keeping use of renewable resources within their replenishment. Applied to energy, non-renewable inputs should be used only as far as they can be substituted in future, and renewable ones only at the rate they can be renewed.

cards.front: A 110 MW coal power plant's R&M raises efficiency from 28% to 32%. Specific coal consumption was 0.7 kg/kWh before. For 7000 h/year, same coal quality, find (a) coal saved per year and (b) CO₂ avoided at 1.53 kg CO₂/kg coal.
cards.back: New SCC = 0.7 × 28/32 = 0.6125 kg/kWh. Generation = 770 million kWh/yr. Coal saved ≈ 67,375 t/yr. CO₂ avoided ≈ 1,03,084 t/yr.
cards.explain: With the same coal quality, specific coal consumption is inversely proportional to efficiency. The saving per kWh times annual generation gives coal saved, and the emission factor converts that to CO₂ avoided. This is the book's short question S-1, worked here.

steps.prompt: Find the specific coal consumption after R&M.
steps.explain: Coal per kWh ∝ 1/efficiency when GCV is unchanged.
Capacity × operating hours.
Saving per kWh × kWh per year.
Apply the emission factor of 1.53 kg CO₂ per kg coal.

cards.front: Why are renewable energy sources described as 'flows' while fossil and nuclear fuels are 'stocks'?
cards.back: Renewables come from essentially inexhaustible, continuously renewed sources (sun, wind, water, waves, geothermal heat, biomass), whereas fossil and nuclear fuels are finite stored quantities that get used up.
cards.explain: The book also notes that renewable energy can generally be used without releasing harmful pollutants and is also called non-conventional energy. Examples: wind, solar, geothermal, tidal, sustainably grown bio-energy and hydropower.

cards.front: What is the solar constant, and what is its average value?
cards.back: The rate at which solar energy at all wavelengths is received per unit area at the top of the earth's atmosphere; on average about 1,368 W/m².
cards.explain: It varies by about 0.3% over the 11-year solar cycle, and each planet has its own solar constant. Don't confuse it with average insolation (342 W/m²), a common exam distractor.

cards.front: Define solar insolation. How does it relate to the solar constant and to the sun's angle?
cards.back: The solar energy striking a square metre of the earth's surface in a day. It is greatest when the surface is normal to the sun and falls with the cosine of the angle from the normal. The average incoming radiation is one-fourth of the solar constant, about 342 W/m².
cards.explain: Insolation is usually expressed in kWh/m²/day and sets collector size: a poor-insolation area needs a larger collector. The more slanted the sun's rays, the longer their path through the atmosphere and the more diffuse they become.

cards.front: What is the 'solar window'?
cards.back: The period of the day, typically 9 AM to 3 PM, when maximum sunlight is available.
cards.explain: Solar collectors are sized and oriented to make best use of this window, when the sun is highest and its rays least slanted.

cards.front: How much solar energy does India receive, and what solar power capacity can a square kilometre of land support?
cards.back: About 5–7 kWh/m² per day for 300–330 days a year, enough to set up about 20 MW of solar power per km² of land.
cards.explain: Solar energy is used through two routes: solar thermal (sun's heat to heat energy) and solar photovoltaic (sunlight to electricity).

cards.front: What temperature does a flat plate collector reach, how is it built, and why does its output vary by season?
cards.back: About 40–60°C. Copper tubes welded to copper sheets, both with a highly absorbing black coating, with a toughened glass cover on top and insulation below, all in a flat box. Its efficiency depends strongly on ambient temperature, so output is higher in summer than in winter.
cards.explain: A solar water heating system consists of a flat plate or evacuated tube collector, an insulated storage tank (water stays hot overnight) and connecting pipes, with the collector facing the sun.

cards.front: How is an evacuated tube collector built, what temperature can it reach, and how do its heat losses compare with a flat plate collector?
cards.back: Two concentric glass tubes fused at the ends with a vacuum between them; the inner tube has a selective absorbing coating, and water flows in through an innermost feeder tube. It reaches up to about 150°C. Heat loss is under 10%, vs about 40% for a flat plate collector.
cards.explain: Because it is insulated like a thermos flask, it needs no separate cover sheet or insulated box, and its efficiency does not drop with ambient temperature the way a flat plate collector's does.

cards.front: Why is an evacuated tube collector more efficient than a flat plate collector?
cards.back: The vacuum stops heat loss by conduction (and convection) back to the atmosphere, and the selective coating converts short-wave radiation to long-wave, preventing re-radiation. More heat is trapped, so it is far less sensitive to ambient temperature.
cards.explain: This is a standard short question (S-5). Sunlight passes through the clear outer tube, the coated inner tube absorbs it, and the trapped long-wave heat cannot escape through the vacuum.

cards.front: Describe how a solar power tower works, including the molten salt temperatures.
cards.back: A field of heliostats (mirrors) focuses sunlight onto a receiver on a tall tower. Molten salt from the cold tank is heated to about 566°C in the receiver and stored in a hot tank. It then passes through a steam generator to drive a turbine, and returns at about 288°C to the cold tank.
cards.explain: The hot and cold salt tanks give thermal storage, so generation can continue when the sun is not shining. The power tower and parabolic trough are the two basic types of solar thermal power station.

cards.front: What is the composition of the molten salt used in solar power towers, and why is it preferred?
cards.back: 60% sodium nitrate and 40% potassium nitrate. It is an efficient, low-cost thermal storage medium and is non-flammable and non-toxic.
cards.explain: Storing heat in molten salt decouples heat collection from electricity generation in a power tower plant.

cards.front: How does a parabolic trough collector work? Give its concentration ratio and fluid temperature.
cards.back: Parabolic trough-shaped reflectors focus sunlight onto a receiver tube along their focal line, concentrating it 30–60 times and heating the fluid to about 400°C to raise steam for a turbine. The troughs lie on an east–west axis and rotate to track the sun.
cards.explain: The book calls it currently the most proven solar thermal electric technology. Such plants can produce many MW but are confined to areas with sufficient solar insolation.

cards.front: What is the photovoltaic effect, and why are solar cells 'tuned' and given an anti-reflective coating?
cards.back: Photons striking two dissimilar materials in close contact knock electrons out of their normal state, producing a voltage. Only photons of the right energy do this, so cells are tuned in manufacture to the most intense part of the sunlight spectrum. Silicon is naturally reflective, so an anti-reflective coating cuts reflection losses.
cards.explain: Because a cell cannot use all wavelengths, solar cell efficiency is low (the book quotes typical efficiencies of 10–15%). Besides silicon, cells are made of gallium arsenide, copper indium diselenide and cadmium telluride.

cards.front: How many silicon cells make a standard PV module, why that number, and what does 'peak watt (Wp)' mean?
cards.back: 36 cells (about 0.5 V each), enough voltage to charge a 12 V battery and run a pump or motor. Wp is the maximum power a module can deliver under standard test conditions; single modules range from about 5 to 120 Wp.
cards.explain: Cells are connected in series and parallel to form modules, and modules form arrays. A PV system comprises panels, a battery, a charge controller and an inverter for AC loads.

cards.front: Write the formula for the energy conversion efficiency of a PV panel.
cards.back: η (%) = Pm / (E × A) × 100, where Pm = maximum power output (W), E = insolation (W/m²) and A = cell or panel area (m²).
cards.explain: It measures how much of the incident solar energy becomes electricity. Commercial silicon panels typically fall in the 10–15% range quoted in the book.

cards.front: Find the energy conversion efficiency of a 175 W solar panel measuring 0.75 m × 1.50 m when insolation is 1,000 W/m².
cards.explain: The panel converts 15.6% of the available solar energy into electricity. The rest is reflected or lost as heat, or is at wavelengths the cell cannot use.

steps.explain: Area intercepting the sunlight.
E × A is the input power.

cards.front: According to Table 11.1, how suitable for power generation are average wind speeds of 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 m/s?
cards.back: Up to 4 m/s: no good; 5 m/s: poor; 6 m/s: moderate; 7 m/s: good; 8 m/s: excellent.
cards.explain: In km/h these are about 15, 18, 22, 25 and 29. Tropics have steady moderate winds all year, while temperate latitudes vary more but have more high-wind occurrences.

cards.front: Why are three-bladed rotors preferred for power generation, and where are multi-bladed rotors used?
cards.back: Three-bladed rotors run more smoothly and generally more quietly than two-bladed ones. Multi-bladed rotors have a large starting torque in light winds and are used for water pumping and low-frequency mechanical power.
cards.explain: Most turbines are horizontal-axis machines with the rotor shaft and generator on top of the tower, pointed into the wind; the rotor can be upwind or downwind of the tower. Blade shape and angle to the relative wind set the aerodynamic performance.

cards.front: In a wind turbine nacelle, what are the typical speeds of the low-speed and high-speed shafts, and which generator is most common?
cards.back: Low-speed (main) shaft: about 30–60 rpm; the gearbox raises this to about 1,000–1,800 rpm on the high-speed shaft. The most common commercial generator is an induction generator producing 50-cycle AC.
cards.explain: The nacelle houses the gearbox, generator and controls. A disc brake on the main shaft or high-speed shaft slows the rotor, and yaw control (sensors plus a yaw motor) turns the nacelle to keep an upwind rotor aligned with the wind.

cards.front: Define cut-in, rated and cut-out (furling) wind speeds, with typical values.
cards.back: Cut-in: minimum speed for reliable useful power, around 5 m/s. Rated: lowest speed at which rated (maximum) power is reached, often 1.5 × the site mean wind speed. Cut-out (furling): speed above which the turbine shuts down to prevent damage, about 20–30 m/s depending on manufacturer.
cards.explain: Together with power output and capacity factor, these are the key operating characteristics shown on a turbine's power curve. The rated speed is chosen to fit the local wind regime.

cards.front: What is the Betz limit, and what fraction of wind energy is actually converted to useful power?
cards.back: The theoretical maximum fraction of wind energy a rotor can capture, about 59%. Allowing for generator and gearbox losses, only about 15–25% becomes useful power.
cards.explain: A rotor cannot be 100% efficient because some air must pass through the blades for the turbine to turn; it extracts energy by slowing the wind. The blade coefficient of performance Cp generally ranges from 0.33 to 0.59.

cards.front: Write the formula for electrical power from a wind turbine, and state what doubling the wind speed vs doubling the swept area does.
cards.back: P = 0.5 × ρ × A × Cp × ηg × ηb × V³ (ρ air density, A swept area, Cp blade coefficient of performance, ηg generator and ηb gearbox efficiency, V wind speed). Doubling V gives 8× power; doubling A only 2×.
cards.explain: It comes from kinetic energy = ½mV² with mass flow = ρAV. Because of the cube law, siting turbines in the highest-wind areas is critical for good economics.

cards.front: A wind turbine has a 6 m diameter rotor, Cp = 0.30, generator efficiency 0.8, gearbox efficiency 0.90 and wind speed 11 m/s. Taking air density as about 1.2 kg/m³, find the expected power output.
cards.explain: This is the book's worked example (the 1.2 kg/m³ density is consistent with its 4,875 W answer). The V³ term dominates: 11³ = 1331.

steps.explain: Area of the circle swept by the rotor.
Combined blade, generator and gearbox efficiency.
Power varies with V³.
P = 0.5ρA·Cp·ηg·ηb·V³.

cards.front: Define the capacity factor of a wind turbine and give its typical range.
cards.back: CF = actual kWh produced in a period (usually a year) ÷ (8760 × nameplate rating in kW). Typically 20–40%, at the upper end only at particularly favourable sites.
cards.explain: It compares actual output with the theoretical maximum if the turbine ran at full rating all year. The variability of the wind is the main reason it is well below 100%.

cards.front: A 2.5 MW wind turbine actually produced 5,000,000 kWh in a year. Find its capacity factor.
cards.explain: The book's example shows that a turbine's real annual output is far below nameplate × hours because of wind variability. 22.8% is within the typical 20–40% range.

steps.explain: Keep units consistent with kWh.
Full rating for all 8760 hours of the year.
CF = kWh produced/(8760 × kW rating).

cards.front: Why is biomass considered 'carbon neutral'?
cards.back: The CO₂ released when biomass is burned is largely balanced by the CO₂ absorbed during its growth through photosynthesis.
cards.explain: Biomass is effectively stored solar energy. It includes wood, straw, crops, algae, sewage sludge and animal and other biological waste; low-density biomass is processed into pellets or briquettes for direct combustion in grate, stoker or fluidised-bed systems.

cards.front: What is biomass gasification? Give its temperature, the calorific value of producer gas and the typical conversion efficiency.
cards.back: Partial combustion of biomass with less than stoichiometric air at about 1000°C, giving combustible CO and H₂ (traces of CH₄) plus tar and dust. Producer gas CV is 1000–1200 kcal/Nm³; conversion efficiency is 60–70%.
cards.explain: Complete combustion would give only CO₂ and water. The key to gasifier design is to reduce biomass to charcoal and then convert the charcoal at a suitable temperature into CO and H₂. Used in a dual-fuel DG set, producer gas can save 65–85% of diesel.

cards.front: Name the four zones of a biomass gasifier in the order biomass passes through them, and the four main stages of a gasification system.
cards.back: Zones: drying (distillation), pyrolysis, combustion, reduction. System stages: feeding of feedstock, gasifier reactions, cleaning of the gas, utilisation of the cleaned gas.
cards.explain: Exothermic reactions in the combustion zone (C + O₂ → CO₂; H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O) supply the heat. In the reduction zone over hot charcoal: C + CO₂ → 2CO and C + H₂O → CO + H₂ (reduction), CO₂ + H₂ → CO + H₂O (water gas), and C + 2H₂ → CH₄ (methanation).

cards.front: 1 kg of dry wood (average CV 3500 kcal/kg) produces 2.5 m³ of producer gas with an average CV of 1000 kcal/Nm³. Find the gasifier conversion efficiency.
cards.explain: Gasifier efficiency = calorific value of gas produced per kg of fuel ÷ calorific value of 1 kg of fuel. The 29% balance is lost as sensible heat, tar, char and dust.

steps.prompt: Find the heat in the gas per kg of wood.
steps.explain: Gas volume × gas CV.

steps.prompt: Identify the heat input per kg of wood.
steps.explain: CV of the dry wood.
Within the 60–70%+ range typical of gasifiers.

cards.front: 20 kg of wood (CV 3200 kcal/kg) produces 46 m³ of producer gas with an average CV of 1000 kcal/Nm³. Find the gasifier's conversion efficiency.
cards.back: Heat input 64,000 kcal; heat output 46,000 kcal; efficiency ≈ 71.88%.
cards.explain: This is the chapter's solved example. It uses the same principle as the per-kg formula, just with total quantities.

steps.explain: Mass of wood × its CV.

steps.prompt: Calculate heat output in the gas.
steps.explain: Gas volume × gas CV.
Efficiency = heat output/heat input.

cards.front: Can a diesel (CI) engine run entirely on producer gas? Compare biomass and diesel use per kWh for CI and spark-ignition engines.
cards.back: No. A CI engine needs pilot diesel: about 1 kg of biomass plus 0.07 litres of diesel per kWh, saving 80–85% diesel. A spark-ignition engine on producer gas gives about 0.55–0.75 kWh per kg of biomass.
cards.explain: CI engines rely on compression ignition, and producer gas cannot ignite that way alone, so a small diesel charge is injected (dual-fuel mode). SI engines use a spark, so they can run fully on producer gas.

cards.front: What is biomethanation, what does gobar gas consist of, and what extra advantage does this process have?
cards.back: Anaerobic (oxygen-free) bacterial digestion of biomass (dung, sewage sludge, MSW, food, distillery and other biodegradable wastes) into biogas. Gobar gas is about 60% methane and 40% CO₂. It is the only biomass process that also gives high-grade manure as a by-product.
cards.explain: Biogas gives higher useful energy from dung than burning it directly: in the book's chart, 25 kg of fresh dung gives about 2,592 kcal of useful energy as biogas vs about 1,046 kcal by burning 5 kg of dried dung. Bio-methane can fully replace natural gas in boilers, furnaces and IC engines.

cards.front: Describe the four stages of anaerobic digestion.
cards.back: 1) Acidic bacteria break complex organic molecules into smaller ones; 2) these break down further into organic acids, CO₂ and ammonia; 3) methanogenic bacteria convert them into acetates and hydrogen; 4) these are converted to methane.
cards.explain: Methane-producing bacteria are very sensitive to ambient conditions, which can slow or stop the process. In a floating-drum plant, a non-return valve keeps air out, since air would kill the bacteria and could create an explosive mixture.

cards.front: How are ethanol and biodiesel produced, and how are they used?
cards.back: Ethanol: fermentation of molasses or any carbohydrate-rich feedstock (sugar beet, sweet corn, ligno-cellulosic straw and wood waste); used as a fuel additive to cut CO and smog emissions, and flexible-fuel vehicles use up to 85% ethanol. Biodiesel: transesterification of plant oil (e.g. non-edible Jatropha) with an alcohol such as methanol; used as a blend (typically 20%) or neat in diesel engines.
cards.explain: Biodiesel can be made from any plant oil, waste cooking oil or animal fat (exam answer: animal and vegetable fat). Jatropha grows on dry, arid land and is non-edible, so it does not compete with food.

cards.front: Classify hydropower by size according to Table 11.2.
cards.back: Large: >25 MW, grid-fed. Small: 2,001 kW–25 MW, usually grid-fed. Mini: 101 kW–2 MW, stand-alone or grid. Micro: 11–100 kW, usually for remote off-grid areas. Pico: a few hundred watts up to 10 kW.
cards.explain: A run-of-the-river micro-hydro scheme needs no storage. It diverts part of the river through an intake weir and settling basin, along a channel to a forebay tank, then down a penstock to the turbine in the power house.

cards.front: Write the formula for the power potential of falling water, and what overall efficiency does the book suggest for small hydro systems?
cards.back: Theoretical P (kW) = 9.81 × Q × H, with Q in m³/s and H in m. For small systems of a few kW, take overall efficiency as about 50%.
cards.explain: Small turbines rarely exceed 80% efficiency, and there are further friction losses in the penstock, so the theoretical power is multiplied by about 0.5 for a realistic figure.

cards.front: A turbine-generator operates at a head of 10 m with a flow of 0.3 m³/s. Taking 50% overall efficiency, how much electricity will it deliver?
cards.explain: The theoretical hydraulic power is 29.43 kW. Applying the book's rule-of-thumb 50% overall efficiency for small systems gives about 14.7 kW of electricity.

steps.explain: Q in m³/s, H in m.
Before losses.
50% overall is typical for small schemes.

cards.front: How much power can a run-of-river mini hydro plant generate with a flow of 20 litres/s and a head of 12 m, assuming 60% system efficiency?
cards.explain: The common mistake is forgetting to convert litres/s to m³/s (divide by 1000). The book writes it as 12 × 20 × 9.81 × 0.6/1000 = 1.4 kW.

steps.explain: 1 m³ = 1000 litres.
Given system efficiency is 60%.

cards.front: Explain how a fuel cell produces electricity.
cards.back: Hydrogen enters the anode, where a catalyst splits it into protons and electrons. The electrolyte lets protons pass to the cathode but not electrons, which flow through an external circuit as current. At the cathode, oxygen combines with the protons and returning electrons to form water and heat.
cards.explain: Since the conversion is electrochemical, not combustion, it is clean, quiet and highly efficient. Cells are stacked in series. Hydrogen is a secondary energy source (from steam reforming of natural gas, electrolysis or biomass gasification), and its high production cost is the biggest hurdle to large-scale use.

cards.front: Match each fuel cell type to its operating temperature: PEMFC, DMFC, PAFC, AFC, MCFC, SOFC.
cards.back: PEMFC: low temperature (high-temperature variants up to 200°C). DMFC: 60–130°C. PAFC: about 180°C. AFC: about 70°C. MCFC: about 650°C. SOFC: about 800–1,000°C.
cards.explain: Electrolytes: PEMFC and DMFC use polymer membranes; PAFC liquid phosphoric acid in a silicon carbide matrix; AFC aqueous potassium hydroxide; MCFC molten carbonate salt in a ceramic matrix; SOFC solid ceramic (stabilised zirconia). MCFC and SOFC run on synthesis gas or methane and are best run continuously.

cards.front: Which fuel cell type is used for each: NASA space shuttles; most megawatt-scale fuel cell power plants; portable devices under 250 W; vehicles; 100–400 kW stationary generators?
cards.back: NASA shuttles: alkaline (AFC). MW-scale plants and large CHP: molten carbonate (MCFC). Portable <250 W: direct methanol (DMFC). Vehicles: PEMFC (variable output, high power density). 100–400 kW stationary: phosphoric acid (PAFC).
cards.explain: PAFC is quite resistant to CO poisoning and can exceed 80% overall efficiency if the heat is used. AFC needs pure hydrogen and oxygen because it is very sensitive to poisoning. Overall, fuel cells span about 1 W to 10 MW.

cards.front: What is landfill gas, and how is it recovered for energy?
cards.back: Biogas (mainly methane and CO₂) formed by natural anaerobic decomposition of organic matter in landfills. Perforated pipes inserted into the landfill collect it under natural pressure for use as fuel, e.g. in a gas engine-generator.
cards.explain: If not captured, landfill methane escapes and adds to greenhouse emissions. In a waste-to-energy direct combustion plant, the remaining ash takes about a tenth of the original space of the trash.

cards.front: Compare wave energy with wind energy: energy content, dependence on height or speed, and power per km of coast.
cards.back: Waves hold roughly 1000 times the kinetic energy of wind. Wave power varies with the square of wave height (wind with the cube of speed), and water is 850 times denser than air. About 40 MW/km of coast is possible with 1 m waves and 1000 MW/km with 5 m waves.
cards.explain: Waves travel long distances with little loss, so wave power is steadier and more predictable than wind or solar, and runs round the clock. In an oscillating chamber, the rising wave pushes air through a turbine, and the falling wave draws air back, so power is generated both ways.

cards.front: What is the basic requirement for tapping tidal energy, and what causes tides?
cards.back: A tidal height difference of at least 5 m. Tides are caused by the combined gravitational pull of the moon and sun.
cards.explain: High and low tides occur twice a day, and bays and inlets amplify them. Water trapped behind a dam at high tide is released through turbines as the tide falls, like a hydro plant; turbines can generate as the tide comes in and as it goes out.

cards.front: How fast does underground temperature rise with depth, and at roughly what depth is rock hot enough to boil water? What is the difference between magma and lava?
cards.back: About 3°C per 100 m, so rock is hot enough to boil water at about 3000 m. Magma is the hot liquid rock in the upper mantle; when it breaks through the surface in a volcano, it is called lava.
cards.explain: Water reaching hot rock can exceed 148°C; where it comes up through a crack it forms a hot spring. A geothermal power plant is like a regular plant except that no fuel is burned to make steam.

cards.front: Name the three types of geothermal power plant and how each works.
cards.back: Dry steam: steam from a production well drives the turbine directly, then is condensed and reinjected. Flash steam: hot water (about 182°C) is flashed to steam in a low-pressure tank. Binary cycle: lower-temperature water (107–182°C) heats a low-boiling organic working fluid (e.g. isobutane) in a heat exchanger, in two closed loops.
cards.explain: In all three, spent fluid is returned to the reservoir through an injection well. Because the binary cycle keeps geothermal water and working fluid in separate closed loops, it has no air emissions.

cards.front: What is the difference between Gross Calorific Value (GCV) and Net Calorific Value (NCV)?
cards.back: GCV includes the latent heat of the water vapour formed in combustion; NCV excludes it (NCV = GCV − latent heat of water vapour).
cards.explain: Hydrogen in the fuel burns to water and any fuel moisture also evaporates. In GCV (higher heating value) that vapour is assumed condensed, so its latent heat is counted. In practice flue gas leaves as vapour, so NCV is the heat actually usable. The difference therefore arises from water vapour/moisture, not from sulphur or ash.

cards.front: What is the flash point of a fuel oil?
cards.back: The lowest temperature at which the fuel vapour momentarily ignites (flashes) when a flame is applied.
cards.explain: Flash point is a safety/storage property, not the temperature of sustained burning (that is the fire point) or of spontaneous ignition (auto-ignition temperature). Furnace oil has a relatively high flash point, which is why it is safe to store and preheat.

cards.front: What is the pour point of a fuel oil and why does it matter?
cards.back: The lowest temperature at which the oil will still flow; it tells the minimum temperature at which oil can be stored and pumped.
cards.explain: Below the pour point the oil gels and cannot be pumped. Heavy oils like furnace oil therefore need tank heating so the oil stays comfortably above its pour point during storage and transfer.

cards.front: Why is viscosity of a liquid fuel important for combustion?
cards.back: It governs atomisation at the burner – oil must be heated to the right viscosity to atomise into fine droplets.
cards.explain: High viscosity gives large droplets, poor atomisation, incomplete combustion, carbon deposits and smoke. Furnace oil is preheated before the burner to bring its viscosity down to what the burner needs. Viscosity also affects pumping and handling.

cards.front: Which type of pump is best suited for transferring viscous liquid fuels such as furnace oil?
cards.back: A positive-displacement gear pump.
cards.explain: Centrifugal pumps lose efficiency and head sharply as viscosity rises. Gear (positive-displacement) pumps deliver a near-constant flow regardless of viscosity, so they are the standard choice for heavy fuel oil.

cards.front: What are the main drawbacks of high sulphur content in fuel?
cards.back: Corrosion (sulphuric acid formation below the acid dew point) and air pollution (SO₂/SO₃).
cards.explain: Sulphur burns to SO₂ and some SO₃; with water vapour these form sulphuric acid that condenses on cold surfaces such as economisers, air preheaters and chimneys. This sets a minimum safe flue gas exit temperature and limits how much waste heat can be recovered.

cards.front: What does proximate analysis of coal report, and what does ultimate analysis report?
cards.back: Proximate: moisture, volatile matter, ash and fixed carbon. Ultimate: elemental C, H, N, S, O (plus ash and moisture).
cards.explain: Proximate analysis is quick and tells how the coal will behave on a grate or in a furnace. Ultimate analysis gives the elemental composition needed to calculate theoretical air, flue gas quantity and indirect boiler efficiency. Proximate analysis does not give % carbon or % hydrogen.

cards.front: What is volatile matter in coal and how does it affect combustion?
cards.back: The gases (methane, hydrocarbons, H₂, CO, tar) driven off when coal is heated; it aids ignition and flame length.
cards.explain: Higher volatile matter makes coal easier to ignite and gives a longer flame, and it needs adequate secondary air for complete burning. Volatile matter is distinct from fixed carbon, which is the solid carbon remaining after volatiles are driven off.

cards.front: What are the '3 T's of good combustion?
cards.back: Time, Temperature and Turbulence.
