steps.prompt: Repeat for the 0.9 m shallow bed.
steps.answer: 0.9 m ÷ 0.0254 = 35.4 in, so ≈ 35 inches of water.
steps.explain: Same rule, shallower bed.

steps.prompt: Which bed needs less fan power, and why?
steps.answer: The 0.9 m shallow bed, because lower bed resistance gives lower pressure drop and fan power.
steps.explain: A deep bed raises pressure drop, which increases the effective gas velocity and fan power.

cards.front: Within what temperature band must an AFBC bed be operated, and what goes wrong outside it?
cards.back: Roughly 800 °C to 950 °C. Above 950 °C there is risk of clinker in the bed; below 800 °C combustion efficiency is lost.
cards.explain: This narrow window is the main special feature of AFBC. Sulphur retention is best at 800 to 850 °C inside this band.

cards.front: What bed temperature range gives efficient sulphur retention in an AFBC?
cards.explain: This sub-range of the 800 to 950 °C window suits limestone sulphur capture. Going above 950 °C risks clinker.

cards.front: How do over-bed and under-bed fuel feeding differ in fuel size and transport?
cards.back: Under-bed pneumatic feeding blows crushed coal (1 to 6 mm) through pipes that pierce the distributor. Over-bed feeding uses a screw conveyor and spreader for 6 to 10 mm coal, accepts oversize fuel and needs no transport lines.
cards.explain: Under-bed feeding needs more feed points as capacity rises, so fuel spreads evenly. Over-bed feeding is simpler because it removes the pneumatic transport lines.

cards.front: What is the purpose of the air distributor in an FBC boiler, and how is it built?
cards.back: It introduces fluidizing air evenly across the bed cross-section, keeps particles moving and prevents de-fluidized zones. It is a perforated metal plate forming the furnace floor, with nozzles or bubble caps to stop solids falling back.
cards.explain: Uneven air distribution creates dead zones in the bed. The distributor plate itself must be protected by refractory, a static bed layer or water-cooled tubes.

cards.front: Why does a shallow bed use less fan power than a deep bed?
cards.back: A shallow bed offers lower bed resistance and so a lower pressure drop. In a deep bed the pressure drop is higher, which raises the effective gas velocity and fan power.
cards.explain: Bed material is typically sand, ash, crushed refractory or limestone at about 1 mm average size. At the same fluidizing velocity, shallow and deep beds fluidize differently, which changes heat transfer to immersed surfaces.

cards.front: What share of total ash in an FBC boiler is bottom ash, and how is it removed?
cards.back: About 30 to 40 percent of total ash is bottom ash; the rest is fly ash. Bed ash is removed by continuous overflow to hold bed height and by intermittent bottom drain for oversize particles.
cards.explain: Oversize particles must be drained to avoid accumulation and defluidization. Firing high-ash washery rejects greatly increases the overflow drain quantity.

cards.front: An FBC boiler produces 2,000 kg/h of total ash. How much is bottom ash and how much is fly ash if bottom ash is 30 to 40 percent?
cards.back: Bottom ash 600 to 800 kg/h; fly ash 1,200 to 1,400 kg/h.
cards.explain: Fly ash is the larger share in FBC, so the fly ash handling system is the heavier duty.

steps.explain: Bottom ash is stated as a share of total ash.
The upper end of the chapter's range.

steps.prompt: Find the fly ash as the balance.
steps.explain: Fly ash is whatever ash is not bottom ash.

steps.prompt: Why does the fly ash share matter for plant design?
steps.answer: Fly ash is much higher than in conventional boilers because particles are elutriated at high velocity.
steps.explain: The chapter notes this makes the dust collection stages (cyclones, bag filters, ESPs) a major part of the design.

cards.front: How does an electrostatic precipitator (ESP) collect fly ash?
cards.back: A high voltage on discharge wires creates an electric field and ionizes the gas. Charged dust particles are pulled by Coulomb force onto collecting plates, which are cleaned by rapping, water washing or hopper removal.
cards.explain: Ions from the discharge wires charge the dust, and the electric field drives it to the plates. ESPs are one of the dust collectors used in FBC systems, alongside cyclones and bag filters.

cards.front: What fraction of fly ash can an ESP remove from flue gas?
cards.back: 95 to 99 percent.
cards.explain: The remaining 1 to 5 percent leaves with the flue gas, so the efficiency directly sets the stack dust load.

cards.front: An ESP receives 500 kg/h of fly ash in flue gas. How much is collected and how much leaves the stack at 95% efficiency and at 99% efficiency?
cards.back: At 95%: 475 kg/h collected, 25 kg/h emitted. At 99%: 495 kg/h collected, 5 kg/h emitted.
cards.explain: Moving from 95% to 99% cuts the stack dust load fivefold in this example.

steps.prompt: Find the collected fly ash at 95%.
steps.explain: ESP efficiency is the fraction of fly ash removed.

steps.prompt: Find the fly ash emitted at 95%.
steps.explain: Whatever is not collected leaves in the flue gas.

steps.prompt: Find the collected fly ash at 99%.
steps.explain: Upper end of the chapter's range.

steps.prompt: Find the fly ash emitted at 99%, and the change in stack load.
steps.explain: Small efficiency gains give large cuts in stack dust at high removal levels.

cards.front: In a CFBC, what share of total combustion air is upward fluidizing air, and where does the rest enter?
cards.back: 60 to 70 percent of total air is upward fluidizing air through the bottom distribution nozzles. The balance enters above the bottom of the furnace as secondary air.
cards.explain: Fuel and limestone are suspended in the fluidizing air stream, which runs at 3.7 to 9 m/s. The secondary air completes combustion above the bed.

cards.front: A CFBC supplies 10,000 m³/h of total combustion air. How much enters as fluidizing (bottom) air and how much as secondary air?
cards.back: Fluidizing air 6,000 to 7,000 m³/h; secondary air 3,000 to 4,000 m³/h.
cards.explain: The 60 to 70 percent split fixes the bottom air. Everything else must be secondary air.

steps.explain: Lower end of the chapter's range for upward fluidizing air.
Upper end of the range.

steps.prompt: Find the secondary air as the balance.
steps.explain: The secondary air is what is left after the bottom air.
Confirms the split is consistent with total air.

cards.front: At what temperature does CFBC combustion take place, and what happens to fine particles?
cards.back: 840 to 900 °C. Fine particles below 450 microns are elutriated out of the furnace by flue gas at 4 to 6 m/s, then collected by solids separators and recycled.
cards.explain: Solids circulation keeps the temperature fairly uniform. The chapter says the controlling parameters are temperature, residence time and turbulence, as in pulverized coal firing.

cards.front: How much solid is recycled in a CFBC per kg of fuel burnt?
cards.back: 50 to 100 kg of solids per kg of fuel.
cards.explain: The large recycle carries bed material back to the furnace, giving longer residence time for carbon and limestone use and efficient heat transfer to the furnace walls.

cards.front: A CFBC burns 12 t/h of coal. How much solids circulate per hour at 50 to 100 kg per kg of fuel?
cards.back: 600 to 1,200 t/h of solids.
cards.explain: Compared with 2 to 4 kg per tonne in an AFBC, the CFBC circulating load is enormous, which is why its separators must be large.

steps.prompt: Convert the fuel rate to kg/h.
steps.explain: The recycle rate is per kg of fuel, so the fuel rate must be in kg.

steps.prompt: Apply the lower rate of 50 kg per kg of fuel.
steps.explain: Lower end of the CFBC range.

steps.prompt: Apply the upper rate of 100 kg per kg of fuel.
steps.explain: Upper end of the range.

steps.prompt: What does this flow require of the separators?
steps.answer: Large mechanical cyclones capable of capturing and recycling the solids, which is why a CFBC needs a tall boiler.
steps.explain: The chapter ties the huge recycle to the cyclone size and boiler height.

cards.front: Name three conditions under which a CFBC is a good choice over other FBC types.
cards.back: Boiler capacity is large to medium; sulphur emission and NOₓ control are important; and the boiler must fire low-grade fuel or fuel of highly fluctuating quality.
cards.explain: CFBC is generally more economical than AFBC for industrial steam above about 75 to 100 t/h, but needs huge cyclones and a tall boiler.

cards.front: What is the principle of a circulating fluidized bed combustion (CFBC) boiler?
cards.back: Crushed fuel and limestone are suspended in upward air (60 to 70 percent of total air). Fine particles are carried out, separated by cyclones and recycled into the furnace. Combustion is controlled by temperature, residence time and turbulence.
cards.explain: Solids circulation moves heat transfer outside the combustion zone (convection section, water walls and riser exit) and gives longer residence time for carbon and limestone use.

cards.front: Explain the difference between CFBC and AFBC.
cards.back: CFBC runs at 3.7 to 9 m/s with 6 to 12 mm fuel and recycles 50 to 100 kg per kg of fuel. AFBC runs at 1.2 to 3.7 m/s with 1 to 10 mm coal and recycles 2 to 4 kg per tonne. CFBC uses calcium more efficiently (1.5:1 against 3.2:1 for AFBC).
cards.explain: AFBC keeps its heat transfer tubes immersed in the bed, while the CFBC has none and moves heat transfer to the convection section and walls. CFBC suits large capacity and low-grade or fluctuating fuel.

cards.front: How does a pressurized fluidized bed combustion (PFBC) system generate power, and what efficiency gain does it give?
cards.back: The bed vessel operates up to 16 ata. Off-gas drives a gas turbine, steam for a steam turbine is raised in tubes immersed in the bed, and turbine exhaust preheats the condensate. Overall conversion efficiency is 5 to 8 percent higher.
cards.explain: Combining gas and steam turbines is why PFBC generates electricity more efficiently than a conventional system, and it suits cogeneration or combined cycle power. Elevated pressure also reduces boiler size considerably.

cards.front: What aspects must be considered in a retrofit project converting a conventional boiler to FBC?
cards.back: Water/steam circulation design; furnace bottom-grate clearance; type of particulate control device; fan capacity; and availability of space.
cards.explain: Retrofits have been carried out successfully in India and abroad. Conversion can be done without major changes after a cost-benefit analysis, and oil-fired boilers can also be converted case by case.

cards.front: What changes does retrofitting a stoker-fired water tube boiler to FBC involve?
cards.back: Replace the grate with a distributor plate having short stand pipes for air from the wind box; add stand pipes to remove bed ash; add horizontal hairpin tubes in the bed with a forced-circulation pump from the drum; and modify the crusher to size the coal/limestone mix for under-bed injection.
cards.explain: The forced-circulation pump moves water from the boiler drum through the hairpin tubes in the bed. The crusher change lets the coal and limestone mix be injected pneumatically under the bed.

cards.front: What combustion efficiency and overall efficiency do FBC boilers achieve?
cards.back: Combustion efficiency over 95 percent irrespective of ash content; overall efficiency around 84 percent, plus or minus 2 percent.
cards.explain: Efficiency holds even with high-ash fuels. The chapter also notes that high heat transfer over a small immersed area reduces overall boiler size.

cards.front: An FBC boiler receives 10 MW of fuel heat. Using the chapter's overall efficiency of 84% plus or minus 2%, what steam heat output should be expected?
cards.back: 8.2 MW to 8.6 MW, with 8.4 MW at the mid-point.
cards.explain: Overall efficiency is useful output divided by fuel heat input, so the balance of 1.6 MW at the mid-point is the total loss.

steps.prompt: Find the output at the lower limit, 82%.
steps.explain: 84 minus 2 percent.

steps.prompt: Find the output at the upper limit, 86%.
steps.explain: 84 plus 2 percent.

steps.prompt: Find the output at the mid-point, 84%.
steps.explain: The chapter's stated overall efficiency.

steps.prompt: How much of the fuel heat is not delivered as output at the mid-point?
steps.explain: This is the total loss the efficiency figure accounts for.

cards.front: What is the highest ash content and lowest calorific value of coal that an FBC boiler can fire at rated output?
cards.back: Ash content up to 62 percent and calorific value as low as 2,500 kcal/kg. Carbon of only 1 percent by weight can sustain fluidized bed combustion.
cards.explain: This is why FBC is suited to low-grade fuels that conventional firing cannot handle well. Fines below 6 mm can also be burnt efficiently.

cards.front: What excess air does FBC operate at, and what does high CO₂ in the flue gas indicate?
cards.back: Only 20 to 25 percent excess air, because CO₂ in flue gas is about 14 to 15 percent at full load.
cards.explain: High CO₂ at low excess air shows that combustion is efficient. Operating at low excess air fits the high combustion efficiency FBC achieves.

cards.front: What fuel saving can a pressurized FBC combined with a gas turbine and steam turbine offer?
cards.back: A potential fuel saving of at least 4 percent.
cards.explain: Operating the bed at elevated pressure produces hot pressurized gases that power a gas turbine, combined with a conventional steam turbine to improve electricity efficiency.

cards.front: What problem does high silica in biomass such as rice husk cause in an FBC boiler?
cards.back: Frequent erosion of super-heater and economizer coils.
cards.explain: The chapter lists this among biomass-firing issues, alongside tube fouling from sand and mud in the fuel.

cards.front: How much chloride can cotton stalk contain, and what does it do in the boiler?
cards.back: About 8 to 9 percent. Chloride combines with sodium and potassium at high temperature and aggravates corrosion of boiler internals, especially super-heater tubes.
cards.explain: Red gram husk and twigs cause a different problem: cold-end corrosion of secondary super-heater and economizer tubes, because of their sulphur content.

cards.front: Why is it hard to set a workable air-to-fuel ratio in a biomass FBC boiler?
cards.back: Fuel mixes often contain 6 to 7 biomass types, each with its own air-to-fuel ratio.
cards.explain: Size variation and high moisture also cause unburnts and steam pressure fluctuations, so one ratio for the whole mix is difficult to set.

cards.front: What does high moisture content in biomass cause in the boiler?
cards.back: Frequent jamming of fuel in feeders, causing steam pressure and temperature fluctuations, and plugging and choking of closely spaced heating surfaces.
cards.explain: Tight super-heater coil spacing, often chosen for compact design, makes the plugging worse.

cards.front: In an FBC boiler, if the bed temperature exceeds 950 °C, what is the likely result: sand heating, ash fusion, melting of limestone or ash carry-over?
cards.back: Ash fusion (clinker formation).
cards.explain: The chapter notes that clinker forms in the bed above 950 °C, and FBC keeps the bed below ash fusion temperature.

cards.front: In a CFBC, which device captures and recycles the bed material: bag filter, settling chamber, cyclone or scrubber?
cards.back: Cyclone.
cards.explain: CFBC needs huge mechanical cyclones to capture and recycle the large amount of bed material. This is also why CFBC boilers are tall.

cards.front: What is the typical overall efficiency of an FBC boiler: 90%, 80%, 60% or 50%?
cards.back: About 80%, the closest option. The chapter gives 84 percent plus or minus 2 percent.
cards.explain: Choose 80 percent from the options given, but note the book states 84 percent plus or minus 2 percent. Read the exact figure before answering.

cards.front: Explain the concept of an FBC boiler with a sketch. What are its major benefits?
cards.back: Air is blown up through a bed of fine solid particles on a distributor. At sufficient velocity the bed fluidizes and burns crushed fuel at about 840 to 950 °C. Major benefits: high efficiency, compact size, fuel flexibility, low SO₂ and NOₓ, low corrosion, no clinker, quick load response and low maintenance.
cards.explain: A sketch should show the air distributor, the bed with in-bed heat transfer tubes, the dust collection path and the boiler. Fluidization gives the turbulence and heat transfer behind these benefits.

cards.front: What is the typical efficiency of a conventional thermal power plant, and what happens to the rest of the energy?
cards.back: About 35%. The other ~65% is lost, mainly as heat rejected to cooling water or air because of the limits of thermodynamic cycles.
cards.explain: Further losses of about 10-15% occur in transmission and distribution on the grid. Cogeneration tackles the problem by using heat that would otherwise be rejected.

cards.front: In the coal-fired power station energy balance (100 GJ input), what is the thermal efficiency and how much energy is lost in total?
cards.back: Thermal efficiency = 36.2%. Total loss = 63.8 GJ.
cards.explain: The book's figure labels the electricity output 36.3 GJ in one place, but its efficiency line uses 36.2 GJ. The itemised losses add up to the balance, which confirms the 63.8 GJ loss.

steps.prompt: Identify the input and output energy.
steps.answer: Input = 100 GJ (coal energy). Output = 36.2 GJ of electricity to the system.
steps.explain: Efficiency is always useful output divided by input on the same basis.
This matches the efficiency line printed under the balance diagram.
Every GJ that is not delivered as electricity appears as a loss in the balance.

steps.answer: Stack 10.2 + hot surfaces 1.0 + boiler leaks 0.8 + cooling tower/condenser 48.3 + unburnt carbon in ash and dust 0.7 + auxiliaries 2.8 = 63.8 GJ.
steps.explain: The items sum to the total loss, so the balance closes. The condenser/cooling-tower loss is by far the largest slice.

cards.front: What overall energy-use efficiency can cogeneration reach?
cards.back: Up to 85%, and above in some cases.
cards.explain: A conventional electricity-only plant manages about 35%. The gain comes from using the heat that a power plant would otherwise reject.

cards.front: What two useful forms of energy does cogeneration produce from one primary energy source?
cards.back: Mechanical energy and thermal energy.
cards.explain: Mechanical energy can drive an alternator or equipment such as a motor, compressor, pump or fan. Thermal energy can serve direct process use or produce steam, hot water, hot air or chilled water.

cards.front: An industry needs 24 units of electricity and 34 units of heat. Compare the fuel needed by separate production (power station 40%, boiler 85%) with cogeneration (85% overall). How much fuel is saved?
cards.back: Separate production needs 100 units; cogeneration needs 68 units. Saving = 32 units (32%).
cards.explain: Cogeneration cuts the losses from 42 units to 10 units. Most of the saving comes from not losing the heat that a separate power station would reject.

steps.prompt: Fuel for the electricity in a separate power station.
steps.explain: A 40% efficient station needs 60 units of fuel for 24 units of electricity.

steps.prompt: Fuel for the heat in a separate boiler.
steps.explain: An 85% efficient boiler needs 40 units of fuel for 34 units of heat.
This is the baseline for the comparison.
One plant at 85% overall efficiency serves both loads.

steps.answer: 100 - 68 = 32 units, which is 32% of the separate-production fuel.
steps.explain: Losses fall from 42 units (100 - 58) to 10 units (68 - 58).

cards.front: What are the macro-level and micro-level benefits of cogeneration?
cards.back: Macro: it shares part of the national utility's financial burden with the private sector and conserves indigenous energy sources. Micro: it can cut a user's overall energy bill, especially where power and heat are needed together and tariffs are rational.
cards.explain: At the national level, cogeneration spreads the investment burden. At site level, the saving depends on having a simultaneous need for both power and heat.

cards.front: Why does on-site cogeneration reduce the burden on the utility network?
cards.back: Electricity is generated on-site, so the grid carries less load and the transmission line losses are eliminated.
cards.explain: Cogeneration also saves fossil fuel and reduces greenhouse gas emissions, particularly CO₂.

cards.front: Name the three cogeneration technologies that have been widely commercialised.
cards.back: (1) Extraction or back-pressure steam turbines. (2) Gas turbine with heat recovery boiler, with or without a bottoming steam turbine. (3) Reciprocating engines with heat recovery boiler.
cards.explain: These three are the mainstream options. The chapter then describes each one in turn, with its heat-to-power characteristics.

cards.front: What is a specific advantage of steam turbines over other prime movers in cogeneration?
cards.back: They can burn a wide range of fuels, including coal, natural gas, fuel oil and biomass.
cards.explain: Some power generation efficiency may be given up to optimise heat supply. Steam turbines are mostly used where electricity demand is above 1 MW, up to a few hundred MW.

cards.front: Why are back-pressure cogeneration plants free of the need for large cooling towers?
cards.back: Their exhaust steam is used by the process, so there is no large condensing system to reject leftover heat.
cards.explain: Condensing turbines need a condenser and cooling tower to reject the heat that is not used. Back-pressure plants avoid that equipment.

cards.front: What size range do gas turbines cover in cogeneration, and which fuel is most common?
cards.back: From a fraction of a MW to about 100 MW. Natural gas is the most common fuel; light fuel oil or diesel can also be used.
cards.explain: Gas turbine cogeneration has grown fast because of natural gas availability, shorter project gestation and modular delivery.

cards.front: What is the main trade-off of gas turbine cogeneration between heat and power?
cards.back: Low heat-to-power conversion efficiency, but more heat can be recovered at higher temperatures.
cards.explain: The high-temperature exhaust suits a wide range of heating and cooling uses. Gas turbines also have a short start-up time and can run intermittently.

cards.front: How can a gas turbine cogeneration unit boost its heat output when the site needs more heat?
cards.back: Supplementary natural gas firing: extra fuel is mixed into the oxygen-rich exhaust gas and burned.
cards.explain: The exhaust still holds oxygen, so the extra firing raises thermal output efficiently. Many large units use this to change their heat-to-power ratio.

cards.front: Why are reciprocating engines popular with smaller energy-consuming facilities?
cards.back: They have high power generation efficiency, their heat recovery is efficient at small sizes, and they suit sites that need more electricity than heat, where low-quality heat (low-pressure steam or hot water) is acceptable.
cards.explain: Reciprocating engines are ideal for intermittent operation. Their performance is not as sensitive to ambient temperature as that of gas turbines.

cards.front: True or false: reciprocating engine performance is more sensitive to ambient temperature than gas turbine performance.
cards.back: False. Engine performance is not as sensitive to ambient temperature changes as gas turbine performance.
cards.explain: The drawback of engines is cost, not temperature sensitivity: a low initial investment, but high operating and maintenance costs from wear and tear.

cards.front: Name the four types of topping cycle cogeneration.
cards.back: (1) Combined-cycle topping: gas turbine, then heat recovery boiler, then steam turbine. (2) Steam-turbine topping: high-pressure boiler steam through a turbine, with low-pressure exhaust for process. (3) Diesel or gas engine with heat recovery from exhaust and jacket water. (4) Gas-turbine topping: gas turbine drives a generator and its exhaust feeds a heat recovery boiler.
cards.explain: In a topping cycle the fuel makes power first, and the leftover heat is the by-product used for process heat. Topping cycles are the most popular form of cogeneration.

cards.front: Which industries mainly use bottoming-cycle cogeneration, and why?
cards.back: Cement, steel, ceramic, gas and petrochemical industries, where high-temperature furnace or kiln heat is rejected at significantly high temperatures.
cards.explain: The rejected heat drives a recovery boiler and turbine-generator to make power. Bottoming-cycle plants are much less common than topping-cycle plants.

cards.front: In base electrical load matching, how is the plant sized and how is the rest of the power supplied?
cards.back: It is sized to the site's minimum electricity demand, taken from the historical demand curve. The rest of the power is bought from the grid.
cards.explain: Thermal demand can be met by the cogeneration system alone or with additional boilers. Surplus heat can be exported to neighbouring customers if the situation permits.

cards.front: In base thermal load matching, how is the plant sized and what covers extra demand?
cards.back: It is sized to the minimum thermal requirement and runs at full load at all times. Standby boilers or burners supply the extra heat, and extra power is bought from the grid.
cards.explain: If local law permits, excess electricity can be sold to the power utility.

cards.front: Which operating scheme makes a facility a stand-alone system, independent of the utility grid?
cards.back: Electrical load matching.
cards.explain: The system must cover all site power needs, including reserves for scheduled and unscheduled maintenance. Auxiliary boilers meet any extra heat demand, and surplus heat is wasted unless it can be exported.

cards.front: In thermal load matching, what does the plant follow, and how are power deficits and surpluses handled?
cards.back: It follows the site's heat demand at any time. A power shortfall is bought from the grid, and excess electricity can be sold to the utility if local legislation permits.
cards.explain: The prime movers are operated according to the thermal demand, so electricity output is set by the heat requirement.

cards.front: Which cogeneration system has the widest heat-to-power ratio range, and what is it?
cards.back: Back-pressure steam turbine, 4.0 to 14.3. For comparison: extraction-condensing steam turbine 2.0 to 10.0; gas turbine 1.3 to 2.0; combined cycle 1.0 to 1.7; reciprocating engine 1.1 to 2.5.
cards.explain: The steam turbine offers a large range of heat-to-power ratios, which is why it fits many different sites. Both heat and power are expressed in the same unit (kW) for the ratio.

cards.front: Under what three conditions is cogeneration most attractive?
cards.back: (a) Steam and power demand are balanced, within the steam-to-power output range of a suitable plant. (b) One plant or a group of plants has enough steam and power demand for economies of scale. (c) Peaks and troughs in demand can be managed, or adequate utility backup is available for electricity.
cards.explain: These conditions link the heat-to-power ratio to the load-matching schemes. Electricity backup is what allows a plant to cover demand peaks.

cards.front: Why does a sugar mill (heat at about 120 °C) suit a topping cycle, while a cement plant (heat at about 1450 °C) suits a bottoming cycle?
cards.back: Lower-temperature heat, such as a sugar mill's 120 °C, fits a topping cycle. Very high-temperature heat, such as a cement plant's 1450 °C, fits a bottoming cycle, which also supplies electricity.
cards.explain: The required quality of thermal energy (temperature and pressure) decides the type of cogeneration system.

cards.front: Why is a rice mill a good candidate for steam turbine cogeneration?
cards.back: It needs mechanical power for milling and heat for paddy drying, and a steam turbine can burn rice husk, the mill's own waste product.
cards.explain: Cheap fuels or waste products often decide whether a cogeneration option is competitive, because they set the running cost.

cards.front: Why should cogeneration for a pulp and paper plant be modular?
cards.back: The plant cannot run long without process steam, so the system should have more than one unit. If one unit shuts down, the energy supply is not seriously affected.
cards.explain: Modularity is a reliability feature for sites that cannot tolerate a prolonged loss of heat or power.

cards.front: How does a grid-dependent cogeneration system differ from a grid-independent (stand-alone) one?
cards.back: A grid-dependent system can buy or sell electricity through the grid. A stand-alone system meets all of the site's energy demands by itself.
cards.explain: For the same facility, the technical configuration differs between the two designs, so the choice must be made early.

cards.front: How can local environmental regulations limit the cogeneration choice?
cards.back: Stringent rules can rule out some fuels, because the cost of treating polluted exhaust gas, or of treating the fuel itself, can be too high.
cards.explain: Environmental rules therefore affect the technology and fuel choice, not only emissions limits.

cards.front: What overall thermal efficiency can a back-pressure cogeneration system reach with an efficient boiler?
cards.back: As much as 90%, when all the exhaust steam is used. The only other losses are gear drive, generator and steam generation.
cards.explain: The chapter's notes on cogeneration efficiency quote up to 85% for back-pressure systems. Both figures appear in the book, so use the number the question asks for.

cards.front: Compared with a back-pressure turbine, what does an extraction-condensing turbine offer, and what does it cost?
cards.back: A higher power-to-heat ratio and higher electricity generation efficiency. The cost is a lower overall thermal efficiency, because exhaust heat is lost in the cooling water.
cards.explain: Condensing systems need more auxiliary equipment, such as the condenser and cooling towers. They suit sites where electricity demand is much higher than steam demand and the load fluctuates.

cards.front: What temperatures apply to gas turbine gases at inlet and exhaust, and why is the exhaust useful?
cards.back: Gases enter at 900-1000 °C and leave at about 450-550 °C. The book gives 400-500 °C for the exit in one place. The hot exhaust makes the gas turbine well suited to high-grade heat supply.
cards.explain: The exhaust can meet all or part of the site's thermal (steam) demand. The OCR of the chapter shows the exit range twice with slightly different numbers.

cards.front: Which fuels suit gas turbines, and why must the hot gas be clean?
cards.back: Natural gas is most used. Gas oil, LPG and naphtha are also suitable. The hot gas must be free of particulates that erode the blades and of contaminants that cause corrosion.
cards.explain: A gas turbine runs at high speed and high temperature, so high-premium fuels are preferred. Distillate oils such as gas oil are also used.

cards.front: What is the efficiency of a stand-alone gas turbine without any heat recovery system?
cards.back: About 35 to 40%.
cards.explain: Losses come from blade efficiency, leakage through clearance spaces, friction and turbulence. Heat recovery in a steam generator is what recovers much of the rest.

cards.front: What share of the turbine's generated energy does the air compressor consume, and what does that do to net efficiency?
cards.back: About 50 to 60%. The 35-40% figures exclude the compressor, fuel pump and other auxiliaries, so the net turbine efficiency is lower than the calculated figure.
cards.explain: In most gas turbine plants the air compressor is an integral part of the turbine plant, so the net figure is the one that counts for usable output.

cards.front: What is turbine heat rate, and in which units is it expressed?
cards.back: The heat input to the turbine needed to produce 1 kWh of electricity. It is expressed in kJ/kWh (or kcal/kWh). 1 kWh = 3,600 kJ = 860 kcal.
cards.explain: Heat rate and efficiency are inversely related only for a pure power plant. For cogeneration, the useful process heat is not counted in the heat rate, so the inverse does not apply.

cards.front: What is a pressure survey on a steam turbine, and what conditions must it meet?
cards.back: Pressure is noted at tapping points along the expansion path and compared with design values to infer the turbine's internal condition. The gauges must be accurate and the readings taken while the load is steady.
cards.explain: A pressure survey should be carried out frequently on each running machine, because it shows deviations in performance early.

cards.front: For Case 1 of the illustrative cogeneration plant (6 MW electrical output, normal process flow), find the heat-to-power ratio. Process extraction: 13,470 kg/h at 3,011.35 kJ/kg with return condensate at 293 kJ/kg. Deaerator bleed: 3,550 kg/h at 2,835.8 kJ/kg.
cards.back: Heat-to-power ratio ≈ 2.16 (thermal output ≈ 12,968 kW against 6,000 kW electrical).
cards.explain: The ratio compares useful thermal output with electrical output in the same unit (kW). Converting kJ/h to kW uses 1 kWh = 3,600 kJ.

steps.prompt: Heat carried away in the process extraction.
steps.explain: The useful heat is the enthalpy drop from the extracted steam to the return condensate.

steps.prompt: Heat carried away in the deaerator bleed.
steps.explain: The book takes the bleed's full enthalpy as useful heat in this calculation.
Dividing kJ/h by 3,600 gives kW, because 1 kWh = 3,600 kJ.
The ratio is dimensionless (kW/kW). A value of 2.16 means 2.16 kW of heat for each kW of electricity.

cards.front: For the same Case 1 plant (boiler efficiency 83%, steam 34,800 kg/h at 3,418 kJ/kg, feed water at 251 kJ/kg), find the Energy Utilisation Factor (EUF).
cards.explain: EUF counts both electrical and useful thermal output against fuel heat input, so it is much higher than the electrical efficiency of the plant.

steps.explain: Each kWh is 860 kcal, the thermal equivalent of electricity.
The two extraction streams from the heat calculation, converted from kJ to kcal with 4.187 kJ/kcal.
Steam heat is divided by boiler efficiency to give the fuel heat input.
Useful output over fuel input. Counting the process heat is what lifts the factor above the power-only efficiency.

cards.front: What is trigeneration?
cards.back: Simultaneous generation of steam (heat), power and refrigeration through integrated systems.
cards.explain: Food processing and cold storage benefit most. A combined-cycle trigeneration plant with a gas turbine, waste heat boiler, steam turbine and absorption chiller can meet 100% of the facility's needs, with surplus power sold to the grid.

cards.front: A chemical plant reduces steam from 17.6 kg/cm²(g) to 1.8 kg/cm²(g) through a PRV for a process needing 5,189 Mcal/h. Replacing the PRV with a back-pressure turbine (8,000 h/yr, fuel 10,000 kcal/kg at Rs 25/kg, grid power at Rs 6/kWh, gearbox 98%, alternator 98%, mechanical 97%, boiler 85%): what is the annual net saving?
cards.back: About Rs 114.5 lakh per year. Power = 434 kW. Extra fuel cost = Rs 1,172.5/h. Grid saving = Rs 2,604/h. Net = Rs 1,431.5/h x 8,000 h.
cards.explain: The turbine needs more steam to deliver the same process heat, because its exit enthalpy is lower. The power it makes is therefore not free, but the grid power it displaces is worth more than the extra fuel.

steps.prompt: Fuel rate with the PRV (steam 9,072 kg/h).
steps.explain: Heat taken from the steam (668 minus condensate 94.5 kcal/kg), divided by boiler efficiency and fuel calorific value.

steps.prompt: Fuel rate with the back-pressure turbine (steam 9,767 kg/h).
steps.explain: The turbine needs more steam so that the process still gets the same heat duty at a lower exit enthalpy.
Rs 25,000 per tonne equals Rs 25 per kg.
Enthalpy drop from 668 to 627 kcal/kg, converted with 860 kcal/kWh, then reduced by gearbox, alternator and turbine mechanical efficiencies.
Grid power saved minus extra fuel cost, before annualising.

steps.answer: 1,431.5 x 8,000 = Rs 11,452,000, i.e. about Rs 114.5 lakh per year.
steps.explain: Operating hours convert the hourly benefit to an annual figure.

cards.front: A back-pressure turbine plant runs round the clock: steam 40 TPH, electrical output 3,200 kW. The process needs 44 TPH, which the existing boiler can supply through the turbine. With the same steam-to-power ratio and grid electricity at Rs 7/kWh, what is the daily saving from extra generation?
cards.back: Rs 53,760 per day (320 kW extra x 24 h x Rs 7/kWh).
cards.explain: The extra steam generates extra power at the existing steam-to-power ratio. Auxiliary power is unchanged, so the whole extra power displaces grid purchases.

steps.explain: This is the steam needed per unit of power in the existing machine. It is assumed to stay the same.
The extra steam the existing boiler can supply.
Divide the extra steam by the steam-to-power ratio.

steps.answer: 320 kW x 24 h x Rs 7/kWh = Rs 53,760 per day.
steps.explain: Extra generated power offsets grid electricity bought at Rs 7/kWh over 24 hours.

cards.front: In the same plant (boiler efficiency 80%, coal GCV 4,300 kcal/kg, steam enthalpy 780 kcal/kg, feed water at 135 °C), how much additional coal is needed per day for the extra 4 TPH of steam?
cards.back: 750 kg/h of coal, which is 18,000 kg (18 tonnes) per day.
cards.explain: The coal calculation uses the enthalpy rise from feed water to steam, divided by boiler efficiency and calorific value. It is the cost side of the extra power.

steps.prompt: Heat added per kg of steam.
steps.explain: The enthalpy rise from feed water at 135 °C to steam at 780 kcal/kg.
Total heat load of the additional 4 TPH.
Divide by boiler efficiency and the coal's GCV.
The plant runs round the clock, so the hourly figure is multiplied by 24.

cards.front: What is waste heat, and what matters more than its amount in a recovery study?
cards.back: Waste heat is heat generated by fuel combustion or a chemical reaction that is dumped into the environment although it could still be reused economically. The essential quality of heat is its 'value', not its amount.
cards.explain: The strategy for recovering heat depends partly on the temperature of the waste gases and on the economics involved. Two streams with the same heat content can have very different value, so temperature decides how practical recovery is.

cards.front: Why is recovering heat from a high-temperature waste stream usually more cost-effective?
cards.back: Higher temperature means higher quality heat, so recovery is usually more cost-effective.
cards.explain: Heat at a higher temperature has more potential value for a useful purpose. Low-temperature waste heat generally needs a use that can accept it directly, such as space heating.

cards.front: What must exist before any waste heat recovery study is worthwhile?
cards.back: There must be some use for the recovered heat, such as preheating combustion air, space heating, or preheating boiler feed water or process water.
cards.explain: The book stresses that recovered heat with no use is not a saving. Identify the sink for the heat before selecting any equipment.

cards.front: What is a cascade system of waste heat recovery?
cards.back: Recovery in stages: the high-temperature stage is used first (for example for air preheating), and the lower-temperature stage is used for process feed water heating or steam raising.
cards.explain: Cascading matches each temperature level with a suitable use. This ensures the maximum amount of heat is recovered at the highest potential.

cards.front: Flue gas from a heat treatment furnace leaves at 900 °C at 2,100 m³/h. It can be cooled to 180 °C. With density 1.19 kg/m³ and Cp 0.24 kcal/kg °C, how much heat is recoverable per hour, using Q = V × ρ × Cp × ΔT?
cards.back: About 4,31,827 kcal/h.
cards.explain: This is the book's worked example of the heat content formula. Only the temperature drop is recoverable, and Cp is per kg, so the volume flow must first be converted to a mass flow.

steps.prompt: Write the formula and list the values.
steps.answer: Q = V × ρ × Cp × ΔT, with V = 2,100 m³/h, ρ = 1.19 kg/m³, Cp = 0.24 kcal/kg °C.
steps.explain: Each term converts the volume flow into a heat quantity per hour.
Only the drop from inlet to exit temperature can be recovered.

steps.prompt: Find the mass flow of flue gas.
steps.explain: Cp is given per kg, so the flow must be in kg/h.
This is the heat available per hour for recovery.

cards.front: Using the book's rule of thumb, what fuel saving comes from a recuperator that cuts flue gas from 900 °C to 180 °C?
cards.explain: The book uses the rule of 1% fuel reduction for every 22 °C reduction in flue gas temperature. This is a rule-of-thumb estimate, not a design calculation.

steps.answer: 1% fuel reduction for every 22 °C reduction in flue gas temperature.
steps.explain: This is the basis of the book's furnace example.
The drop is the inlet temperature minus the final exhaust temperature.
Each 22 °C of drop gives 1% of fuel.
The book states the result as 33%.

cards.front: For a waste heat source that is a vapour stream, what extra heat becomes recoverable?
cards.back: When the vapour is condensed, its latent heat is also recoverable, in addition to its sensible heat.
cards.explain: Latent heat is released at a constant temperature during condensation. For steam or vapour streams it can be a large share of the total heat content.

cards.front: When is heat lost in providing chilled water a high-grade waste heat source?
cards.back: High grade if it can be used to reduce the demand for refrigeration. Low grade if the refrigeration unit is used as a form of heat pump.
cards.explain: The grade depends on whether the recovered heat reduces refrigeration load or only provides low-temperature heat. The book classes this source in Table 8.1.

cards.front: What are the typical waste gas temperature ranges of a glass melting furnace and of a dry-process cement kiln?
cards.back: Glass melting furnace: 1000–1550 °C. Dry-process cement kiln: 620–730 °C.
cards.explain: Both are high-temperature sources in the book's Table 8.2. The high-temperature range is where heat recovery usually gives the most valuable heat.

cards.front: What are the typical exhaust temperature ranges of steam boilers and gas turbines in the medium-temperature band?
cards.back: Steam boiler exhausts: 230–480 °C. Gas turbine exhausts: 370–540 °C.
cards.explain: The book's Table 8.3 lists these as medium-temperature sources. Recovery here usually means steam generation or air heating.

cards.front: True or false: a turbocharged reciprocating engine has a higher exhaust temperature range than a non-turbocharged one?
cards.back: False. Turbocharged: 230–370 °C. Non-turbocharged: 315–600 °C.
cards.explain: The book's Table 8.3 gives both ranges, and the turbocharged range is the lower one. Check these values against the table when answering trap questions.

cards.front: What are the two categories of benefit from waste heat recovery?
cards.back: Direct benefits: lower utility consumption and cost, and lower process cost, because process efficiency improves. Indirect benefits: reduced pollution, smaller equipment sizes, and lower auxiliary energy use.
cards.explain: Direct benefits show up in the energy and process cost lines. Indirect benefits come from a smaller flue gas flow, which allows smaller fans, pumps and other equipment.

cards.front: Which combustible wastes can be burnt in incinerators to recover heat and reduce pollution?
cards.back: Carbon monoxide gas, sour gas, carbon black off-gases, oil sludge, acrylonitrile and other plastic chemicals.
cards.explain: Burning these wastes in incinerators serves two purposes: the heat is recovered, and the release of toxic material to the atmosphere is reduced.

cards.front: Which plant documents should be reviewed to understand a process before designing a waste heat recovery system?
cards.back: Process flow sheets, layout diagrams, piping isometrics, and electrical and instrumentation cable ducting drawings.
cards.explain: This review identifies sources and uses of waste heat, upset conditions caused by recovery, available space, and constraints such as dew point in equipment.

cards.front: Name the economic parameters used to evaluate a waste heat recovery system.
cards.back: Investment, depreciation, payback period and rate of return. Advice from experienced consultants and suppliers should also be obtained.
cards.explain: The economic evaluation supports the choice of system. The book stresses that consultant and supplier advice is needed for a rational decision.

cards.front: Why do recuperators often use parallel flow rather than the more efficient counterflow arrangement?
cards.back: Because the recuperator also cools the exhaust duct that carries the gases away, which extends that duct's service life.
cards.explain: Counterflow would transfer heat more efficiently. Parallel flow is kept because it keeps the duct wall cooler.

cards.front: Why is the metallic concentric-tube recuperator called a 'radiation' recuperator?
cards.back: A substantial part of the heat passing from the hot gases to the inner tube is transferred by radiation. The cold air in the annulus is almost transparent to infrared, so it is heated only by convection.
cards.explain: The hot gas flows in the inner tube and the combustion air flows in the outer annulus. Only the radiant part of the transfer depends on the gas side being hot.

cards.front: How do baffles change a tube-type (convective) recuperator?
cards.back: Baffles make the air pass over the hot tubes more than once: two baffles give a three-pass recuperator, and one baffle giving two passes is a two-pass design. Baffling raises effectiveness but also raises cost and the pressure drop in the combustion air path.
cards.explain: More passes give a larger effective heat transfer area and better effectiveness. The trade-off is extra cost and extra resistance to air flow.

cards.front: Why are shell-and-tube recuperators more compact and more effective than radiation recuperators?
cards.back: They provide a larger heat transfer area through multiple tubes and multiple gas passes.
cards.explain: The book says shell and tube type recuperators are generally more compact and have higher effectiveness. This is why they are used where space and efficiency matter.

cards.front: What temperature limits do ceramic recuperators allow on the gas side and on the preheated air side?
cards.back: Gas side up to 1550 °C; preheated air side up to 815 °C. Metal recuperator liners lose life at inlet temperatures above about 1100 °C.
cards.explain: Ceramic tube recuperators were developed to overcome the temperature limit of metal recuperators. Later designs use short silicon carbide tubes joined by flexible seals.

cards.front: What happens to regenerator performance if the time between reversals is made very long?
cards.back: Thermal storage must be larger, which raises cost. The average preheat temperature is lower, which reduces fuel economy.
cards.explain: Regenerators are widely used in glass and steel melting furnaces for large capacities. The reversal period is a key design choice, balancing storage cost against preheat temperature.

cards.front: What sensible heat transfer efficiency can a heat wheel reach, and how large have heat wheels been built?
cards.back: Up to 85%. Heat wheels have been built up to 21 m in diameter with air capacities up to 1130 m³/min.
cards.explain: A heat wheel is a rotating porous disk with high heat capacity that carries heat from the hot duct to the cold duct. It suits low to medium temperature recovery.

cards.front: What are the three elements of a heat pipe?
cards.back: A sealed container, a capillary wick structure fused to the inner surface of the tube, and a working fluid.
cards.explain: The wick is sealed under vacuum with the working fluid. It returns the condensed liquid to the evaporator region.

cards.front: How does a heat pipe move heat from the hot end to the cold end?
cards.back: At the hot end the working fluid evaporates and absorbs latent heat. The vapour travels to the cool end, condenses and gives up its latent heat. The liquid then flows back through the wick.
cards.explain: The heat pipe has no moving parts and needs no input power. Heat transfer depends on repeated evaporation and condensation of the working fluid.

cards.front: What operating temperature and heat recovery capability do heat pipe heat exchangers offer?
cards.back: They can operate at 315 °C with 60% to 80% heat recovery.
cards.explain: The book also notes that heat pipe systems are lightweight and compact. They lower fan horsepower and need no cooling water or lubrication systems.

cards.front: A heat pipe can transfer up to how many times more thermal energy than copper, the best known conductor?
cards.back: Up to 100 times.
cards.explain: Heat pipes absorb and transfer thermal energy with no moving parts, so they need minimal maintenance.

cards.front: By how much does each 22 °C reduction in flue gas temperature reduce boiler fuel use?
cards.back: About 1% of the boiler's fuel.
cards.explain: This applies whether the heat goes to an economiser (feed water) or an air preheater (combustion air). The book uses it as the standard rule of thumb for boiler heat recovery.

cards.front: How much feed water temperature rise in an economiser, and how much combustion air temperature rise in an air preheater, gives 1% boiler fuel saving?
cards.back: 6 °C rise in feed water temperature, or 20 °C rise in combustion air temperature, gives 1% fuel saving.
cards.explain: These are the book's conversion figures for boiler heat recovery. They make it easy to estimate the saving from a measured temperature change.

cards.front: When must a shell-and-tube heat exchanger be used for waste heat recovery?
cards.back: When the waste heat medium is a liquid or vapour that heats another liquid, because both paths must be sealed to contain their pressures. A condensing vapour is normally kept in the shell.
cards.explain: The higher-pressure fluid is circulated in the tubes, since the shell is inherently weaker. Vapour condensing inside small parallel tubes causes flow instability, so it is placed in the shell.

cards.front: Why is a plate heat exchanger used when the temperature difference is small?
cards.back: When temperature differences are small, the cost of heat exchange surface is a major factor. Thin corrugated plates separated by gaskets give a large surface in a compact unit. Typical uses are milk pasteurisation and food evaporation.
cards.explain: The hot and cold streams flow in alternate channels between the plates. The corrugations improve heat transfer.

cards.front: What is a waste heat boiler, and how does it produce steam?
cards.back: It is usually a water-tube boiler in which hot exhaust gases from gas turbines, incinerators and similar sources pass over water-filled tubes. The water is vaporised in the tubes and the steam is collected in a steam drum.
cards.explain: Because the exhaust gases are usually in the medium-temperature range, the water tubes are often finned to increase the gas-side heat transfer area and make the boiler compact.

cards.front: What is the rule-of-thumb temperature limit for waste heat recovery, and why?
cards.back: Below about 120 °C (or better, 150 °C, for a safe margin) is usually the limit, because of the risk of condensation of corrosive liquids.
cards.explain: Rising fuel costs can make even low-temperature heat worth using for space heating. The corrosion risk sets the practical floor for recovery.

cards.front: Describe the four steps of the vapour compression heat pump cycle.
cards.back: 1) The evaporator extracts heat from the waste heat source and boils the working fluid. 2) The compressor raises its pressure and temperature, using external work. 3) The condenser delivers heat to the user. 4) The throttling valve reduces the pressure back to the evaporator condition, and the cycle repeats.
cards.explain: It is a closed cycle: the circulating substance is kept separate from the source and user streams and reused each time round.

cards.front: How much heat can a heat pump upgrade, relative to the energy the device consumes?
cards.back: More than twice the energy consumed by the device.
cards.explain: A heat pump lifts low-grade heat from ambient air, water or earth to a useful temperature by doing compression work with an electric motor-driven compressor.

cards.front: Why are heat pump applications most promising when both heating and cooling are used?
cards.back: Example: in a plastics factory, chilled water from the heat pump cools the injection moulding machines, while the heat output warms the factory or office.
cards.explain: Using both outputs makes the heat pump's cost go further. The book also lists product drying and maintaining dry storage atmospheres as applications.

cards.front: What is a direct contact heat exchanger, and where is it typically used?
cards.back: Low pressure steam is condensed directly in incoming water, which is sprayed over trays or packed beds, heating it. The typical application is the deaerator of a steam generating station.
cards.explain: Direct contact works only where the steam and water are miscible, as the book notes. The steam is completely condensed in the incoming water.

cards.front: A crude oil furnace heats 500 m³/h of crude (SG 0.85, Cp 0.6 kcal/kg °C) from 255 °C to 360 °C, firing 3.4 t/h of fuel oil with GCV 9,850 kcal/kg. An air preheater heats 57 t/h of combustion air (Cp 0.24) from 28 °C to 195 °C. What is furnace efficiency before and after the air preheater?
cards.back: Before: 80%. After: 85.8%.
cards.explain: The air preheater returns heat to the furnace, so less fuel is needed for the same heat gain in the crude. The heat gain by the crude does not change; only the heat input falls.

steps.prompt: Find the heat gain by the crude.
steps.explain: Volume (m³) × 1000 × SG gives mass in kg/h.

steps.prompt: Find the heat input before the air preheater.
steps.explain: Fuel in t/h is converted to kg/h and multiplied by GCV.

steps.prompt: Find the furnace efficiency before the air preheater.
steps.explain: Efficiency is heat gain divided by heat input.

steps.prompt: Find the heat recovered by the air preheater.
steps.explain: Air is heated from the 28 °C ambient, not from zero.

steps.prompt: Find the new heat input and the efficiency after the air preheater.
steps.explain: The heat saved from the flue gas reduces the fuel input for the same heat gain.

cards.front: A boiler economiser cuts flue gas temperature from 260 °C to 150 °C. Using the book's rule, what is the fuel saving?
cards.back: About 5% of boiler fuel.
cards.explain: The rule is 1% fuel saving per 22 °C drop in flue gas temperature. The 1,000 kg/h fuel figure in the explanation is only an example to show scale.

steps.prompt: Find the flue gas temperature drop.
steps.explain: The drop is the gas temperature entering minus the gas temperature leaving.

steps.answer: 1% boiler fuel saving per 22 °C drop in flue gas temperature.
steps.explain: This is the book's rule for economisers and air preheaters.
Five steps of 22 °C give five percent.

steps.answer: Result: 5% of boiler fuel; for example, 5% of 1,000 kg/h = 50 kg/h.
steps.explain: Rule-of-thumb estimate only; the actual saving depends on the boiler and the operating conditions.

cards.front: A hospital cooling plant recovers 28,225 kcal/h of heat from exhaust air and its capacity falls by 9.33 TR. If plant capacity costs Rs 12,000 per TR, what is the capital cost saving?
cards.explain: This is the book's case example, which states the saving as Rs 1,12,000. The chapter does not date the cost figures, so the year is not known from the text.

steps.answer: Plant capacity reduction = 9.33 TR; capital cost = Rs 12,000 per TR.
steps.explain: The 28,225 kcal/h recovered heat gives the 9.33 TR reduction in the book.

steps.prompt: Multiply capacity reduction by capital cost.
steps.explain: This is the capital cost avoided by not installing the extra capacity.
The book states Rs 1,12,000 as the capital cost saving.

steps.answer: Operating electricity cost is Rs 268 per million kcal (based on 0.8 kW/TR) in the book.
steps.explain: Capital saving and operating cost are separate figures and must not be added together without the operating data.

cards.front: A carbon black plant vents CO-rich gas. An incinerator with a waste heat boiler and steam turbine costs about Rs 350 lakh and saves about Rs 160 lakh a year in power. What is the simple payback period?
cards.explain: The book does not state a payback for this case. This simple payback is derived from its cost and saving figures and ignores interest, running costs and the pollution benefit.

steps.prompt: Identify the capital cost and the annual saving.
steps.answer: Capital cost Rs 350 lakh; annual saving about Rs 160 lakh per annum.
steps.explain: Both figures are given in the case example.

steps.prompt: Divide the cost by the annual saving.
steps.explain: Simple payback is capital cost divided by annual net saving.
The saving is an approximate figure (tilde in the book), so the answer is approximate too.

steps.prompt: Check what the estimate leaves out.
steps.answer: Simple payback ignores the time value of money and the running costs of the new equipment.
steps.explain: Treat the result as a first estimate, as the book suggests for investment decisions.

cards.front: A furnace flue gas stream of 2,000 kg/h (Cp 0.25 kcal/kg °C) drops from 800 °C to 250 °C across a heat exchanger of 98% efficiency. (a) How much heat is recovered? (b) How many litres per hour of water can be heated by 50 °C from this heat?
cards.back: (a) 2,69,500 kcal/h. (b) 5,390 litres/h.
cards.explain: This is short question S-2 in the book, which gives no answer key. The working uses Q = m × Cp × ΔT × efficiency, and assumes water density of 1 kg/L.

steps.prompt: Find the temperature drop of the flue gas.
steps.explain: Only the temperature drop across the exchanger is recovered.

steps.prompt: Find the heat available from the gas stream.
steps.explain: This is mass flow × Cp × ΔT.
The exchanger does not recover all the available heat.

steps.answer: 2,69,500 ÷ (1 × 50) = 5,390 kg/h, which is about 5,390 litres/h at water density 1 kg/L.
steps.explain: Water heat needed per kg is Cp × ΔT, with Cp of water taken as 1 kcal/kg °C.

cards.front: What are the three ways heat flows from a warm medium to a cooler one?
cards.back: Radiation (warm surface to a cooler surface across an air space), conduction (through solid or fluid materials) and convection (by physical movement of air).
cards.explain: Heat transfer is the flow of thermal energy from a hotter object to a cooler one. Radiation needs no medium, conduction moves heat through material without bulk movement, and convection carries heat along with moving air or fluid.

cards.front: What four criteria govern the rate of heat transfer between a hot and a cold fluid?
cards.back: (1) Temperature difference between the fluids; (2) area of the conductive barrier; (3) resistance to heat flow in each fluid; (4) material of the barrier, which must be compatible with the process fluids and must not corrode or contaminate them.
cards.explain: A larger temperature difference and a larger area both raise the heat flow. High resistance on either fluid side slows the overall rate, so the barrier material is chosen for compatibility as well as conductivity.

cards.front: What is a heat exchanger?
cards.back: A device that transfers heat energy from one fluid to another, generally without mixing the two fluids.
cards.explain: Heat only flows from hotter to cooler, so the two fluids must be at different temperatures and in thermal contact. They stay separate, which is why the design uses walls or tubes between them.

cards.front: Name the five purposes a heat exchanger can serve.
cards.back: (1) Heat a cooler fluid with a hotter one; (2) cool a hot fluid with a cooler one; (3) boil a liquid with a hotter fluid; (4) condense a gas with a cooler fluid; (5) boil a liquid while condensing a hotter gas.
cards.explain: The purposes cover sensible heating or cooling and phase change. Recognising the purpose tells you whether the exchange is sensible, latent or both.

cards.front: Is the heat lost by the hot fluid exactly equal to the heat gained by the cold fluid in a real heat exchanger?
cards.back: No. In theory they are equal, but environmental heat losses make them differ slightly. Calculations assume they are equal to simplify the work, and insulation keeps the losses small.
cards.explain: The energy balance (heat lost by hot side = heat gained by cold side) is the basis of exchanger calculations. Insulating equipment and piping minimises the losses that the simplification ignores.

cards.front: What does Q = m × Cₚ × ΔT give, and what are its units?
cards.back: Heat transferred Q in kW, where m is mass flow in kg/s, Cₚ is specific heat in kJ/kg·°C and ΔT is the temperature difference between the fluid's inlet and outlet in °C.
cards.explain: This is the sensible heat gained or lost by a fluid with no phase change. Apply it to each stream separately, then use the energy balance to link the hot and cold sides.

cards.front: What is the basic heat exchanger design equation?
cards.back: Q = U × A × ΔT_LMTD, where Q is the heat transfer rate, U the overall heat transfer coefficient, A the heat transfer surface area and ΔT_LMTD the log mean temperature difference.
cards.explain: The equation links the heat duty to the driving force and the surface. For a known duty, a higher U or a higher ΔT_LMTD means less area is needed. It can be rearranged to size the area.

cards.front: What LMTD value is used when the temperature difference between the two fluids is the same at both ends of the exchanger?
cards.back: The log mean formula gives zero in this case, so the LMTD is taken as the temperature difference at each end (the terminal temperature difference). In the book's example that is 30 °C.
cards.explain: When the temperature difference is constant along the length, the log formula breaks down. Using the terminal difference keeps the design equation usable.

cards.front: What does the overall heat transfer coefficient U depend on?
cards.back: The conductivity of the wall separating the fluids, the convection coefficients on the hot and cold sides, the wall thickness and the fouling coefficients. In practice U is often found by measuring the other parameters and calculating it.
cards.explain: U combines all the resistances between the two fluids. Fouling deposits add resistance, so they lower U.

cards.front: Between what limits does the temperature correction factor F usually lie, and when can F be taken as 1?
cards.back: F usually lies between 0.85 and 0.98. F can be taken as 1 only when the flow is purely counter-current.
cards.explain: F corrects the LMTD for exchangers that are not truly counter-current, which is common in cross-flow and multi-pass designs. Charts or a numerical method are used to find F for a given configuration.

cards.front: What are the three broad flow-pattern classes of heat exchangers?
cards.back: Counter flow, parallel flow and cross flow.
cards.explain: The classes describe how the hot and cold fluids move relative to each other. Flow pattern, along with available space and economics, sets the type and configuration of an exchanger.

cards.front: When is a counter-flow design most valuable?
cards.back: When there is a temperature cross, meaning the desired outlet temperature of one fluid lies between the inlet and outlet temperatures of the other fluid.
cards.explain: In counter flow the hottest cold-side outlet meets the hottest hot-side inlet, so the cold fluid can be heated above the hot fluid's outlet temperature. A true counter flow is hard to build for many applications, but plate, double-pipe and spiral exchangers come close.

cards.front: Where are cross-flow designs commonly used, and why?
cards.back: In most shell-and-tube and air-cooled exchangers, because a counter-flow layout is sometimes impractical due to high flow volumes or space restrictions.
cards.explain: In cross flow the two fluids move at right angles. Most applications use multiple passes, which combine cross flow and counter flow and can produce a partial temperature cross.

cards.front: What is a double-pipe heat exchanger and where is it used?
cards.back: Two concentric tubes, with one fluid in the inner tube and the other in the annular space between the tubes. It is used for cooling process fluids where only small heat transfer areas are needed.
cards.explain: It is one of the simplest configurations. It can run in parallel or counter flow, and several units can be combined in series or parallel to form a system.

cards.front: In a shell-and-tube exchanger, why is the process fluid usually placed inside the tubes?
cards.back: For ease of cleaning, and to use the higher pressure capability inside the tubes.
cards.explain: Tubes handle higher pressure better than the shell, and the tube side is easier to clean. Baffles on the shell side direct the flow across the tubes and support them.

cards.front: What are the main advantages and the main limitation of plate heat exchangers?
cards.back: Advantages: high heat transfer coefficients and area, low pressure drop and very high effectiveness. Limitation: relatively low pressure capability.
cards.explain: Corrugated plates increase turbulence and heat transfer. Plate exchangers suit duties with modest pressure where high effectiveness is needed.

cards.front: How does the overall heat transfer coefficient of a plate exchanger compare with a traditional shell-and-tube exchanger?
cards.back: Plate exchangers can reach about 8,000 W/m²·°C under favourable conditions. Traditional shell-and-tube exchangers are usually below 2,500 W/m²·°C.
cards.explain: The much higher U of plate units means a smaller area for the same duty. This is one reason plate units suit close temperature approaches.

cards.front: Why is counter flow usually preferred, and when is parallel flow chosen instead?
cards.back: Counter flow gives a larger effective LMTD, so a smaller area and greater potential energy recovery. Parallel flow is chosen for a high initial heating rate, for moderate tube wall temperatures (useful where fouling is aggravated by high temperature) or for rapid heating of viscous fluids.
cards.explain: A larger LMTD means less area for the same heat transfer. Parallel flow gives cooler tube walls and a fast start, which can cut pumping needs for viscous fluids.

cards.front: How do surface condensers differ from barometric condensers?
cards.back: Surface condensers circulate cooling water through tubes, so steam condenses on a cool surface and the condensate is collected. Barometric condensers rely on direct contact between the cooling water and the steam.
cards.explain: Surface condensers keep the condensate separate from the cooling water, so it can be returned and reused. Barometric units are simpler but mix the cooling water with the steam.

cards.front: What is the role of a condenser in a steam turbine or ejector system?
cards.back: In turbine applications it runs under vacuum and removes a significant amount of latent heat from the exhaust steam, which is recovered as condensate. In ejector applications it condenses the motive steam and condensable vapours, reducing the motive steam needed.
cards.explain: Recovering the condensate returns hot water to the system instead of losing it. In ejector systems, condensing the motive steam cuts the steam the ejector consumes.

cards.front: Why is steam injected into the bottom of a distillation tower?
cards.back: To reduce the partial pressures of the hydrocarbons, which facilitates their separation and reduces coke formation on tray surfaces.
cards.explain: Distillation separates crude oil or feedstock into components by their boiling points. The lower partial pressure helps the components separate, and it also reduces coking on the trays.

cards.front: What does an evaporator do and how is it usually built?
cards.back: It reduces the water content of a liquid, usually by heating it with steam, to concentrate the product. Most are shell-and-tube exchangers with steam on the shell side and the product being concentrated in the tubes.
cards.explain: Evaporators are used widely in food processing, chemicals, steel, forest products and textiles. They can be single-effect or multiple-effect.

cards.front: Roughly what fraction of the steam of a single-effect evaporator is needed after adding a first effect, and then a second effect?
cards.back: Adding one effect cuts steam use to nearly 50% of the original. Adding another effect brings it to nearly 33%.
cards.explain: Each effect reuses the latent heat of the vapour from the previous effect. The savings drop off with each added effect, which is why the number of effects is limited.

cards.front: Why does reduced heat transfer in an exchanger matter for a process?
cards.back: It almost always affects cycle time and product cost. Exchanger performance should be monitored and maintained at regular intervals set by cost-benefit criteria.
cards.explain: Efficient heating and cooling depend on good heat transfer from the surfaces. A good operation and maintenance policy starts at installation and continues in later years.

cards.front: What happens to utility requirements and to exchanger area when the minimum approach temperature (ΔTmin) in pinch analysis is increased?
cards.back: Utility requirements (steam and cooling) increase, and area requirements decrease.
cards.explain: A larger ΔTmin means less heat is recovered, so more hot and cold utility is needed. A larger approach temperature also means the exchangers can be smaller.

cards.front: In pinch analysis, what is the defining parameter that decides whether a hot and cold stream match is suitable?
cards.back: Quality, which for heat means temperature.
cards.explain: Pinch treats a process as supplies and demands of commodities such as energy or water. Inefficient transfer between mismatched streams wastes the imported utility.

cards.front: What do the hot and cold composite curves show in pinch analysis?
cards.back: The hot composite curve shows the process's heat availability and the cold composite curve shows its heat demands. The degree to which they overlap is the potential for heat recovery.
cards.explain: Building the curves needs a complete and consistent heat and mass balance. Sliding one curve horizontally changes only the relative position, not the stream data.

cards.front: In the chapter's composite-curve example with ΔTmin = 10 °C, what are the minimum hot and cold utility loads?
cards.back: Minimum hot utility Q_Hmin = 900 kW. Minimum cold utility Q_Cmin = 750 kW.
cards.explain: The heating and cooling that remain after maximum internal recovery between the composite curves give these targets. They set the energy target before any heat exchanger is designed.

cards.front: What is the main advantage of pinch technology over conventional design methods?
cards.back: It sets energy and capital cost targets for a process or a whole site before design, so the scope for energy savings and the investment needed can be judged before projects are identified.
cards.explain: Targets come from stream data alone. Pinch also guides debottlenecking, choice of combined heat and power, and recovery of low-grade waste heat.

cards.front: For a given heat duty and temperature difference, does a higher heat transfer coefficient need a larger or a smaller area?
cards.back: A smaller area. From A = Q / (U × ΔT_LMTD), a higher U reduces A.
cards.explain: A higher U means heat passes through the wall more readily, so less surface is needed. This is why high-U plate exchangers can be compact.

cards.front: Does an exchanger's effectiveness depend on the LMTD?
cards.back: No. Effectiveness is the ratio of the actual heat transferred to the heat that an exchanger of infinite size could transfer. It is built from the flow heat capacities and inlet temperatures, not the LMTD.
cards.explain: Effectiveness is the best way to compare different types of exchanger. The LMTD is an average temperature difference used in the design equation and is not part of the effectiveness definition.

cards.front: How much heat does 1,000 kg of water gain when it is heated from 30 °C to 70 °C (Cₚ = 1 kcal/kg·°C)?
cards.explain: This is a direct use of the sensible heat formula, with the specific heat of water given in kcal, so the answer is in kcal.

steps.prompt: Which formula gives the heat gained by a fluid with no phase change?
steps.explain: This is the sensible heat formula used throughout the chapter.
The rise is the outlet temperature minus the inlet temperature.
Specific heat is 1 kcal/kg·°C, so the result is in kcal, not kJ.

cards.front: A process stream is cooled from 94 °C to 65 °C while cooling water is heated from 30 °C to 46 °C. What is the log mean temperature difference (LMTD)?
cards.back: About 41.2 °C.
cards.explain: The LMTD is an average driving force between the two end temperature differences. It lies between the two end differences and is lower than their arithmetic mean.

steps.prompt: Find the temperature difference at the first end.
steps.explain: Pair the hot inlet with the cold outlet, as in the book's example.

steps.prompt: Find the temperature difference at the other end.
steps.explain: Pair the hot outlet with the cold inlet.
The log mean of the two end differences is the single average used in Q = U × A × ΔT_LMTD.

cards.front: In the chapter's pipe-cooler example, milk (0.4 kg/s, Cₚ 3,890 J/kg·°C) is cooled from 49 °C to 18 °C in a 2.5 cm bore pipe. The bath is at 10 °C and U = 900 J/m²·s·°C. What pipe length is needed?
cards.back: About 34.8 m, which gives 2.73 m² of surface.
cards.explain: Heat removed is found from the energy balance, then the design equation gives the area, and the pipe geometry gives the length.

steps.prompt: Find the heat removed from the milk.
steps.explain: Mass flow times specific heat times the temperature drop.

steps.prompt: Find the log mean temperature difference with the bath at 10 °C.
steps.explain: The bath is the constant second fluid, so both ends are measured from 10 °C.
This is the design equation Q = U × A × ΔT rearranged for A.
The heat transfer area of a pipe is its circumference times its length.

cards.front: In a counter-flow exchanger, brine (1.8 kg/s, Cₚ 3.38 kJ/kg·°C) enters at −8 °C and leaves at 10 °C, cooling water (1.05 kg/s, Cₚ 4.18 kJ/kg·°C) that enters at 32 °C. The area is 55 m². Find the water outlet temperature and the overall U.
cards.back: Water leaves at about 7 °C. U ≈ 0.11 kW/m²·°C (about 110 W/m²·°C).
cards.explain: Heat balance gives the unknown outlet temperature. The LMTD then gives U from the design equation.

steps.prompt: Find the heat gained by the brine.
steps.explain: Heat lost by the brine equals heat gained by the water.
Solve the water heat balance for the unknown outlet temperature.

steps.prompt: Find the two end temperature differences.
steps.explain: In counter flow the water inlet is paired with the brine outlet, and the water outlet with the brine inlet.
Log mean of the two end differences.
kW divided by m² and °C gives kW/m²·°C, which is the same as kJ/m²·s·°C.

cards.front: A counter-flow double-pipe exchanger heats 10.5 m³/h of water from 30 °C to 90 °C (Cₚ 4.18 kJ/kg·°C). The process liquid enters at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C. With U = 814 W/m²·°C, find (a) the counter-flow area and (b) the % increase in area if the flows were parallel.
cards.back: (a) About 9.5 m². (b) About 14% more area (10.8 m²) for parallel flow.
cards.explain: The same duty needs more area in parallel flow because its LMTD is smaller. This is the book's solved example.

steps.prompt: Find the water mass flow and the heat duty.
steps.explain: Divide kJ/h by 3,600 to get kW.
Counter flow pairs the hot inlet with the cold outlet.
Design equation with Q in W.
Parallel flow pairs the two inlets and the two outlets.

steps.prompt: Find the parallel-flow area and the % increase.
steps.explain: The smaller LMTD of parallel flow needs more area for the same duty.

cards.front: Stream 1 is cooled from 200 °C to 100 °C, releasing 2,000 kW. What is its heat capacity flow rate CP?
cards.back: CP = 20 kW/°C.
cards.explain: CP is the slope of the stream's enthalpy against temperature. It equals mass flow times specific heat.

steps.prompt: Identify the heat duty and the temperature change.
steps.explain: Use the stream's own data.
Heat duty divided by temperature change gives the slope of the stream line.

steps.answer: CP = (mass flow) × (specific heat), so 20 kW/°C is the product of the flow rate and Cₚ.
steps.explain: This is why CP is used to build composite curves from several streams.

cards.front: In the 150 °C to 100 °C interval of the hot composite curve, Stream 1 (CP 20 kW/°C) and Stream 2 (CP 40 kW/°C) are both present. What is the hot composite CP in this interval?
cards.explain: Hot composite CP in each temperature interval is the sum of the CPs of the streams present in it.

steps.prompt: Identify which hot streams cover the interval 150 °C to 100 °C.
steps.answer: Stream 1 (200 to 100 °C) and Stream 2 (150 to 60 °C) both cover it.
steps.explain: A stream contributes only within its own temperature range.
Stream 2 has a duty of 3,600 kW over 90 °C, so CP = 40.

steps.prompt: Add the CPs of the streams present.
steps.explain: The sum gives the slope of the hot composite curve in that interval.

cards.front: Why is power transmitted over long distances at high voltage?
cards.back: For the same power, current falls as voltage rises, so I²R line losses fall roughly with 1/V².
cards.explain: Power P = √3·V·I·cosφ; doubling voltage halves current for the same power, cutting resistive losses to a quarter. This is why generation at 11–33 kV is stepped up for transmission and stepped down at substations, whose main role is voltage transformation. HVDC is preferred for very long distances because it avoids reactive power flow and has lower losses there.

cards.front: A plant receives 96 MU at its end and the T&D efficiency is 80%. How much generation is required?
cards.explain: Energy delivered = energy generated × T&D efficiency, so generation = delivered ÷ efficiency. A common trap is to multiply (96 × 0.8 = 76.8) instead of dividing. The 24 MU difference is the T&D loss.

cards.front: How is the AT&C (Aggregate Technical & Commercial) loss of a distribution utility calculated?
cards.back: AT&C loss = 1 − (Billing efficiency × Collection efficiency).
cards.explain: Billing efficiency = energy billed (metered + unmetered assessed) ÷ input energy. Collection efficiency = amount actually collected for current bills (excluding arrears) ÷ amount billed. Example: billing 80% and collection 75% gives AT&C loss = 1 − 0.6 = 40%. Revenue realised per kWh input = current collections ÷ input energy.

cards.front: What makes up a two-part industrial electricity tariff?
