cards.front: An engine room of 30 m × 20 m × 5 m needs 20 air changes per hour. The ventilator fan has a 15 mm WC static rise and 70% fan efficiency. At 90% motor efficiency, what motor power is drawn?
cards.back: About 3.9 kW (fan shaft about 3.5 kW).
cards.explain: Airflow comes from room volume times air changes. The static efficiency formula gives fan shaft power, and motor efficiency gives the electrical input.

steps.explain: Length × breadth × height.
Convert air changes per hour to m³/s.
Rearranged static efficiency formula: kW = Q × SP ÷ (102 × η).
Motor input = shaft power ÷ motor efficiency.

cards.front: A boiler ID fan is to be sized for 30,000 m³/h at 240 mm WC. Applying the book's ID fan safety margins, what is the design duty?
cards.back: 36,000 m³/h at about 312 mm WC.
cards.explain: The book gives ID fans a 20% margin on volume and a 30% margin on head. Margins are normally agreed with the process supplier.

steps.explain: 20% on volume for ID fans.
30% on head (pressure) for ID fans.
This is the duty to specify when sizing the ID fan.

cards.front: A VSD for boiler fans costs Rs 0.65 million and saves Rs 0.33 million a year. What is the simple payback?
cards.back: About 2.0 years (1.97). The book says it paid back in under 2 years.
cards.explain: Simple payback is investment divided by annual saving. It ignores interest and inflation.

steps.explain: Simple payback formula.

steps.prompt: Note the basis of the saving.
steps.answer: Rs 0.33 million a year comes from the average power cut of about 41 kW.
steps.explain: The payback depends on the annual saving the study measured.
The case study reports a payback under 2 years.

cards.front: After a retrofit, a primary air fan's power falls from 57 kW to 22 kW. What is the percentage reduction?
cards.back: About 61%.
cards.explain: Percentage reduction is the drop divided by the original power. The book's case study gives these two values for the belt-driven to direct-coupled retrofit.

steps.explain: Original minus new power.

steps.answer: The retrofit changed a belt-driven arrangement to a direct-coupled fan with a more efficient impeller.
steps.explain: Both transmission and impeller losses were removed.
Drop divided by original power, times 100.

cards.front: How are pumps classified by operating principle?
cards.back: As dynamic or displacement pumps. Dynamic pumps are centrifugal or special-effect pumps; displacement pumps are rotary or reciprocating pumps.
cards.explain: Dynamic pumps add velocity to the liquid and convert it to pressure. Displacement pumps trap a volume and push it through. Centrifugal pumps are the common dynamic type and rotary and reciprocating are the displacement sub-types.

cards.front: What are the two main parts of a centrifugal pump and what does each do?
cards.back: The impeller, the only moving part, is attached to a shaft and gives the water velocity. The diffuser (volute) houses the impeller, collects the water and converts velocity to pressure.
cards.explain: Water enters the eye of the impeller and is thrown outward by centrifugal force, creating low pressure at the eye that draws in more water. The diffuser passages then direct the flow to the discharge, or to the next stage in a multi-stage pump.

cards.front: What sets the head (pressure) and the capacity of a centrifugal pump?
cards.back: Head depends on impeller diameter, number of impellers (stages), eye size and shaft speed. Capacity depends on the exit width of the impeller.
cards.explain: Head and capacity together set the motor horsepower needed. The more water pumped, the more energy required.

cards.front: True or false: a centrifugal pump is positive acting and always delivers the same volume.
cards.back: False. It is not positive acting. Flow falls as the depth of water to be lifted increases, and falls further when it pumps against rising pressure.
cards.explain: Because of this, a centrifugal pump must be selected for the specific job. The head it generates is set by the system it works against.

cards.front: What are the axes of a standard centrifugal pump performance curve?
cards.back: Flow is on the horizontal axis. Head, efficiency, power and NPSH required are on the vertical axis, each plotted against flow.
cards.explain: Head falls gradually as flow rises, and efficiency peaks at one flow. Reading all the curves against the same flow lets you read the duty point, its efficiency and its power together.

cards.front: What is static head, and is it affected by flow?
cards.back: Static head is the difference in height between the supply and destination reservoirs. It is independent of flow.
cards.explain: A system with only static head also includes pumping into a pressurised vessel with short pipe runs. Graphically, static head is a flat line against flow.

cards.front: How does friction head vary with flow, and how are pipe and fitting losses given?
cards.back: Friction head is proportional to the square of flow rate. Friction tables give loss per 100 feet (or metres) of pipe at various flows; fittings are given as an equivalent length of the same-size pipe.
cards.explain: Doubling the flow roughly quadruples the friction loss, which is why friction becomes costly at high flow. Friction is the loss on the liquid in pipes, valves and equipment.

cards.front: Where is a pump's operating point?
cards.back: Where the pump curve and the system curve intersect.
cards.explain: Superimposing the two curves gives the actual flow and head. If the real system curve differs from the calculated one, the pump will run at a different flow and head from the expected ones.

cards.front: A pump moves 68 m³/h against 47 m head with pump A (50% efficient) and pump E (60% efficient). Pump A must be throttled to 76 m head. How much extra motor power does pump A draw, and what is the extra yearly cost at 8000 h/yr and Rs 5.50/kWh?
cards.back: Pump A draws about 14.9 kW more motor power than pump E (31 kW vs 16.1 kW). That is 1,19,200 kWh/yr, about Rs 6,55,600/yr, more than the price of a new pump.
cards.explain: Pump A is oversized, so it must be throttled to deliver 68 m³/h. Throttling raises its head to 76 m and its efficiency is only 50%, so motor power rises. The chapter concludes the extra electricity cost exceeds the cost of a new pump.

steps.prompt: Hydraulic power of pump E at 47 m head and 68 m³/h?
steps.explain: Hydraulic power = Q (m³/s) × head (m) × density × g / 1000, with 68 m³/h = 0.01889 m³/s.

steps.prompt: Shaft and motor input power for pump E (pump 60%, motor 90%)?
steps.explain: Shaft power divides by pump efficiency. Motor input divides by motor efficiency.

steps.prompt: Hydraulic power of pump A throttled to 68 m³/h at 76 m head?
steps.explain: Throttling forces the pump to develop more head for the same flow, so hydraulic power rises with no gain in water delivered.

steps.prompt: Motor input power for pump A at 50% pump and 90% motor efficiency, and the extra over pump E?
steps.explain: The 50% pump efficiency is the main reason the extra power is so large.

steps.prompt: Extra annual energy and cost at 8000 h/yr and Rs 5.50/kWh?
steps.explain: Compare this running cost with the capital cost of a correctly sized pump. Here the running cost is the bigger figure.

cards.front: A pump runs at 3000 rpm giving 100 m³/h, 100 m head and 40 kW. Using the affinity laws, what are the flow, head and power at 1500 rpm?
cards.back: Flow 50 m³/h, head 25 m, power 5 kW.
cards.explain: Flow is proportional to speed, head to speed squared, and power to speed cubed. Halving the speed halves the flow, quarters the head and cuts the power to one-eighth.

steps.explain: Flow is directly proportional to speed (Q1/Q2 = N1/N2).
Head is proportional to the square of speed.
Power is proportional to the cube of speed, so the drop is steep.

steps.prompt: Why is the power saving bigger than the flow saving?
steps.explain: Cubic dependence on speed means small speed cuts give large power savings, which is the basis for energy saving in centrifugal pumps with varying flow.

cards.front: What is the difference between NPSHA and NPSHR?
cards.back: NPSHA (available) is the margin by which pressure at the pump eye exceeds the liquid's vapour pressure. It is a property of the system design. NPSHR (required) is the suction head the pump needs to avoid cavitation. It is a property of the pump design.
cards.explain: NPSHA falls when suction friction losses rise. NPSHR rises with flow. Cavitation is likely when NPSHA is not safely above NPSHR.

cards.front: Name the three undesirable effects of cavitation in a pump.
cards.back: 1) Erosion of impeller vanes, especially with water-based liquids. 2) Increased noise and vibration, with shorter seal and bearing life. 3) Partial choking of impeller passages, reducing performance and, in extreme cases, total loss of developed head.
cards.explain: Erosion usually starts before any noticeable loss of head, so it is often the first sign of trouble. Cavitation begins where the liquid pressure at the vane inlet drops below vapour pressure.

cards.front: How is the onset of cavitation defined by manufacturers and standards?
cards.back: As the NPSHR at which head drops by 3% compared with cavitation-free head. Prolonged running at that point usually causes damage, so NPSHA should exceed NPSHR by a margin.
cards.explain: Erosion begins at different NPSHA values than the head drop does. The 3% definition gives a consistent, standard reference point.

cards.front: How does NPSHR change with flow and with speed?
cards.back: NPSHR increases with flow. It varies approximately with the square of speed. At very low speeds NPSHR reaches a minimum plateau and does not fall to zero.
cards.explain: Higher flow also increases suction friction, lowering NPSHA, so both effects raise cavitation risk. The plateau at low speed means NPSH must be checked carefully in variable-speed pumping.

cards.front: A pump has NPSHR of 4 m at 1480 rpm. What is its approximate NPSHR at 1000 rpm?
cards.back: About 1.83 m, using NPSHR proportional to speed squared.
cards.explain: The square-law drop is large. The chapter warns that NPSHR does not fall to zero at low speed, so the formula overstates the reduction near the plateau.

steps.explain: Use the ratio of the new speed to the original speed.
NPSHR varies approximately with the square of speed.
This is the approximate NPSHR at 1000 rpm.

steps.answer: Near very low speed NPSHR levels off, so the formula is not reliable there.
steps.explain: Check NPSH against the manufacturer's curve for variable-speed operation.

cards.front: In a friction-only system, what happens to the operating point and power when pump speed is reduced?
cards.back: The operating point slides along a line of constant efficiency, so the pump stays in its best region and power falls substantially. Variable speed is the ideal control for friction-dominated systems.
cards.explain: The affinity laws hold in this case, so the reduction in flow and head comes with a large cut in power absorbed.

cards.front: What is the risk of a deep speed reduction in a system with high static head?
cards.back: Flow and efficiency fall sharply and the pump can run in a damaging region. At the lowest speed in the chapter's example (1184 rpm), the pump cannot lift liquid, flow and efficiency are zero, and the energy input heats the liquid. The pump then becomes a water heater.
cards.explain: Static head does not fall with speed, so the operating point moves away from the efficient region. The benefit of variable speed is therefore smaller and must be checked case by case.

cards.front: Why does a lower pump speed also extend bearing and seal life?
cards.back: Hydraulic forces on the impeller fall roughly with the square of speed, so bearing loads drop. Vibration and noise fall and seal life improves, provided the duty point stays in the allowable range.
cards.explain: The chapter also says bearing life rises as speed falls, but the exponent is unreadable in the OCR, so it is not given here.

cards.front: Is speed regulation or a control valve the more efficient way to control pump flow?
cards.back: Speed regulation is always more efficient than a control valve.
cards.explain: A valve wastes energy as a head drop at a given flow. Reducing speed lowers the energy given to the liquid instead, and also lowers bearing load and noise.

cards.front: What does stop/start control need, and what are its caveats?
cards.back: It needs storage (reservoir, wet well, elevated tank or accumulator) so the pump can run intermittently. Stop/start adds load on transmission parts and heats the motor, so cycle frequency must suit the motor and be checked with the pump maker.
cards.explain: It saves energy only when intermittent flow is acceptable. Run times can also be shifted into off-peak tariff periods.

cards.front: For minimum energy, should one pump run at full capacity continuously or two pumps alternate under stop/start?
cards.back: One pump at full capacity running continuously is better than two pumps alternating under stop/start control.
cards.explain: Pumping at the lowest flow the process allows minimises pipe friction. The chapter's example: pumping at half the flow for twice as long reduces energy to a quarter.

cards.front: Why does a throttle valve waste energy even at maximum flow?
cards.back: Usual practice is to keep the valve about 10% shut even at maximum flow, so energy is always spent overcoming its resistance. The flow multiplied by the head drop across the valve is wasted energy.
cards.explain: Pump power falls a little at lower flow, but throttling still wastes energy. Control valve maintenance is also costly on corrosive or solids-laden liquids.

cards.front: Why is bypass control less energy efficient than a control valve, and what is the small bypass line for?
cards.back: With bypass control the pump runs at maximum demand all the time, so its power does not fall with demand. A small bypass line installed to stop the pump running at zero flow is a safety feature, not a means of flow control.
cards.explain: A fixed-duty pump feeding a tank that overflows back to suction shows the same waste. The energy lost in bypass lines only shows up when the whole system is analysed.

cards.front: Why is impeller trimming used instead of buying a smaller impeller?
cards.back: The next smaller impeller is often too small for the load, and smaller impellers may not be made for that pump size. Trimming is then the only practical option short of replacing the pump and motor.
cards.explain: Trimming lowers the energy given to the liquid, removing the excess head. The affinity relations are non-linear for trimmed impellers, so predictions are approximate.

cards.front: A pump with a 300 mm impeller delivers 120 m³/h at 40 m head and 20 kW. The impeller is trimmed to 240 mm. What are the new flow, head and power?
cards.back: Flow 96 m³/h, head 25.6 m, power 10.2 kW.
cards.explain: Flow is proportional to diameter, head to diameter squared and power to diameter cubed. A 20% diameter cut reduces power by almost half. This is within the chapter's usual limit of trimming to about 75% of the original diameter.

steps.prompt: Diameter ratio D2/D1 and whether it is within the usual trim limit?
steps.explain: The chapter says impeller diameters are rarely reduced below 75% of original.

cards.front: How do multiple-speed motors differ from variable speed drives (VSDs)?
cards.back: Multiple-speed motors have separate windings for each speed, cost more and are less efficient than single-speed motors, and offer only discrete speeds. VSDs give continuous speed adjustment without jumping between speeds.
cards.explain: The two serve separate applications, so the choice depends on whether the load needs fine or only step-wise speed changes.

cards.front: Name the mechanical and electrical types of variable speed drive.
cards.back: Mechanical: hydraulic clutches, fluid couplings, adjustable belts and pulleys. Electrical: eddy current clutches, wound-rotor motor controllers and variable frequency drives (VFDs).
cards.explain: VFDs change the supply frequency to change motor speed. They are by far the most popular type of VSD.

cards.front: What soft-start benefit does a VFD give a motor?
cards.back: A VFD cuts the start-up current from about 5 to 6 times normal operating current to about 1.5 times, which reduces wear on the motor and its controller.
cards.explain: A direct start draws a large in-rush current that fades as the motor reaches speed. The VFD ramps the speed up, so the starting current stays low.

cards.front: Why do boiler feed water pumps often waste energy, and what fixes are possible?
cards.back: They are sized for design pressure, but most boilers run below it, so excess head is dropped across pressure-reducing and manual valves. Fixes: a VFD, trimming the impeller, reducing the number of stages, or changing the pump.
cards.explain: A VFD can cut pump power and improve control. The best option depends on how much the boiler load varies.

cards.front: Name the three ways a VFD can control a boiler feed pump.
cards.back: 1) One pump, one boiler, no feed water regulating valve: pump speed follows boiler water level. 2) Constant discharge pressure at a set value regardless of plant load. 3) Constant differential pressure of about 3.5 to 5.5 kg/cm² across the feed regulating valve.
cards.explain: Removing the regulating valve removes its throttling loss and some capital cost. Constant discharge pressure keeps the pump away from shut-off pressures.

cards.front: A boiler feed pump draws 53 kW with 6 stages, and 35 kW after two impellers are removed (4 stages). What is the saving in kW and as a percentage?
cards.back: 18 kW, about 34% of the original power.
cards.explain: Removing stages lowers the pressure the pump develops, so less head is thrown away across the throttling valves. The chapter reports these measured figures from an actual case.

steps.explain: Subtract the power after the change from the power before.

steps.prompt: Saving as a percentage of the original power?
steps.explain: Divide the saving by the original power.

steps.prompt: Why does removing stages save energy?
steps.answer: Less head is developed, so less pressure is throttled away at the valves.
steps.explain: The boiler runs below design pressure, so the extra stages were generating unused head.

cards.front: What are the sub-systems of a municipal water pumping system?
cards.back: Raw water pump house at the intake, pure water pump house with filtration plant, booster stations as required, and elevated storage reservoirs in the distribution system.
cards.explain: A water pumping station's capacity is normally stated in million litres per day (MLD).

cards.front: When is a vertical turbine pump used, and what are its drawbacks? What is a submersible pump?
cards.back: It is used where the pumping water level is below the limit of a volute centrifugal pump. Drawbacks: higher initial cost and harder to install and repair. A submersible pump is a vertical turbine pump close-coupled to a small submersible motor fixed below the intake, used in very deep tube wells.
cards.explain: A single impeller gives limited head, so more head is obtained by adding bowl assemblies (stages). A long drive shaft would be impractical in very deep wells, which is why the motor is submerged.

cards.front: How do sewage pump impellers differ from clear-water pump impellers, and why do sewage pumps use volutes?
cards.back: Sewage impellers are designed to pass solids that clog clear-water pumps. They are single-suction (no shaft in the intake) and radial-flow. They use volutes because a diffuser is prone to clogging.
cards.explain: Solids and fibrous matter would block diffuser passages, so the open volute is preferred for sewage handling.

cards.front: What efficiency do agricultural pump sets typically reach, and why?
cards.back: 30 to 55%. Efficiency varies because the water level in the intake changes, which pushes the pump away from its best efficiency point. Pumps are often oversized and locally made, chosen for low initial cost rather than efficiency.
cards.explain: Oversizing lets the pump draw water from declining depths and withstand large voltage fluctuations. Centrifugal pumps of 1 to 25 HP are most common, with higher ratings in some areas.

cards.front: Name five energy conservation opportunities in pumping systems.
cards.back: Ensure adequate NPSH at the site; provide basic instruments such as pressure gauges and flow meters; operate pumps near best efficiency point; modify the system to minimise throttling; adapt to wide load variation with variable speed drives or sequenced control of multiple units.
cards.explain: These are among the chapter's list. Other measures include avoiding free-fall gravity returns, repairing seals to stop dripping and fitting a booster pump for a few high-head areas.

cards.front: If pump speed doubles, by how much does power go up?
cards.back: Eight times, because power is proportional to the cube of speed (2³ = 8).
cards.explain: Flow doubles and head quadruples at the same time. Small speed increases therefore sharply raise shaft power, shaft stress and bearing loads.

cards.front: In a cooling water circuit, pipe A (100 mm, 1.5 m/s), pipe B (100 mm, 1.8 m/s) and pipe C (200 mm, 2.0 m/s) feed three heat exchangers. Total head is 34 m discharge less 2 m suction. Motor power is 50.7 kW at 90% motor efficiency. Find the pump efficiency.
cards.back: About 61%.
cards.explain: Total flow is the sum of the three pipe flows. Hydraulic power is flow × head × 9.81, and pump efficiency is hydraulic power divided by shaft power. The chapter uses 22/7 for pi and treats 3.4 kg/cm² as about 34 m head.

steps.explain: Flow = area × velocity; area = pi × d²/4.

steps.prompt: Flows in pipes B and C?
steps.explain: Use the same area × velocity relation with each pipe's diameter.
Parallel branches from one pump add their flows.
The chapter treats 3.4 kg/cm² as about 34 m head and subtracts the 2 m suction head.
Hydraulic power = Q × head × density × g, with density 1000 kg/m³.
Shaft power is motor input × motor efficiency; pump efficiency is hydraulic power / shaft power.

cards.front: The shaft power of a motor driving a pump is 30 kW. Motor efficiency is 0.9 and pump efficiency is 0.6. What power is transmitted to the water?
cards.back: 16.2 kW (option a in the chapter's quiz).
cards.explain: The chapter gives no answer key. This reading applies both efficiencies in series: 30 kW × 0.9 = 27 kW at the pump shaft, then 27 kW × 0.6 = 16.2 kW to the water. If the 30 kW is taken as the pump shaft power, the answer would be 18 kW.

steps.explain: Motor efficiency applies to the power taken in by the motor.
Pump efficiency is the ratio of hydraulic power to shaft power.

steps.answer: Option a, 16.2 kW (per the chapter's option list, given the reading above).
steps.explain: Option b (18.0 kW) would result only if the 30 kW were already the pump shaft power.

cards.front: A pump delivers 35 m³/h at 1440 rpm with a discharge gauge of 4.4 kg/cm². The suction is 2 m below the pump centreline. Pump efficiency is 68% and motor efficiency 90%. If speed is halved, what are the new flow, head and motor power?
cards.back: Flow 17.5 m³/h, head 11.5 m, motor power about 0.9 kW (down from about 7.2 kW).
cards.explain: The gauge reading is taken as 44 m head, plus 2 m suction lift, giving 46 m. Flow scales with speed, head with speed squared and power with speed cubed. This assumes 1 kg/cm² is about 10 m of head.

steps.prompt: Total head at the present duty?
steps.answer: 4.4 kg/cm² ≈ 44 m; plus 2 m suction lift = 46 m
steps.explain: Head is the gauge pressure in metres of liquid plus the static suction lift.

steps.prompt: Hydraulic and motor input power at present duty?
steps.explain: Hydraulic power divides by pump efficiency, then by motor efficiency, to give motor input.
Flow is proportional to speed.
Head is proportional to speed squared.

steps.prompt: New motor power at half speed?
steps.explain: Power is proportional to speed cubed, so halving speed cuts power to one-eighth.

cards.front: A pillar furnace cooling pump gives 60 m head and draws 13.4 kW, but the furnace needs 12.5 l/s at only 3.0 kg/cm². Estimate the new shaft power if the pump speed or impeller is adjusted to match the duty, and the saving.
cards.back: About 4.7 kW, a saving of about 8.7 kW (about 65%).
cards.explain: The required head is about 30 m, half the existing 60 m. Using the affinity relations, head scales with speed squared, so the speed ratio is about 0.71 and power falls with the cube, to about 35% of the original. This estimate assumes the 13.4 kW is at the current 60 m duty.

steps.prompt: Required flow and head in SI units?
steps.explain: Convert the furnace requirement to the same units as the pump data.

steps.answer: 30 / 60 = 0.5 head ratio, so speed (or diameter) ratio = √0.5 ≈ 0.71
steps.explain: Head is proportional to speed squared.
Power is proportional to speed cubed.
Recommended measures are speed reduction (VFD) or impeller trimming. Check the answer against the pump manufacturer's curve.

cards.front: What are the pump capacity control methods covered in this chapter?
cards.back: Speed control (VFD, multiple-speed motor, impeller trimming or a smaller impeller), flow control valve (throttling), bypass control, stop/start control, and parallel pumps switched to meet demand.
cards.explain: Speed control is the most efficient method. Throttling and bypass waste energy, and stop/start needs storage in the system.

cards.front: What are the two main categories of cooling tower?
cards.back: Natural draft and mechanical draft.
cards.explain: Natural draft towers use very large concrete chimneys to draw air through the media and are generally used for water flow above about 45,000 m³/hr. Mechanical draft towers use fans, are far more widely used, and are the focus of this chapter.

cards.front: What are the three airflow arrangements of mechanical draft towers?
cards.back: Counter flow induced draft, counter flow forced draft, and cross flow induced draft.
cards.explain: In counter flow induced draft, hot water enters at the top and air is introduced at the bottom and exits at the top. In cross flow towers, water passes over the fill while air enters from one side (single-flow) or from opposite sides (double-flow).

cards.front: Name the basic components of an evaporative cooling tower.
cards.back: Frame and casing, fill, cold water basin, drift eliminators, air inlet, louvers, nozzles and fans.
cards.explain: Fill maximises water-air contact to aid heat transfer. Drift eliminators capture droplets carried in the air stream, and nozzles wet the fill with water spray.

cards.front: What are the two types of fill, and which is more efficient?
cards.back: Splash fill and film fill. Film fill is more efficient.
cards.explain: Film fill gives the same heat transfer in a smaller volume than splash fill. Splash fill breaks water into droplets as it falls over horizontal splash bars, and plastic splash fill performs better than wood splash fill.

cards.front: What is the function of drift eliminators?
cards.back: They capture water droplets entrapped in the air stream that would otherwise be lost to the atmosphere.
cards.explain: Drift is water lost as droplets, separate from evaporation loss. The chapter gives typical drift specifications in its drift loss section.

cards.front: Which fan types are used in induced draft and forced draft towers?
cards.back: Propeller (axial) fans are used in induced draft towers. Propeller and centrifugal fans are both found in forced draft towers.
cards.explain: Depending on size, propeller fans can be fixed or variable pitch. Fixed-pitch and variable-pitch fans differ in how they adjust airflow to load.

cards.front: How does a fanless cooling tower move air without a fan?
cards.back: Pressure from the existing water circulation pump forces water through ejector nozzles at high velocity. The low pressure created sucks cold ambient air into the tower.
cards.explain: Ejector nozzles convert water pressure into kinetic energy of the air. The chapter states the minimum pressure required at the jet ejector nozzles is 0.5 bar.

cards.front: What are the energy and noise advantages of a fanless cooling tower?
cards.back: No fan or motor is needed, so fan power is saved (the pump needs only marginally more power). Noise from fans and motors is also eliminated.
cards.explain: Fan and motor vibration reinforces noise resonance in a conventional tower, and the fanless design removes that source. The chapter also notes very low maintenance when circulating water is kept clean.

cards.front: Define cooling tower range.
cards.back: The difference between the cooling tower water inlet (hot) and outlet (cold) temperatures.
cards.explain: Range is set by the process heat load and the water circulation rate through the exchanger, not by the tower itself. Both range and approach should be monitored.

cards.front: Define cooling tower approach. Which is the better indicator of tower performance, range or approach?
cards.back: Approach = cold water outlet temperature minus ambient wet bulb temperature. Approach is the better indicator.
cards.explain: Approach shows how close the tower brings the cold water to the ambient wet bulb temperature. Range is still monitored alongside it.

cards.front: What is cooling tower effectiveness, and what is its formula?
cards.back: Effectiveness (%) = Range / (Range + Approach) × 100.
cards.explain: Range + approach equals the ideal range, which is the cold water inlet temperature minus the ambient wet bulb temperature. Effectiveness therefore compares actual range with the ideal range.

cards.front: What is the empirical formula for evaporation loss in a cooling tower?
cards.back: Evaporation loss (m³/hr) = 0.00085 × 1.8 × circulation rate (m³/hr) × (T1 − T2), where T1 − T2 is the inlet-outlet water temperature difference.
cards.explain: The 1.8 factor is the evaporation (m³) per 10,00,000 kcal of heat rejected. The chapter cites Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook as the source of the relation.

cards.front: What are cycles of concentration (COC)?
cards.back: The ratio of dissolved solids in the circulating water to dissolved solids in the make-up water.
cards.explain: COC links directly to blow down. For the same evaporation, a higher COC means less blow down is needed.

cards.front: How is cooling tower blow down calculated?
cards.back: Blow down = Evaporation loss / (COC − 1).
cards.explain: Blow down depends on the cycles of concentration and the evaporation loss. The chapter advises optimising the blow down flow rate to the site COC limit.

cards.front: What thermodynamic relation links the L/G ratio to the water temperatures and air enthalpy in a cooling tower?
cards.back: L(T1 − T2) = G(h2 − h1), so L/G = (h2 − h1) / (T1 − T2). L/G is in kg/kg.
cards.explain: Heat removed from the water must equal heat absorbed by the air. T1 and T2 are the hot and cold water temperatures (°C), and h1 and h2 are the air-vapour enthalpies at the inlet and exhaust wet bulb.

cards.front: How does cooling tower size vary with heat load, range, approach and entering wet bulb, when the other three are held constant?
cards.back: Size varies directly with the heat load and inversely with the range, the approach and the entering wet bulb temperature.
cards.explain: A larger heat load needs a bigger tower. A wider range, a larger approach or a higher wet bulb each allow a smaller tower for the same duty.

cards.front: What is the coldest approach to design wet bulb that a manufacturer will typically guarantee?
cards.back: About 2.8°C.
cards.explain: The closer the approach, the larger and more expensive the tower. Initial selection is based on the average maximum wet bulb for the summer months at the site.

cards.front: A tower cools 4540 m³/hr from 48.9°C to 32.2°C at a 26.7°C design wet bulb. Find the range, approach and effectiveness.
cards.back: Range 16.7°C, approach 5.5°C, effectiveness about 75.2%.
cards.explain: This is the chapter's own example of how the cold water temperature is fixed by the wet bulb plus approach. The same method applies to any tower duty.

steps.explain: Range is the hot water inlet temperature minus the cold water outlet temperature.
Approach is the cold water outlet temperature minus the design wet bulb temperature.
Effectiveness is range divided by the ideal range (range plus approach).

steps.answer: A 5.5°C approach is wider than the 2.8°C closest approach manufacturers usually guarantee.
steps.explain: The chapter notes the closer the approach, the larger and costlier the tower, so a wider approach allows a smaller tower.

cards.front: Why is the ambient wet bulb, rather than the inlet wet bulb, normally specified for a tower?
cards.back: Recirculation of discharge vapour raises the inlet wet bulb, and the recirculation factor is not known in advance. The ambient wet bulb is therefore specified, and the supplier must cover the extra rise from its own equipment.
cards.explain: The ambient wet bulb is the temperature that generally exists in the tower area. Inlet wet bulb is the temperature of the air entering the tower and can be raised by recirculated discharge.

cards.front: Can a cooling tower cool water down to the entering wet bulb temperature when a heat load is applied?
cards.back: No. Without a heat load the tower can cool water to the entering wet bulb in theory, but a thermal potential is needed to reject heat, so the approach is always above it.
cards.explain: The approach obtained depends on thermal conditions and the tower's capability. This is why a design wet bulb cannot be treated as a guaranteed cold water temperature.

cards.front: What is the effective heat exchange area of film fill compared with splash fill?
cards.back: Film fill about 150 m²/m³; splash fill about 30–45 m²/m³.
cards.explain: Film fill also allows a higher possible L/G ratio (1.5–2.0 against 1.1–1.5 for splash). Because it needs less air and pumping head, film fill gives a large power saving.

cards.front: Air enters a tower at 26.67°C wet bulb carrying 24.17 kcal/kg and leaves at 37.8°C wet bulb carrying 39.67 kcal/kg. How much heat does each kg of air pick up?
cards.back: About 15.5 kcal/kg, compared with the 12.1 kcal/kg the chapter quotes for the cooler 21.1°C wet bulb case.
cards.explain: Air at a higher wet bulb can carry more heat, so the same tower rejects more heat per kg of air. This is one reason a higher design wet bulb gives a smaller tower.

steps.prompt: Find the heat picked up per kg of air.
steps.explain: Heat gained by the air equals its enthalpy at exit minus its enthalpy at entry.

steps.answer: The chapter quotes 12.1 kcal/kg for air going from 21.1°C to 32.2°C wet bulb.
steps.explain: Higher entering wet bulb air picks up more heat per kg, so the warmer case rejects more per kg of air.

cards.front: Rank these tower designs from least to most power consumption: cross flow splash fill, counter flow film fill, counter flow splash fill.
cards.back: Counter flow film fill (least), then counter flow splash fill, then cross flow splash fill (most).
cards.explain: Counter flow heat exchange is more effective than cross flow. The chapter's comparison (Table 7.4) is for a 16,000 m³/hr water flow.

cards.front: What are the main water-side problems of an open cooling system?
cards.back: Corrosion and/or scale formation, and biological or micro-biological fouling. Deposits from turbidity, sand, silt and corrosion products add to the problem.
cards.explain: Corrosion can lead to leaks in heat exchangers and to deposits of corrosion products. Algae can block tower nozzles and reduce the temperature drop across the tower.

cards.front: Name the main factors that promote corrosion in cooling water systems.
cards.back: High salinity, low pH, low alkalinity, corrosive gases (mainly oxygen and CO₂), and dissimilar metals.
cards.explain: Corrosion is not precisely understood, but these factors are the main drivers. It can cause heat exchanger leaks and deposits of corrosion products.

cards.front: When does an open condenser water circuit on softened water face severe scaling?
cards.back: When the pH of the circulating water is above 9.0, total alkalinity (as CaCO₃) is above 550 ppm, or temporary hardness of the make-up is above 200 ppm.
cards.explain: High calcium and magnesium levels, together with high pH and alkalinity, are the main sources of scale in open evaporative condenser circuits.

cards.front: What does a side stream filter handle, and how often should the total system water be filtered?
cards.back: A side stream filter handles 2% to 5% of the total circulation rate, sized so that the total system water (hold-up volume) is filtered about once every 12 hours.
cards.explain: Side stream filters are needed where circulating water has very high turbidity or suspended impurities.

cards.front: Which oxidising biocide is the most effective and most economical, and what do bio-dispersants do?
cards.back: Chlorination. Bio-dispersants remove the upper layer of biological masses so that biocides can penetrate the lower layers.
cards.explain: For volumes above 100 m³, suitable gas chlorinators are used. The safest are vacuum gravity feed types, installed on 50 kg or 100 kg chlorine cylinders.

cards.front: What drift loss do most end-user specifications call for, and what can modern PVC drift eliminators achieve?
cards.back: Most specifications call for 0.02% drift loss. Modern PVC drift eliminators can reach 0.003–0.001%.
cards.explain: Drift is water carried out of the tower as droplets in the air stream, separate from evaporation. Better eliminator shapes made from PVC made these lower values possible.

cards.front: What fan energy saving has been reported from replacing metal or GRP fan blades with hollow FRP blades, and what payback?
cards.back: Fan energy savings of about 20–30%, with a simple payback of 6 to 7 months.
cards.explain: Hand-moulded FRP blades can achieve an optimum aerodynamic profile. They are lightweight, need lower starting torque (so smaller motors), and extend gearbox, motor and bearing life.

cards.front: Rank cooling tower fan control methods from least to most effective.
cards.back: ON-OFF of single-speed fans (least effective), then two-speed fans, then three-speed fans, then automatic adjustable pitch or variable speed fans (closest control of cold water temperature).
cards.explain: In multi-cell towers, adjacent cells may run at different speeds, or some may be on while others are off, depending on load and the required water temperature.

cards.front: By how much may a 1°C rise in cooling water temperature increase the kW of an A/C compressor?
cards.back: About 2.7%.
cards.explain: The chapter also states that a 1°C drop in cooling water temperature can give a heat rate saving of about 5 kcal/kWh in a thermal power plant.

cards.front: Name five energy saving measures for cooling towers.
cards.back: Optimise fan blade angle seasonally or by load; correct excessive or uneven fan blade tip clearance; replace splash bars with PVC cellular film fill; replace slat drift eliminators with low pressure drop PVC cellular units; cover hot water basins to limit algae growth.
cards.explain: The chapter lists about twenty measures. Others include periodic cleaning of plugged nozzles, balancing flow to hot water basins, and optimising blow down to the COC limit.

cards.front: How is closed-loop VFD control of a cooling tower fan set up?
cards.back: An RTD sensor at the tower outlet sends a 4–20 mA signal to the drive's PID controller. The set point is entered in °C or °F, and the drive adjusts fan speed to remove any error.
cards.explain: If outlet temperature rises (from a higher wet bulb or plant load), the drive raises fan speed to bring it back to the set point. An optional bypass lets the fan run from mains supply if the drive fails.

cards.front: Why does a VFD save energy on a cooling tower fan that is rated for worst-case conditions?
cards.back: The fan is rated for the worst wet and dry bulb conditions, which occur for only a small part of the year. A VFD slows the fan in milder conditions, saving energy.
cards.explain: Savings need annual wet and dry bulb data, or a trial with and without the VFD. Savings are small in hot periods when the drive must run at full speed.

cards.front: A cooling tower cell circulates 1565 m³/hr from 44°C to 37.6°C at a 29.3°C wet bulb, and runs at 2.7 cycles of concentration. Find the range, approach, effectiveness, evaporation loss, blow down and make-up per cell.
cards.back: Range 6.4°C; approach 8.3°C; effectiveness 43.5% (rated 64.5%); evaporation 15.32 m³/hr; blow down 9.01 m³/hr; make-up 24.33 m³/hr per cell.
cards.explain: This is the chapter's trial on a thermal power plant cooling tower, which found the cell flow about 16.5% below rated. The same steps apply to any tower trial, using measured temperatures and the site COC.

steps.explain: Range is the inlet hot water temperature minus the outlet cold water temperature.
Approach is the outlet cold water temperature minus the ambient wet bulb temperature.
The rated value is 100 × (43 − 33) / (43 − 27.5), so the actual cell is well below its design effectiveness.

steps.prompt: Calculate the evaporation loss per cell.
steps.explain: Evaporation depends on the circulation rate and the temperature drop across the tower.

steps.prompt: Calculate the blow down at 2.7 COC.
steps.explain: Blow down removes concentrated water so that dissolved solids do not build up beyond the COC limit.

steps.prompt: Calculate the make-up water per cell.
steps.explain: Make-up replaces water lost both to evaporation and to blow down.

cards.front: A tower's L/G ratio is found from a trial: water flow 1565 m³/hr, air flow 989,544 m³/hr at a density of 1.08 kg/m³. Find the L/G ratio and compare it with the design value.
cards.back: L/G = 1.46 kg/kg, against a rated value of 1.74 kg/kg.
cards.explain: A lower L/G than design means relatively more air for the water being cooled. The chapter links the lower flow per cell to a need to investigate the CW pump and system.

steps.prompt: Find the water mass flow rate.
steps.explain: Water density is taken as 1000 kg/m³ for mass flow.

steps.prompt: Find the air mass flow rate.
steps.explain: Air mass flow is volume flow multiplied by air density.
L/G is the ratio of water to air mass flow rates.

steps.answer: Rated L/G is 1.74 kg/kg, so the actual L/G is lower.
steps.explain: The book notes the flow per cell is about 16.5% below rated, which helps explain the lower L/G.

cards.front: A cooling tower handles 3000 m³/hr of water, with the hot water at 41°C, the cold water at 31°C and a wet bulb of 24°C. Find the range, approach, effectiveness and cooling capacity in kcal/hr.
cards.back: Range 10°C; approach 7°C; effectiveness 58.8%; cooling capacity 30 million kcal/hr.
cards.explain: This is the chapter's solved example. Cooling capacity is the mass flow times specific heat times temperature difference, which for water is kg/hr × 1 kcal/kg°C × range.

steps.explain: Range is hot water inlet minus cold water outlet temperature.
Approach is cold water outlet minus the wet bulb temperature.
Effectiveness is range divided by the ideal range (range plus approach).
Flow in m³/hr is converted to kg/hr (×1000), then multiplied by the temperature drop, since water's specific heat is 1 kcal/kg°C.

cards.front: A cooling tower fan's manual control uses 392 kWh/day and VFD control uses 254 kWh/day. The fan runs 26 days a month for 12 months, and the drive panel costs Rs 2,50,000. Find the daily saving, the percentage saving, the annual saving and the payback period.
cards.back: Daily saving 138 kWh (35.2%); annual saving Rs 2,15,280; payback about 1.16 years.
cards.explain: The chapter's figures are extrapolated annual estimates. In hot periods the VFD runs at full speed, so the real average annual saving is lower.

steps.explain: Saving is the manual control consumption minus the VFD consumption.
Percentage saving is the daily saving divided by the manual control consumption.
Multiply the daily saving by the operating days per month and by 12 months.

steps.prompt: Find the implied unit energy cost and check the annual money saving.
steps.answer: The chapter states Rs 2,15,280 per year. This implies about Rs 5 per kWh (215,280 / 43,056). The unit cost line is not legible in the OCR, so the Rs 5 figure is derived, not quoted.
steps.explain: Annual money saving is annual kWh saved multiplied by the unit energy cost.
Simple payback is the capital cost divided by the annual saving.

cards.front: A cooling tower circulates 1250 m³/hr with a range of 7°C. Blow down is 1% of the circulation rate. Estimate the evaporation loss and the cycles of concentration.
cards.back: Evaporation about 13.4 m³/hr; blow down 12.5 m³/hr; COC about 2.07.
cards.explain: Blow down is found from the circulation rate, then COC is found by rearranging the blow down formula. Evaporation loss uses the empirical 0.00085 × 1.8 relation from the chapter.

steps.explain: The range of 7°C is used as the temperature difference T1 − T2.
Blow down is given as a percentage of the circulation rate.

steps.answer: COC − 1 = Evaporation / Blow down = 13.39 / 12.5 = 1.07, so COC ≈ 2.07.
steps.explain: Rearranging blow down = evaporation / (COC − 1) gives COC = 1 + evaporation / blow down.

cards.front: True or false: range is a better indicator of cooling tower performance than approach.
cards.back: False. Approach is the better indicator. Range is set mainly by the process heat load.
cards.explain: Both should be monitored, but approach shows how closely the tower brings cold water to the ambient wet bulb. The chapter's objective question uses this same distinction.

cards.front: How many lumens is 1 watt equal to at 555 nm, the wavelength the eye sees best?
cards.back: 683 lumens (683 lm/W). The lumen is the photometric equivalent of the watt, weighted to the standard observer's eye response.
cards.explain: Yellowish-green light at 555 nm gives the most visual response per watt. Blue or red light of the same radiant power looks dimmer to the eye. This is why 683 lm/W is the ceiling for luminous efficacy.

cards.front: What is illuminance, and what is its unit?
cards.back: Illuminance is the luminous flux incident on a surface per unit area. Its unit is the lux (lx), where 1 lux = 1 lumen per square metre.
cards.explain: Illuminance is measured on the working plane, the main plane where tasks are carried out. It affects both task performance and how the space looks. Average maintained illuminance is the average of readings taken across an area.

cards.front: State the inverse square law for illuminance from a point source.
cards.back: E = I / d², where E is illuminance (lx), I is luminous flux (lm) and d is distance (m). Illuminance falls with the square of distance. The alternate form is E₁ × d₁² = E₂ × d₂².
cards.explain: Doubling the distance cuts illuminance to one quarter. Distance is measured from the test point to the first luminating surface, such as the filament of a clear bulb or the glass envelope of a frosted bulb.

cards.front: What is lamp circuit efficacy, and how does it differ from lamp efficacy?
cards.back: Lamp circuit efficacy is the lumens emitted per circuit watt, which includes control gear losses. It is the more meaningful measure for lamps that need control gear.
cards.explain: Lamp efficacy counts only the lamp's own watts. Circuit efficacy also counts the ballast losses, so it gives the true energy cost of the light. Its unit is lumens per circuit watt (lm/W).

cards.front: What does the Colour Rendering Index (CRI) measure, and what does a CRI of 100 mean?
cards.back: CRI measures the effect of a lamp's light on the perceived colour of standard colour chips, compared with a reference source of the same correlated colour temperature. A CRI of 100 means the chips look identical under the lamp and the reference. A low CRI means some colours look unnatural.
cards.explain: CRI is found by measuring the colour appearance of the chips under the lamp and under the reference. Any difference from the reference pulls the CRI below 100. Lamps with low CRI are poor for colour-critical work.

cards.front: What is the function of a ballast in a fluorescent lamp circuit?
cards.back: A ballast is a current-limiting device that counters the negative resistance of a discharge lamp. It aids the initial voltage build-up needed to start the lamp and acts as a stabiliser in the circuit.
cards.explain: A fluorescent tube cannot run from the mains directly. The ballast is the auxiliary circuit housed in a casing that provides the start-up and steady operation. Ignitors do a similar starting job for HID lamps by sending a high-voltage pulse.

cards.front: Into which three groups are lamps classified by construction and operating characteristics?
cards.back: Incandescent, fluorescent and high intensity discharge (HID). HID lamps are further classified as sodium vapour, mercury vapour and metal halide.
cards.explain: The group determines efficacy, colour, lamp life and how much light the lamp loses over its life. Knowing the three groups makes the individual lamp types easier to place.

cards.front: How does the halogen cycle stop the filament of a halogen lamp from thinning?
cards.back: Tungsten evaporates from the hot filament and combines with halogen at the cooler bulb wall to form tungsten oxyhalide. This vapour drifts back to the hot filament, where it breaks apart and tungsten is re-deposited on the filament.
cards.explain: The re-deposited tungsten does not return to the exact spot it left. Breaks still tend to occur near the lead-in connections, where temperature drops sharply. Halogen lamps are more efficient and last longer than standard incandescent lamps.

cards.front: How much more efficient and how much longer-lived is a fluorescent tube lamp than a standard incandescent lamp?
cards.back: About 3 to 5 times as efficient, and it can last about 10 to 20 times longer.
cards.explain: These are the general comparison figures given in the chapter. Fluorescent lamps need a ballast and a starter circuit, and their luminous flux depends strongly on ambient temperature.

cards.front: What diameters do the T12, T8 and T5 linear fluorescent tubes have?
cards.back: T12 = 38 mm (1.5 in), T8 = 25 mm (1 in) and T5 = 16 mm (5/8 in). The T number is the diameter in eighths of an inch.
cards.explain: T5 and T8 are the thinner tubes. The chapter says T5 and T8 give about 5% higher efficacy than 40 W T12 lamps and have become the most popular choice for new installations.

cards.front: Why is low pressure sodium (LPSV) a poor choice where colour matters?
cards.back: LPSV is monochromatic, so all colours appear black, white or shades of grey under it. It is used for outdoor security and street lighting and for low-wattage indoor areas such as stairwells.
cards.explain: LPSV is the most efficacious light source of all the lamp types, but it gives the poorest quality of light. Many municipalities do not allow it for roadway lighting because the colour rendition is so poor.

cards.front: What does a metal halide lamp add to a high pressure mercury vapour lamp, and why does it render colour better?
cards.back: It adds metal halides, usually rare-earth iodides or a mixture of sodium and scandium iodide, so that metal radiation augments the mercury spectrum. Its colour rendering is significantly better than mercury vapour and can be tailored by the choice of halides.
cards.explain: The halides act like the tungsten halogen cycle. At high temperature the halide compound dissociates and releases the metal into the arc. The halides also stop the quartz wall being attacked by alkali metals.

cards.front: How does an LED produce light?
cards.back: By electroluminescence. Current drives electrons from N-type material (extra electrons) into holes in P-type material (extra positive gaps). When an electron drops into a hole it releases its extra energy as light.
cards.explain: The LED chip is usually less than one square millimetre, and additional optical components shape and direct the light. Different inorganic semiconductor materials produce different colours.

cards.front: True or false: LEDs are inherently white light sources.
cards.back: False. LEDs emit nearly monochromatic light, so white light has to be produced by phosphor conversion, RGB colour mixing or a hybrid method.
cards.explain: That is why coloured LEDs are used directly in traffic lights and exit signs. A general-purpose white LED needs a conversion or mixing method to make white light.

cards.front: What are the three ways to produce white light from LEDs?
cards.back: Phosphor conversion (a blue or UV LED with a phosphor), RGB colour mixing of red, green and blue LEDs, and a hybrid method that combines phosphor-converted and monochromatic LEDs.
cards.explain: In a phosphor-converted LED, the phosphor on or near the LED turns the blue or near-UV light into white light. In RGB mixing, the proper amounts of the three colours combine to give white.

cards.front: What efficacy do LEDs reach in the laboratory and in typical products?
cards.back: Up to 200 lumens per watt in the laboratory and in some products on the market. More typical LEDs average 50 to 130 lumens per watt.
cards.explain: Low power requirements make solar panels with battery backup practical and economical for remote LED applications. LEDs direct their light instead of radiating it in all 360 degrees.

cards.front: What is the recommended scale of illuminances in lux?
cards.explain: A factor of about 1.5 represents the smallest significant difference in the subjective effect of illuminance. Each recommended range spans three successive steps of this scale, with R as the middle value.

cards.front: When is the Zonal Cavity Method used, and why is it preferred?
cards.back: It is the accepted method for average illuminance indoors, unless the light distribution is radically asymmetric. It is an accurate hand method because it accounts for the effect of inter-reflectance on illuminance.
cards.explain: For outdoor lighting the chapter uses a different route: the coefficient of utilisation is read from a curve and the standard lumen formula is applied.

cards.front: What are the three cavities in the Zonal Cavity Method?
cards.back: The ceiling cavity (between ceiling and fixtures), the room cavity (between fixtures and work plane) and the floor cavity (between work plane and floor).
cards.explain: The method treats the room as three stacked spaces. The room cavity is the space the luminaires light, and its height is what the room index uses.

cards.front: What is the room index formula used in the Zonal Cavity Method?
cards.back: Room index = (L × W) / [mounting height × (L + W)], where mounting height = luminaire height minus work plane height.
cards.explain: In the chapter's example a 10 m × 10 m room with a 2.0 m mounting height gives RI = 100 / (2 × 20) = 2.5. The room index is then used to read the utilisation factor from the manufacturer's table.

cards.front: Define utilisation factor (UF) and state where its value comes from.
cards.back: UF is the percent of rated bare-lamp lumens that leave the luminaire and reach the work plane, counting both direct and reflected light. Manufacturers supply a CU or UF table for each luminaire from a photometric test report.
cards.explain: UF depends on the luminaire type, the room index, and the ceiling and wall reflectances. For a twin tube fixture at room index 2.5, the chapter gives UF = 0.66.

cards.front: What is the lumen-method formula for the number of luminaires required?
cards.back: N = (E × A) / (F × UF × LLF). E is the required lux on the working plane, A is the room area (L × W), F is the total lumens from all lamps in one fitting, UF is the utilisation factor and LLF is the light loss factor.
cards.explain: Use the room area in m² and the required lux, so that the units cancel to give a count of fittings. Round the result to whole fittings as the design requires.

cards.front: What does the light loss factor (LLF) cover, and what are the typical values for an air-conditioned office, a clean industrial site and a dirty industrial site?
cards.back: LLF covers the depreciation of lamp output over time and dirt on fittings and walls. LLF = lamp lumen MF × luminaire MF × room surface MF. Typical values are 0.8 (air-conditioned office), 0.7 (clean industrial) and 0.6 (dirty industrial).
cards.explain: MF is the maintenance factor. A lower LLF means more light is lost, so more fittings are needed for the same lux level.

cards.front: What is the space-to-height ratio (SHR) of a luminaire, and what is the recommended value for the example fitting?
cards.back: SHR = spacing between luminaires / mounting height. The recommended value for the example luminaire is 1.5. A larger SHR means fewer fittings and a lower connected load.
cards.explain: If the actual SHR is more than the recommended value, the uniformity of lighting becomes less. Luminaires closer to a wall should be spaced at half the spacing or less.

cards.front: Name four daylighting methods the chapter gives for using natural light in buildings.
cards.back: North lighting by single-pitched saw-tooth trusses; skylights with FRP material and a transparent or translucent false ceiling; light shelves at windows; and solar tubes on the roof that direct sunlight deep into the building.
cards.explain: North lighting suits latitudes north of 23 degrees, such as North India. In South India it needs diffusing glass to cut out direct sunlight. Atriums with FRP domes can remove the need for electric lights in tall-building passages.

cards.front: What is de-lamping, and under what conditions does it work?
cards.back: De-lamping means removing lamps to reduce lighting energy. It works when the mounting height is reduced and efficient luminaires are fitted, so the illuminance is hardly affected. It also suits empty spaces where no active work is done.
cards.explain: De-lamping sits alongside task lighting and daylighting as a way to cut lighting energy without changing the lamps themselves.

cards.front: What energy saving have industries reported from reducing lighting feeder voltage with reactors or transformers?
cards.back: 5% to 15% of lighting energy. Industries with high night-time voltage also get fewer premature lamp failures.
cards.explain: Night-time grid voltages are often higher than normal. Lowering the voltage saves energy and still gives the rated light output, because gas discharge lamps change their light output and power with voltage.

cards.front: Which electronic ballast advantages does the chapter give over an electromagnetic choke for tube lights?
cards.back: Electronic ballast losses are about 1 W, against 10 to 15 W for an electromagnetic choke, saving about 15 to 20 W per tube light. The starter is eliminated and the tube lights instantly without flicker.
cards.explain: Electronic ballasts are oscillators that convert the supply to about 20,000 to 30,000 Hz. They ignite the lamp, stabilise the gas discharge and supply power to the lamp.

cards.front: How much can ageing lamps and dirt cut illumination, and why is maintenance important?
cards.back: Together they can reduce total illumination by 50 percent or more, while the lights keep drawing full power. Basic maintenance is cleaning lamps and fixtures, cleaning and repainting interiors, and relamping.
cards.explain: Lighting maintenance is vital to lighting efficiency. Cleaning and relamping restore the light level without adding any connected load.

cards.front: Which sensing technologies are used for occupancy-linked lighting control?
cards.back: Infra-red, acoustic, ultrasonic or microwave sensors, which detect either movement or noise in a room.
cards.explain: The sensors switch lights on when occupancy is detected and off after a set period with no movement. They are designed to override manual switches, so lights are not left on in empty spaces.

cards.front: What is the trade-off in choosing the time span of a timed-turnoff switch?
cards.back: Shorter time spans waste less energy, but they raise the chance that the lights switch off while someone is still in the space. For most applications the best choice is an electronic unit with a fixed interval set by engineering staff.
cards.explain: Timed-turnoff switches are the least expensive type of automatic lighting control. Spring-wound dial timers let occupants set the span, which is unlikely to be set with efficiency in mind.

cards.front: Why is an internally mounted photoelectric dimming control better than simple on/off daylight switching?
cards.back: It senses the total light in the area and adjusts the electric lighting so that daylight plus electric light always meets the design level. Electric light can be turned off completely when daylight alone is enough. Dimming saves more energy and is more acceptable to occupants.
cards.explain: Time delays are needed in the control system so that fast-moving clouds do not cause repeated rapid switching.

cards.front: How many street lights does a typical municipal area have, and what is the typical municipal lighting load?
cards.back: 20,000 to 50,000 street lights, depending on the kilometres of road lit within municipal limits. The typical electrical load of a municipal lighting system is 2 MW to 7 MW.
cards.explain: Street lighting is one of the major electrical loads in municipal areas. Lamps in use include fluorescent tubes, mercury vapour, sodium vapour and metal halide, with high mast towers at strategic junctions and LEDs for traffic signals.

cards.front: Name five controls the chapter lists to reduce street lighting energy use.
cards.back: Timer control (switch on and off as per set timing); daylight control based on illumination level; selective or alternate switching of low-traffic areas after midnight; lux-level switching after midnight; voltage controllers operated after midnight; and PLC-controlled lighting panels for control and monitoring.
cards.explain: Several of these controls work only after midnight, when traffic is low. PLC-controlled panels add effective monitoring on top of the switching.

cards.front: Which fluorescent lamps does the BEE Standard and Labelling programme cover, and up to what wattage?
cards.back: 4-foot tubular fluorescent lamps (FTL) up to 40 W. Halo-phosphate lamps are covered at 6500 K. Tri-phosphate lamps are covered at 6500 K, 4000 K and 2700 K.
cards.explain: The S&L programme covers FTL because of the large number of these lamps in use. The star rating scheme for FTL is set out in Table 8.4, though the scheme's columns are hard to read in the source text.

cards.front: The illuminance is 10 lm/m² from a lamp at 1 m. What is the illuminance at 0.5 m?
cards.back: 40 lm/m² (40 lx).
cards.explain: This is the chapter's worked example of the inverse square law. Halving the distance multiplies illuminance by four.

steps.prompt: Write the inverse square law in the chapter's alternate form.
steps.explain: Illuminance changes with the square of the distance ratio.

steps.prompt: Substitute the values E₁ = 10 lm/m², d₁ = 1.0 m and d₂ = 0.5 m.
steps.explain: Keep the distances in the same unit.
Squaring the ratio is what makes the effect non-linear.

steps.prompt: Multiply to get the new illuminance.
steps.explain: Halving the distance quadruples the illuminance.

cards.front: The illuminance is 17 lm/m² at 2 m from a lamp. What is the illuminance at 1.5 m?
cards.explain: This is an exam-style question built directly on the inverse square law. Moving closer to the source increases illuminance by the square of the distance ratio.

steps.prompt: Write the inverse square relation between the two positions.
steps.explain: Same law as the chapter's worked example.

steps.prompt: Substitute E₁ = 17 lm/m², d₁ = 2 m and d₂ = 1.5 m.
steps.explain: Check that the distances are in the same unit.
The closer position gives a ratio above 1.
Illuminance is higher at the closer distance, as expected.

cards.front: A 10 m × 10 m air-conditioned office needs 200 lux on the working plane. The fittings are twin-tube 36 W lamps with 3050 lm per lamp, UF 0.66 and LLF 0.8. How many fittings are needed? The luminaire is 2.9 m high and the work plane is 0.9 m high.
cards.back: 6 twin-tube fittings (12 lamps). The formula gives 200 × 100 / (2 × 3050 × 0.66 × 0.8) = 6.2, which the book rounds to 6.
cards.explain: This is the chapter's worked example of the zonal cavity method. The book rounds 6.2 down to 6. Strictly, 6 fittings give about 193 lux, so exam answers should follow the book's 6.

steps.explain: The room index links the room geometry to the utilisation factor table.

steps.answer: UF = 0.66 for the twin-tube fitting at room index 2.5
steps.explain: The UF comes from the manufacturer's table for this luminaire.
Typical values are 0.8 air-conditioned office, 0.7 clean industrial and 0.6 dirty industrial.

steps.prompt: Compute the total lumens from all lamps in one fitting.
steps.explain: A twin-tube fitting carries two lamps.
E is 200 lux and A is 100 m².
The book's answer is 6 fittings.

cards.front: Luminaires are spaced 3.33 m apart and mounted 2.0 m above the work plane. What is the space-to-height ratio, and is it acceptable against the recommended value of 1.5?
cards.back: SHR = 3.33 / 2.0 = 1.66. It is slightly above the recommended 1.5, and the book accepts it as close to the limit.
cards.explain: Because SHR is above 1.5, the uniformity of lighting is slightly less than ideal. The book notes that a larger SHR is better, since it can reduce the number of fittings and the connected load.

steps.explain: This is the spacing worked out in the chapter's example.
Mounting height is luminaire height minus work plane height.
SHR is spacing divided by mounting height.

steps.answer: 1.66 is above 1.5, so it is close to the limit and accepted in the chapter
steps.explain: Values above the recommendation slightly reduce uniformity.

cards.front: Forty T12 fluorescent fixtures (40 W lamp plus 12 W ballast) run 12 hours a day, every day of the year. What is the connected load and the annual energy use?
cards.back: About 2.1 kW connected load and about 25 kWh per day, or 9,125 kWh per year.
cards.explain: This is the existing case in the chapter's lighting case study on campus security lighting. The book rounds 2.08 kW to 2.1 kW.

steps.prompt: Find the power of one fixture.
steps.explain: Ballast losses are part of the fixture's real draw.

steps.prompt: Find the connected load for 40 fixtures.
steps.explain: Connected load is the total of all fixtures running together.
Hours of operation times the load gives the daily energy.
Matches the book's annual figure.

cards.front: The 40 T12 fixtures are replaced with 18 W LEDs that draw 0.72 kW for 12 hours a day. At Rs 5 per unit and Rs 2,500 per lamp, what is the annual saving and the simple payback?
cards.back: Saving of 5,840 kWh per year, worth Rs 29,200 per year. The investment is Rs 1.0 lakh, so the simple payback is about 3.4 years (book figures).
cards.explain: The book gives 3,285 kWh per year for the LED case. The arithmetic 0.72 kW × 12 h × 365 days gives about 3,154 kWh, so the book's figure is slightly higher. Exam answers should follow the book's numbers.

steps.explain: Replacing the lamps removes the ballast losses as well.

steps.prompt: Find the proposed annual energy (book value).
steps.explain: Note the small gap between the book figure and the simple calculation.
Saving is the existing energy minus the proposed energy.
Uses the tariff given in the book.
Investment is the lamp cost for all 40 lamps.
Simple payback is investment divided by annual money saving.

cards.front: An 18 W LED with an efficacy of 130 lm/W gives how many lumens?
cards.back: 2,340 lumens (18 × 130), matching the book's proposed LED output.
cards.explain: The chapter's proposal gives an efficacy of about 120 to 140 lm/W, which gives 2,160 to 2,520 lumens for an 18 W lamp. The book's figure of 2,340 lumens corresponds to 130 lm/W.

steps.explain: Efficacy is lumens per watt, so multiplying by watts gives lumens.

steps.prompt: Substitute efficacy 130 lm/W and power 18 W.
steps.explain: Use the efficacy mid-point of the chapter's 120 to 140 lm/W range.
This is the book's total output for the replacement lamps.
The book's figure sits inside this range.

cards.front: A 250 W HPSV lamp is to be replaced by two 28 W CFLs running 3,000 hours a year. What is the annual energy saving, and should the change be recommended?
cards.back: Saving of 582 kWh per year (750 − 168). The watts alone do not settle it: check that the light output and colour meet the task before recommending the change.
cards.explain: The chapter gives this as an exam question without a model answer. The chapter stresses matching the lamp type to the work and keeping adequate light levels, so the output check is the key point.

steps.explain: Energy is power times hours.
Two CFLs replace one HPSV lamp.
Multiply by the tariff to get the money saving, which the question does not give.

steps.prompt: Decide whether to recommend the change.
steps.answer: Recommend only if the light output and colour rendering meet the task; check the lumen output of the CFLs against the HPSV
steps.explain: The chapter says to establish adequate light levels without compromising productivity, safety or security.

cards.front: A municipal corporation has 30,000 lamps of 250 W HPMV each, run 3,600 hours a year, at a tariff of Rs 4.75 per kWh. What is the annual energy consumption and the annual energy cost?
cards.back: 27,000,000 kWh per year, costing about Rs 12.825 crore (Rs 128.25 million) per year.
cards.explain: This is the energy part of exam question L-2. The same question asks for demand cost at Rs 150 per kVA with 0.7 PF, but the chapter does not state the billing period, so that part is not carded.

steps.explain: Total load is the number of lamps times the wattage per lamp.
Energy is load times annual operating hours.
Multiply energy by the tariff per kWh.

cards.front: What are the two basic types of reciprocating engines used to generate electricity?
cards.back: Spark ignition (SI) engines and compression ignition (CI) engines.
cards.explain: Spark ignition engines use a spark plug to ignite a compressed fuel-air mixture. Compression ignition engines compress air until it is hot enough to ignite injected fuel, and their higher compression ratio gives them higher efficiency.

cards.front: Which fuels are typically used in spark ignition engines?
cards.back: Gasoline, natural gas, and sewage and landfill gas.
cards.explain: Spark ignition engines suit gaseous and light fuels that are mixed with air before combustion. Diesel and heavy fuel oil are normally used in compression ignition engines.

cards.front: Which fuel is normally used in compression ignition engines, and how does a dual-fuel engine work?
cards.back: Diesel or heavy fuel oil is normally used. In a dual-fuel engine, natural gas is compressed with the combustion air and diesel oil is injected at the top of the compression stroke to start combustion.
cards.explain: The diesel oil acts as the ignition source for the gas-air mixture. The engine can therefore run mainly on natural gas while still using diesel to initiate combustion.

cards.front: What compression ratio range is typical for a diesel engine, and what temperature does the compressed air reach?
cards.back: 14:1 to 25:1. The air is heated to about 700-900°C, which ignites the injected diesel spontaneously.
cards.explain: Because the fuel ignites from compression heat, the diesel engine is also called a compression ignition (CI) engine. The high compression ratio is why CI engines are more efficient than spark ignition engines.

cards.front: Name the four strokes of a four-stroke diesel engine in order.
cards.back: Induction, compression, ignition and power, exhaust.
cards.explain: On induction the descending piston draws in fresh air. During compression the valves are closed and the air is compressed to up to 25 bar. Fuel is injected and ignites on the power stroke, and the exhaust stroke discharges the spent gases.

cards.front: What is the approximate electrical efficiency of a modern lean-burn spark ignition gas engine?
cards.back: Close to 45%.
cards.explain: In a lean-burn gas engine, gas is mixed with air before the inlet valves, and a small prechamber with a richer mixture is ignited by a spark plug. Flames from the prechamber nozzle ignite the lean mixture in the main cylinder, so combustion is fast.

cards.front: List the five components that make a diesel generating set a system.
cards.back: (a) Diesel engine and accessories, (b) AC generator, (c) control systems and switchgear, (d) foundation and power house civil works, (e) the connected load and its components such as heating, motor drives and lighting.
cards.explain: The set performs well only when these components are well matched. The chapter asks that each component be chosen for highest efficiency and run near its optimum efficiency level.

cards.front: By how much should the engine power rating exceed the end-use power demand?
cards.explain: The margin stops the machine being overloaded when motors start, when some lighting switches on, or when wear raises power consumption. The engine should not be sized exactly at the demand.

cards.front: What speed range do diesel engines typically run at, and where should an engine be run?
cards.back: Typically 1300-3000 RPM. Run the engine as close as possible to its rated speed.
cards.explain: Running at rated speed avoids poor efficiency and deposit build-up from incomplete combustion, which raises maintenance and running costs. Speed is measured at the output shaft, and fuel efficiency is greatest at one optimum speed.

cards.front: What captive power output range do diesel engine plants most frequently cover?
cards.back: Most frequently used sizes are 4 to 15 MW.
cards.explain: Diesel plants dominate small captive (non-utility) power because diesel engines are more efficient than gas turbines and small steam turbines in this range. For continuous operation a low speed engine is more cost-effective than a high speed engine.

cards.front: Give four advantages of a captive diesel power plant.
cards.back: Any four of: low installation cost; short delivery and installation period; efficiency as high as 43-45%; better performance at part loads; minimum cooling water needs; short start-up time.
cards.explain: Diesel plants also suit a range of fuels, from light distillates to residual fuel oils. They can use air cooled heat exchangers where water is scarce.

cards.front: How has the specific fuel consumption of diesel engines changed since the 1970s?
cards.back: It has fallen from about 220 g/kWh in the 1970s to about 160 g/kWh at present.
cards.explain: Modern high efficiency turbochargers allow an exhaust gas driven turbine generator to add output. This lowers fuel consumption per kWh and raises overall thermal efficiency.

cards.front: Can a gas turbine burn the poorest quality fuel oils as easily as a diesel engine can?
cards.back: No. A diesel engine can burn the poorest quality fuel oils, while a gas turbine needs costly fuel treatment equipment to do so.
cards.explain: This is a common exam trap. Slow speed dual fuel engines using high-pressure gas injection also give the same thermal efficiency and power output as a regular fuel oil engine.

cards.front: What is the normally accepted definition of a high speed engine?
cards.back: An engine running at 1500 rpm.
cards.explain: High speed sets have been developed in India, while slow speed engines of higher capacity are often imported. Slow speed engines suit continuous use, and high speed engines suit intermittent use.

cards.front: Which engine type has the longer period between overhauls, and what are the typical intervals?
cards.back: The slow speed engine, at about 8000 hours. The high speed engine is about 3200 hours (typical manufacturer recommendations).
cards.explain: Slow speed engines have lower BMEP, less wear and tear, a higher weight-to-power ratio and lower direct operating cost. These features make them suitable for continuous use.

cards.front: A plant has a 650 kW connected load, a diversity factor of 0.54, a 70% set loading and 0.8 PF. What DG set rating in kVA is needed?
cards.back: About 625 kVA (maximum demand 350 kW, set rating 500 kW).
cards.explain: Diversity factor here is maximum demand divided by connected load. The set should run at about 70% loading, and the kW rating is converted to kVA using the power factor.

steps.prompt: Find the maximum demand from the connected load and diversity factor.
steps.answer: Maximum demand = 650 kW × 0.54 = 351 kW, taken as 350 kW.
steps.explain: The diversity factor is demand divided by connected load, so demand = connected load × factor.

steps.prompt: Find the set rating in kW for 70% loading.
steps.explain: The set is sized so that the demand is about 70% of its rating.

steps.prompt: Convert the kW rating to kVA at 0.8 PF.
steps.explain: Generators are specified in kVA, so the kW rating is divided by the power factor.

cards.front: Why is one large DG set usually preferred over two or more smaller sets?
cards.back: One large set is more economical in space, operation, maintenance and initial capital investment.
cards.explain: Parallel sets have their own benefits. Only the power shortfall needs to be met, one set can be stopped while another carries at least 50% of the requirement, and one set can serve as 100% standby in low power-cut periods.

cards.front: Which protections are recommended on all DG sets, and which relay is essential for parallel operation?
cards.back: Short circuit, overload and earth fault protection, plus high temperature and low lube oil pressure cut-outs. A reverse power relay is essential when sets run in parallel.
cards.explain: Full circuit protection may be uneconomical on small sets, but it is strongly recommended. The reverse power relay prevents one alternator from back feeding another.

cards.front: What is the largest direct-on-line (DOL) motor a DG set can start, and what starting method raises that limit?
cards.back: Roughly 50% of the DG set kVA rating in HP with DOL starting. Star-delta or auto-transformer starting raises the limit to about 75% of the kVA rating.
cards.explain: DOL starting draws up to six times rated current for a few seconds, and the starting current should not exceed about 200% of alternator full load capacity. Voltage and frequency recover well before the motor reaches full speed.

cards.front: What does the electricity rules require for earthing a DG set?
cards.back: Two independent earths, one to the equipment body and one to the neutral.
cards.explain: Two independent earths give adequate protection against earth faults. They also drain away any leakage potential from the equipment for safe working.

cards.front: A 500 kVA DG set is to start the largest possible motor. What is the limit in HP with DOL starting, and with star-delta or auto-transformer starting?
cards.back: About 250 HP with DOL starting, and about 375 HP with star-delta or auto-transformer starting.
cards.explain: The chapter gives these as approximate guides for the largest motor the set can start. Reduced-voltage starting cuts the starting current, which allows a larger motor.

steps.prompt: State the rule for the largest motor started by DOL.
